changes_bullets: crates/wz-capture/src/pcapng.rs (new, 17 unit tests): the pcapng reader. Blocks SHB / IDB / EPB / SPB and the obsolete Packet Block; unknown block types skipped by their declared length, which is what the format's self-describing structure is for (name-resolution, statistics, decryption-secret and custom blocks all appear in real wireshark output).

Its own module and its own Packet type rather than a variant of pcap::PcapFile, because pcapng keeps per-SECTION byte order and per-INTERFACE link type and timestamp resolution where classic pcap keeps all three per-file. Folding it in would mean applying one interface's link type to every packet, which for a `dumpcap -i any` or two-`-i` capture decapsulates half the file as the wrong link layer -- silently, since a wrong link header parses into a plausible IP packet often enough to produce flows.

Timestamps resolve to milliseconds where the interface's own if_tsresol exponent is in hand, in BOTH directions: finer than a millisecond divides (micro, nano), coarser multiplies (if_tsresol 3 is milliseconds, 0 is whole seconds), and the high bit selects base 2.
The 64-bit timestamp is read as ONE count with the high word first, not as the seconds/fraction pair the classic layout invites.
A new SECTION clears the interface list, because ids in the next section index ITS interfaces and the link type may differ.
A packet naming an undescribed interface is a hard error, not a guess: the interface carries the link type.
The trailing block_total_length is checked against the leading one -- the format duplicates that field precisely so a reader can detect the mismatch.

The quiet outcome is the worse one and is what makes this a defect rather than a local inconvenience: where /usr/local is NOT writable the build dies with a permission error naming neither the compiler nor the cache (that is how it presented), and where it IS writable -- a container as root, a developer who owns /usr/local -- it SUCCEEDS, installing a shared library outside the build tree.

THE PLANE THAT LEAKS IS THE ONE THE BOUND WAS MOST NEEDED ON. A scouting group gives every host its own 5-tuple, none of them ever closes, and SCOUTs arrive for as long as the process runs -- and scouting is precisely the path that returns before the frame path's accounting.

carry_forward_bullets: NOTHING IS WIRED YET. This crate opens a record handed to it; `wz-capture` holds the records and does not call it, and the two are in different dependency worlds on purpose. The join is its own round and it has a shape: `Framing::Encrypted` already keeps a per-direction pending tail, and what it does NOT keep is the record sequence number, which restarts at zero on every key change and is the one input `open` cannot infer.

THE KEYS HAVE NO PATH INTO THE PROCESS. `pcapng.rs` reports that a Decryption Secrets Block EXISTS (R311y626) and does not parse it, and no keylog file reader exists anywhere. Until one does, this crate has no caller that could supply a secret from a capture.

KEY UPDATE IS UNHANDLED AND IS NOT AN EDGE CASE. A long-lived zenoh session will send `key_update`, after which the traffic secret is re-derived (`application_traffic_secret_N+1`) and the sequence number RESTARTS. A decryptor that missed it reports authentication failures that read exactly like a wrong key.
TLS 1.2 AND QUIC ARE OUT, and QUIC is not a small extension of this: its packet protection is a different construction with header protection on top, so none of `open` applies.

THE AES-128 RECORD LEG RIDES ON THE OTHER TWO SUITES. Its derivation is differential like theirs, but no oracle seals a 16-byte-key record for it, so its nonce/AAD/content-type path is exercised only by the shared code being shared. Stated because a reader would otherwise assume three suites are covered three times.

Round 1682.decision_summary: R311y657 (§1.2a) -- the first decryption in this workspace: a new crate on the far side of the wz-capture seam turns a traffic secret and a ciphertext record into plaintext, and the split between borrowed primitives and wz's own protocol layer was read off the pinned versions rather than chosen
verification_bullets: THE SEAM WAS READ OFF THE PINNED VERSIONS, WHICH IS WHAT R311y649's CARRY DEMANDED BEFORE THE FIRST LINE. ring 0.17.14 makes `hkdf::Prk::new_less_safe` public (src/hkdf.rs:117) -- the entry point for a caller who already holds a secret, which is the position an offline analyzer is in -- while rustls 0.23.40 keeps `hkdf_expand_label` `pub(crate)` (src/tls13/key_schedule.rs:889). So the primitives are borrowed and the PROTOCOL layer is this crate's own, and that division was measured rather than preferred.

BOTH ARE ALREADY IN THIS WORKSPACE'S LOCK: `cargo tree -i ring` reaches them through `wz-runtime-tokio`'s `transport-link-tls` (tokio-rustls -> rustls -> ring) and through `wz-runtime-tokio-test-support`'s dev-dependencies. This crate adds no new third-party NAME to the tree.

THE DERIVATION IS DIFFERENTIAL, NOT SELF-CONSISTENT. rustls's own key schedule, assembled from the pieces it does export (`expander_for_okm` + `expand_slice`), derives the same key and iv from the same secret for all three suites. The label bytes for the oracle are rebuilt BY HAND in the test rather than taken from `hkdf_label`, so an error in the encoder cannot cancel itself out.

AND THE RECORD ACTUALLY OPENS: rustls SEALS a record and this crate opens it, at sequence numbers 0, 1, 2, 255, 256, 65536 and 0x0102030405060708. Past zero on purpose -- at `seq == 0` every nonce construction agrees, so a fixture that only opened the first record of a connection would pass with the sequence XORed into the wrong end of the iv.

THE ORACLE'S REACH IS BOUNDED AND THE BOUND IS STATED IN THE TEST: `AeadKey`'s only public constructor is `From<[u8; 32]>` (rustls src/crypto/cipher.rs:327), so rustls can seal for the two 32-byte suites and NOT for `TLS_AES_128_GCM_SHA256`. The test asserts that EXACTLY ONE suite is skipped and which, so a future narrowing of the oracle cannot pass quietly.

SEVEN FALSIFICATIONS, each from a fresh snapshot of the file and each reverted from that snapshot. Dropping the `"tls13 "` prefix, writing the output length little-endian, omitting the 6 from the prefixed label length, XORing the sequence into the FRONT of the iv, passing an empty AAD, reading the content type off the FRONT of the plaintext, and using SHA-256 for the SHA-384 suite -- every one reds, and the three label probes red the byte-for-byte encoding test as well as the differential.

THE ORACLE'S OWN TYPE IS FEATURE-DEPENDENT, AND ONLY TWO LANES TOGETHER SHOW IT. `SupportedCipherSuite` matched exhaustively compiles alone and FAILS `cargo test --workspace` with E0004, because workspace feature unification turns on rustls's `tls12` and a variant appears; given a wildcard arm it compiles under the workspace and fails `-D warnings` alone, because the arm is unreachable. Layer C1 caught the first half after the isolated build was green. The accessor `SupportedCipherSuite::tls13()`, which rustls cfgs internally, is the only spelling correct in both.

carry_forward_bullets: THE CHAIN IS NOW CAPTURE -> SECRETS -> KEYS AND STOPS THERE. Nothing selects a connection's secrets FOR a flow: that needs the ClientHello's 32-byte random, which `wz-capture` parses no part of -- R311y649's `client_hello_verdict` deliberately checks only the record's internal consistency and never reads the body. The random is at a fixed offset in the ClientHello and reading it is the next round's first move.

A DSB's PAYLOAD IS NOW RETAINED WITHOUT A BOUND. Every other accumulation in `wz-capture` is capped and counted (`skipped_packets`, `frames_per_flow`, `max_flows`); this one is not, and a file with a large embedded key log grows the parse by its size. No limit field mentions it.

KEY UPDATE IS VISIBLE IN THE PARSER NOW AND STILL UNHANDLED: `CLIENT_TRAFFIC_SECRET_1` and later are REFUSED BY NAME, so a capture that key-updates reports a refused label rather than silently missing records -- which is better than R311y657 and is not support.

THE SECRETS TYPE IS NOT CHECKED. `DecryptionSecrets::secrets_type` is carried and no caller looks at it, so a DSB holding something other than `0x544c534b` ("TLSK") would be handed to the key log parser, which would count every line as unparsed. Honest but unhelpful; the check belongs at the join.

Five rounds each proved one link, and a chain of separately-proven links is not a proven chain -- the joins are where an index or a coordinate goes wrong with neither side noticing.
THE INDEX IS LOAD BEARING AND THE TEST SAYS SO: the second record must NOT open at the first one's index. Without that leg "it decrypted" would say only that something was decryptable.

THE CONTENT-TYPE GATE IS NOT DEFENSIVE CODING. TLS 1.3 leaves the outer type reading `application_data` on every record after the ServerHello, so a post-handshake NewSessionTicket -- which servers send routinely, mid-session -- is indistinguishable from traffic until it is opened. The probe that feeds it onward decodes it as a zenoh message.

carry_forward_bullets: THE RESYNC AND THE EPOCH TRIAL CAN STILL DISAGREE ABOUT ONE RECORD. A CORRUPT RECORD STILL ADVANCES THE EPOCH POINTER. carry_forward_bullets: QUIC IS RECOGNISED AND NOT DECRYPTED, and the boundary is deliberate rather than a shortfall to paper over: packet protection is two layers (header protection unmasks the packet number before the AEAD applies), the keys come off the TLS secret through a QUIC-specific `quic key` / `quic iv` / `quic hp` schedule, and the zenoh bytes then live inside STREAM frames that must be reassembled before any of this crate's framing applies. That is a TRACK. What is closed is the misread; what remains is the plaintext.

A QUIC CAPTURE THAT BEGINS MID-CONNECTION IS NOT RECOGNISED. Recognition needs a long header, so a capture of only 1-RTT packets is still fed to the zenoh decoder and can still misread -- the same precondition, and the same honest failure direction, as `NoSessionIdentity` for a mid-session TLS flow. The Initial packet's keys are derivable from the version and the original DCID alone, so reading THAT is the one part of QUIC decryption needing no key log, and it would also settle this.

THE `quic` CENSUS IS NOT PER DIRECTION. One census per flow, so a capture where one side speaks QUIC and the other does not shows a single set of counts. Every other per-flow census in this crate is `[A, B]`.

`analyze_with_limit`'s CAP HAS NO COMMAND-LINE FLAG. The library takes it and `wz-analyze` always passes `None`, so the bound is reachable only by a Rust caller -- which is exactly the `a library nobody runs` shape, one argument deep.

changes_bullets: [REDACTED-REQ]'s LIVE LEG IS BUILT. `crates/wz-replay/src/live.rs` (NEW) dials a peer, opens a real session, and publishes the plan's emissions as real application Pushes. IT DIALS RATHER THAN LISTENS, and that is a decision rather than a default. Every `wz-e2e-*` binary in this workspace is an ACCEPTOR, which is right for a fixture whose peer is a harness and wrong for a replay tool: an operator points it AT a running deployment, and asking that deployment to connect out inverts who has to be reconfigured. `--connect <locator>` takes zenoh's own locator dialect through `parse_any_locator`.

THE EMISSION RUNS OFF THE RUNTIME'S WORKERS. `play` is the single driver of a plan and it is synchronous because the delay belongs to the SINK -- the contract `Sink` states. A synchronous wait on a runtime worker would stall the writer task that has to put the previous sample on the wire, so `play` runs under `spawn_blocking` while the session FSM is driven on the runtime and the two are RACED rather than sequenced: the FSM must keep running for a Push to reach the wire, and the drive loop only ends when the session does. Duplicating `play` as an async loop was the alternative and it is worse -- the dry run and the live run would then iterate the plan in two places, and the property this crate sells is that `--dry-run` prints what a live run does.

THE FEATURE, AND THE REFUSAL THAT MAKES IT SAFE. `live` is ON by default because a replay tool that cannot replay is not the tool the requirement asks for, and it is a feature at all because the plan half -- schedule, mutation, selection, extraction -- must stay buildable and testable without the session runtime's dependency graph. With it off, `--connect` is REFUSED and names the feature: a build that printed the plan and exited zero would tell an operator their replay ran. That is this workspace's rule about a lower layer degrading silently, applied at the layer a person types into.

THE FACADE SUBSET IS PINNED, not inherited. `wz` is taken with `default-features = false` and verbatim the subset `wz-e2e-pubsub` pins for the same planes, plus `session-unicast-accept` for this crate's own in-process peer. Teardown is the order the e2e harness established: drop every action sender clone so the writer observes its channel close, then await `writer_handle.drain()` -- a wall-clock tail window can cut a writer still making progress.

changes_bullets: RP4 CLOSED, AND THE ROUND BEGAN BY REFUTING ITS OWN PREMISE. R311y700 wrote that a capture's per-message timing could not be reused -- a sample carries a framing coordinate rather than a clock, and on a stream link that coordinate is a byte offset -- and R311y702 repeated it as a carry naming the datagram half as the only reachable one. `wz_capture::FlowDissection::packet_for` is PUBLIC, answers "which capture packet carried the byte at this stream offset", and its own doc names `PassiveFrame::stream_offset` as the thing to compose it with. Both halves now carry the clock, and the correction is recorded on the types rather than only in a ledger entry.

`wz_analyze::Sample::captured_at_millis` (NEW) -- when the capture recorded the packet this message arrived in. The datagram half is a direct lookup (that coordinate IS the packet index); the stream half is the composition `packet_for`'s doc prescribes. `Reread::ts_millis` resolves it for both file kinds -- pcapng through the packet's own interface, classic pcap through the file's timestamp unit -- and `samples` now takes ONE second read serving both halves rather than one for the datagram bytes and another for the clock.

`None` IS A REAL ANSWER AND THERE ARE THREE WAYS TO REACH IT, said on the field rather than left to be inferred: a capture block that carried no timestamp (pcapng permits it), a stream offset whose bytes the assembler had already discarded, and a capture this reader could not parse a second time. A consumer must not read it as zero -- the fabricated-measurement rule the throughput plane's `unmeasured` state already answers to one layer down.

`Schedule::timing` + `Timing::{Declared, Capture}` + `TimingSource::{Declared, Measured, Unmeasurable}`. `Declared` REMAINS THE DEFAULT: the plan is this tool's contract and what an existing invocation does is not changed silently. Under `Capture` the gap is the interval between the two samples the plan KEEPS -- not between consecutive samples -- because a selector that drops the message between two kept ones widens the real interval, and reproducing the narrower one would play a conversation at a pace it never had. Speed scales a measured gap exactly as it scales a declared one and the ceiling applies to both.

`Unmeasurable` IS A THIRD STATE RATHER THAN A FALLBACK TO `Declared`. The two produce the same NUMBER and mean opposite things: one is the caller's choice, the other is a measurement that was wanted and missing. `PlannedEmission::timing` carries it and `render` prints it per row -- appended so the declared case reads exactly as it always did, and a reader who did not ask for capture timing gets no new words on any row.

`--timing declared|capture` at the command line, REFUSED for any other word on the rule `--side` and `--payload-format` already settled: a reader who typed `--timing real` and silently got the declared gaps would believe they were replaying the capture's own pace.

changes_bullets: THE OBSERVATION UNIT WAS THE 5-TUPLE AND THE QUESTION IS ABOUT NODES. Every plane in `wz-capture` folds a flow; a flow is what the wire hands out and it is the wrong unit for "which nodes are talking to which" -- one node reconnecting from a new source port is two flows, and a NAT between the tap and the peer makes the address a fiction while the zid stays exactly what it was. `wz-capture/src/node.rs` keys the capture by ZID instead, from the three places the wire carries one: the INIT of a unicast handshake, the JOIN a multicast peer announces itself with, and the HELLO answering a SCOUT.

A LINK NEEDS BOTH ENDS TO NAME THEMSELVES -- an INIT each way on one flow. One INIT proves a node sent one and not that a session exists. R311y608's rule is ENFORCED here rather than restated: a frame carrying `inadmissible_on_link` is a message the link cannot act on (pico gives a raweth link the multicast transport, whose receive path takes an INIT and does nothing with it), so its zid is recorded as SEEN and never establishes anything. A census without that distinction would report a topology assembled from messages no participant acted on.

THE COMPILER FOUND THE THIRD ROW PRODUCER. `Hello` was an unconstructible evidence kind, because a scouting message never enters `frames` -- it advances no session, so `DatagramDissection` keeps it in its own list. A census built from the frames of both tables still reports ZERO nodes on a discovery-only capture, which is exactly what a first look at a deployment is. The plane walks `flows()`, `datagram_flows()` and the scouting list, after the decryption pass.

[REDACTED-REQ] OCCUPANCY, AT BOTH AXES. Per NODE: unit bytes are credited to the direction's SENDER (settled by the handshake, so the attribution pass runs after it), counted once per UNIT and not once per message -- `unit_len` rides on every message of a batch, so a per-message sum multiplies a batch by its own message count. Per TOPIC: `ThroughputTable::share_bp` over the plane's sized total. Both are truncated integer basis points, and both say so.

THE DENOMINATOR IS THE WHOLE CAPTURE, and what cannot be credited is counted and printed rather than divided away. A mid-session capture has no handshake, so no direction has an owner; sharing out only the attributed part would make such a capture read as a tidy 100% for whoever happened to be identified, and the figure would IMPROVE as attribution got worse. `--nodes` renders nodes, evidence, shares and both byte totals in text and JSON.

`Dissection::feed_quic_stream` / `feed_quic_stream_with_sink` (`wz-capture/src/lib.rs`) is the QUIC twin of `decrypt_with` / `decrypt_with_sink`, and the seam points the other way for a stated reason: TLS records arrive inside a byte stream this crate already reassembles, so the loop belongs in wz-capture and the cipher is a caller's trait; a QUIC stream is reassembled AFTER decryption, both behind a cipher wz-capture may not carry, so the caller owns the loop and hands the RESULT back. What the caller may not own is the framing -- zenoh's QUIC link is streamed (`zenoh-link-quic/src/unicast.rs:184`) and opens one bidirectional stream per link (`:330`, acceptor at `:524`), so the bytes inside it are the ordinary length-prefixed batch stream this crate already frames.

`DatagramDissection::quic_streams` holds one `QuicStreamDissection` per QUIC stream id, each with its own `PassiveSession`. One session per ID and not per direction, because a bidi stream's two halves share an id and the zenoh handshake is an exchange; a list and not one session, because `one stream per link` is a property of today's zenoh and not of QUIC. A SEPARATE list from `frames` because `PassiveFrame::stream_offset` means the packet index there and a byte offset here, and folding them would put a third meaning into a field two consumers already resolve.

`DatagramDissection::frame_lists()` is the enumeration every plane now walks. Four census planes named `flow.frames` directly -- throughput (`agg.rs`), exchanges (`exchange.rs`), payloads (`payload.rs`), nodes (`node.rs`) -- so a second list would have reached whichever plane its author remembered. That omission has shipped four times here (R311y668, y678, y699, y700), twice in consecutive rounds, so the fix is a method rather than a convention.

The QUIC pass MOVED above the census planes in `wz-analyze::analyze_request`. It now frames what it recovers, so a plane built before it would census the pre-QUIC view and report a floor as a total -- the same order rule the decryption pass states four lines up, and the same mistake R311y716 shipped in the alert path.

The verdict rule at `report.rs` was `stream_bytes > 0 || datagram_bytes > 0`, whose own comment said it would lift `when a decoder exists rather than when someone edits this line`. It now subtracts TWO terms via one shared `quic_application_unread` helper: bytes nobody offered a framer, plus bytes a framer took and decoded nothing out of (`QuicStreamDissection::undecoded_bytes`, measured from the session's own frame coordinates). Dropping the second term would let the verdict call a capture whole because its bytes reached a stall.

`--fields` reaches QUIC: `feed_quic_stream_with_sink` offers the recovered bytes to the same `PlaintextSink` the TLS half uses, in the one window where bytes, frames and coordinates coexist. `FieldSink` rows now CARRY their `OffsetSpace` instead of each render site asserting one, because a recovered QUIC stream has no ciphertext record to point back at. An offer that APPENDS is framed but not walked and counted in `appends_not_walked`, since walking a tail at an offset into the whole names the wrong bytes as a message's fields.

`DissectionLimits::quic_streams_per_flow` (16 in `for_live_tap`) bounds the new table by REFUSING rather than evicting -- the streams already held carry this connection's session state, so dropping the oldest would discard the handshake and leave the survivor decoding a stream it has no session for. The exhaustive-destructuring preset test caught the new field at compile time, as designed.

changes_bullets: R311y720 closes M4 BY MEASURING IT, which is what the item asked for and what four rounds restated instead. The register has carried it since R311y660 as 'three planes walk the same frames three times -- cost UNMEASURED, so whether it is debt has to be measured first', and the missing piece was always the harness: the planes are cheap per frame, so the answer only appears at a size no unit fixture has. `agg::tests::m4_the_cost_of_walking_the_same_frames_four_times` builds 20 000 records, times the parse and each plane, and times a BARE traversal beside them -- because fusing four walks removes the iteration and never the per-record work inside it, so iteration is the ceiling on what fusing could buy.

THE ANSWER: over 20 000 decoded messages the parse costs 73.3 ms, the four planes 17.4 ms (23.8% of it), and four bare traversals 258 us -- 1.5% of the plane time. Fusing the walks could save at most that, at the cost of fusing four independently-testable planes into one. M4 IS NOT DEBT and should be struck rather than carried.

PF4 closes the only way it honestly can: DECLARED. protobuf's wire format carries no names, so every closure that ENDS in the analyzer is a closure that invents them. `FormatMap::name_field` takes `(keyexpr pattern, field path, name)` and `--payload-name 'demo/**:1=temperature'` is the command line for it. Keyed by pattern AND path, because one deployment's field 1 is a temperature and another's is a sequence number. `PayloadField::name` is `Option<String>`, ALWAYS `None` as a decoder returns it -- the invariant is stated on the field -- and filled in where the resolved keyexpr and the decoded paths are both in hand.

The name is rendered BESIDE the path (`1 (temperature)`) and not instead of it, so a reader can check the declaration against the bytes, and JSON carries `"name":null` for an undeclared path rather than omitting the key.

SERIAL DECAP closes off a DECLARED link type, which is the shape the register's standing warning demanded: `LINKTYPE_RTAC_SERIAL` (250) has a pseudo-header this machine cannot verify -- `pcap/dlt.h` gives the number and no layout -- so nothing here parses one. `--serial <linktype>` declares it, exactly as `--quic` declares a port, and what `wz-capture::serial` then reads is only what it can check: the COBS envelope, the CRC32, and the handshake flags, all pinned against `vendor/zenoh-pico/include/zenoh-pico/protocol/definitions/serial.h:53-55`.

DIRECTION comes from the wire where the wire proves it. A bare INIT is the initiator's and INIT|ACK the responder's (`serial_protocol.c:257-276`); the capture's INTERFACE ID -- a real field of the file -- stands in for which of the two wires, one reader each because interleaving two COBS streams resynchronises into garbage. First interface seen is provisionally A and a handshake frame CORRECTS it. A one-interface capture cannot separate the directions at all and says so (`direction_unattributed`) rather than letting a positional A read as a measurement.

The decode was MOVED to `finish`, and the move is a defect this round measured rather than a tidy-up: decoding as packets arrive fixes a frame's direction before the handshake that names it can arrive, so a capture reported the positional guess for its early frames and the measured answer for its later ones, with nothing saying which was which. Buffered per line and decoded once the mapping is final.

The link is UNICAST with a DATAGRAM flow (`vendor/zenoh-pico/src/link/unicast/serial.c:67-68`), so each frame's payload is ONE transport message through `next_datagram_on` with `LinkHandshake::Present`, and `transport-link-serial` is non-optional in wz-capture on exactly the argument R311y597 made for raweth -- a `--serial` flag that silently read nothing because a feature was off is the silent degradation this workspace turns into a refusal everywhere else.

THE GATE. `scripts/lib/message_producer_lint.py` (Layer C0) reds when a `Vec<PassiveFrame>` field exists that `Dissection::message_lists` does not reach. That type IS the population -- it is the only thing the four census planes consume -- so the rule is mechanical and the compiler maintains the list, which is the difference from a hand-kept register of producers that the same person who forgot the producer would have to update.

The scan follows ONE hop: a field the enumeration names, or a field named by a method the enumeration calls (`frame_lists`). One and not a full call graph, deliberately -- a deeper walk starts proving things about code the gate cannot read, and the shape it exists to catch is a field nobody mentions anywhere.

THE BOUND, and it is a COMMITMENT rather than a discard. A serial frame read before the handshake has no knowable direction and must be held; a capture whose handshake never arrives holds everything. But those frames are EVIDENCE, and discarding them to save memory would trade the capture's contents for its budget -- which no other bound in this crate does, they all trade recency. So `DissectionLimits::serial_frames_before_attribution` (256 on the live-tap preset) stops the WAIT: past it the mapping is committed, everything held is decoded under it, and `SerialCensus::committed_positionally` says the attribution is positional.

A late handshake is then IGNORED, and that is not an optimisation: taking it would leave one capture with two mappings, which is the exact defect R311y720 measured and moved the decode to `finish` to fix. The rendering reads `committed_positionally` BEFORE `roles_witnessed`, so a committed line can never be reported as measured.
The buffer also DRAINS once the mapping settles -- by handshake or by commitment -- so it stops growing at the moment it stops being necessary, rather than holding until `finish`.

`FlowKey::serial_line` takes no argument now. It used to carry the interface count in the `port`, argued as 'a real fact in the only field that can hold one'. That was the wrong argument: the field is a PORT, a reader matching a row against their deployment reads it as one, and a count sitting there is a fabricated fact in the column that must hold none. The interface count already lives in the census, and putting it here as well was one number with two homes.

LAYER 1, THE TYPE. `wz-capture/src/messages.rs` holds `MessageList`, a newtype over `Vec<PassiveFrame>` whose `Deref`/`DerefMut` target is a SLICE and never the `Vec`. That single choice is what made the change tractable and what makes it strong: every READ compiles unchanged -- `len`, `iter`, `first`, indexing, `&list` at a `&[PassiveFrame]` parameter, and `&mut list[..]` for an in-place remap -- while nothing can GROW or SHRINK the list, because a slice has no `push`, no `extend` and no `remove`. MEASURED: converting the five producers produced exactly SEVEN compile errors, every one of them a growth or a removal, out of roughly 217 call sites.

The removal door hands back a `#[must_use] Discarded` whose destructor PANICS unless the caller took the frame. carry_forward_bullets: THE VERDICT-REASON GATE IS A NECESSARY CONDITION, NOT A SUFFICIENT ONE, and it says so in its own doc: a test that names a variant and asserts nothing about it satisfies it. The wire-name half of that gate binds a variant when a test asserts the exported string, but only in a test that also reaches the verdict surface (`reasons(`, `is_complete`, `VerdictReason`). carry_forward_bullets: The mutation sweep proves a leg is load-bearing; it does not prove the test that kills it asserts the RIGHT thing. A test that merely counts `reasons().len()` would kill every leg. That is the honest limit of mutation testing and there is no cheaper gate underneath it -- the two gates together say a leg is named, documented and depended upon, and the quality of the depending is the author's.

Only ONE mutation operator is applied: delete the push. A leg raised under the WRONG CONDITION -- `> 0` where it should be `>= 0`, or a counter read from the wrong plane -- survives this sweep untouched, because the push is still there and still reachable. Condition mutation is the natural next operator and it is a much larger space.

`Layer C0mut` compiles and runs the suite once per leg, so its cost grows with the number of legs and with the suite. Twenty-three legs at 2m16s local is comfortable; the shape to watch is a leg count that doubles, at which point running only the crates that bind each leg stops being enough and the sweep wants a cache of which tests touch `reasons()` at all.

`Declarations` lives in `wz-analyze` because the analyzer is the only consumer of `FormatMap`. A second consumer -- the replay half is the plausible one -- would want the same ledger and would either duplicate this type or force it down into `wz-capture`, and pushing it down would put run state back in the crate that was just cleared of it. The right move then is a third home, not a move back.
changes_bullets: R311y726 pays what R311y725 wrote down as unfinished, and both payments are structural rather than another assertion on top of the old shape.

N14 -- `scripts/lib/verdict_leg_mutation.py` (run-ci Layer C0mut, registered in ci.yml). For each `VerdictReason` it replaces the `out.push(...)` that raises it with a statement of no effect, runs the suite, and requires a test to REDDEN. This is the sufficient condition the static gate cannot express: R311y725's lint proves a leg is NAMED by a test, this proves one DEPENDS on it. R311y715 ran exactly this sweep by hand and a hand-run sweep gates nothing.

The sweep refuses three ways that are NOT findings about the code: a mutant that will not compile, a mutant that hangs, and a non-zero exit with no test report at all. Each is a failure of the TOOL, because a severing that cannot be expressed cannot answer the question, and counting it as red would be the false pass the whole thing exists to refuse. The unmutated baseline must be green first, or every mutant is red for the wrong reason.

It mutates `report.rs` in place and restores it byte for byte on every exit path, verifying the restore before reporting anything; a backup left behind means a previous run died and the next run REFUSES rather than guessing which copy is real. A hermetic copy was considered and rejected -- this workspace's cargo root reaches `../vendor/`, so the copy is most of the repository.

Per leg it runs only the crates whose tests name that leg, and ESCALATES to the full set before calling anything a survivor. A kill in a subset is a kill (running fewer tests can only make a mutant harder to catch); a survival in a subset is not yet an answer. Twenty of twenty-three legs are named only inside `wz-capture`.

N14 second half -- the static lint's wire-name binding path was REMOVED. Measured first: all 23 variants are bound by the `VerdictReason::X` code form and not one relied on the string form, so the path bound nothing and could only ever have bound something by accident.

N15 -- `FormatMap` is configuration again. The `Cell<bool>` R311y725 put beside every rule is gone; the map hands out an opaque `DeclarationId` with each answer and lists its `declarations()`, and `wz-analyze`'s new `Declarations` type borrows the map, forwards the two questions the field layer asks, and remembers which handles came back. `DeclarationKind` moved to `wz-capture` (the rule/name distinction is the map's), while the flag name, note kind and remedy stayed in the reader (a command line is not the map's business).

THE SWEEP'S OWN FIRST RUN WAS WRONG AND FAILED CLOSED, which is the lesson worth keeping. Its discriminator read any line opening `error: ` as a build failure, and `cargo test` prints `error: test failed, to rerun pass ...` for a FAILING TEST -- so all 23 mutants were reported uncompilable. It refused to report OK, which is the right direction to be wrong in, and it still measured nothing. The rule now is cargo's own words (`could not compile`), plus a `test result:` line as proof that a suite actually ran.

Survivor path probed rather than assumed: with the suite artificially restricted to a crate that binds almost nothing, the sweep reports SURVIVED for the legs that lose their killer and exits non-zero. The green run proves the kill path; this proves the other one.

N15 has a witness that fails under the R311y725 shape: two `Declarations` over the SAME map, where the first applies both declarations and the second must still report both unused. Probed by re-creating the old behaviour with a thread-local sticky set -- the second ledger then reported 0 unused against an expected 2, red.

MEASURED AND CORRECTED: the carry said the `Cell` had cost `FormatMap` its `Sync`. It had not. `FormatMap` holds `&dyn PayloadFormat`, a trait object carrying no auto-trait bounds, so it was never `Sync` and the `Cell` changed nothing about that -- verified by compiling a struct of the pre-R311y725 shape against a `Sync` bound. THE MIDDLE OF THE RANGE IS STILL UNTESTED, and this is the honest limit of the pair. `sever` is the guard always false and `widen` is the guard always true; both are extremes. A guard wrong by a STEP -- `> 1` where `> 0` was meant, a counter read off the neighbouring plane, an off-by-one on a length -- keeps raising the leg on every fixture that trips it hard and stays quiet exactly where the old guard did. Neither operator perturbs it. Boundary mutation reaches it and needs the condition PARSED rather than wrapped, which is a different order of tool.

The widen axis is THIN over the plane legs, and the sweep's own numbers say where. The legs outside a plane die under sixteen tests apiece; five of the plane legs die under exactly one -- `ExchangeGaps`, `ExchangeUnread` and `ExchangesUnclosed` all on `one_undecided_plane_makes_the_page_a_floor_when_it_is_the_only_plane`, `ExchangeUndecided` and `PayloadUndecided` on one test each of their own. A capture with a plane attached and nothing wrong with it is asserted in very few places.

Measured, not assumed: weakening that single test to the pre-R311y725 `contains` shape did NOT produce a survivor, because `wz-replay`'s alert e2e caught the mutant instead. A backup that happens to exist is not a backup the gate asked for -- nothing requires the alert witness to keep its clean half, and if it loses it several plane legs go unwitnessed on this axis at once.
changes_bullets: R311y727 pays N16, the carry R311y726 wrote down about its own sweep: one mutation operator asks only half the question a guard can fail.

`scripts/lib/verdict_leg_mutation.py` gains a second operator. `sever` replaces the `out.push(...)` so no capture can raise the leg; `widen` rewrites the single-line `if` guarding that push to `(COND) || true` so EVERY capture raises it. The first asks whether anything notices the reason going away, the second whether anything notices it arriving over captures that are fine.

The second operator is the one that reaches the defect R311y726 named and could not test for: a guard too WIDE keeps its push, keeps reddening every fixture that trips it, and walks through a severing sweep untouched. The failure it hides reads worse than a missing reason -- a verdict that cries incomplete over whole captures teaches an operator to stop reading verdicts.

The condition is kept inside the widened guard rather than replaced by a bare `true`, so every binding it reads stays read. A bare `true` orphans the `let`s above it and the sweep would then be reporting its own unused-variable warnings as findings about the verdict.

Reachability is established for BOTH operators before any mutant runs: a leg whose guard is not a single-line `if` directly above the push is named and the run FAILS. Skipping it would answer half the question in silence, which is the population-of-zero green this file exists to refuse. All 23 legs are reachable today.

`--only VARIANT` narrows the sweep to one leg, for the probes that keep the gate honest -- re-running 46 mutants to learn about one is how a probe stops being run. It prints PROBE in the headline and `A PARTIAL POPULATION` in the OK line, because a partial run reporting a plain OK is the same false green wearing this tool's own words.

A REPORTING DEFECT INHERITED FROM R311y726 IS FIXED: after escalating from the crates that name a leg to the full package set, the evidence line still printed the narrow set. An escalated kill was therefore attributed to a package set the killing test is not in. Found by a probe, not by reading -- it printed a `wz-replay` test as killed "in wz-capture".
`scripts/run-ci.sh` Layer C0mut's header records the second operator and that the population it compiles and runs is now 46 rather than 23.

carry_forward_bullets: `boundary` reaches 15 of 23 guards and the remaining eight are a real gap rather than a rounding: `drops().any()`, `!gaps().is_clean()` and `!selection().is_decisive()` each hide their thresholds inside a method, so moving one means following the implementation rather than editing the guard. Those eight are exactly the plane and bounds legs -- the ones whose fixtures are hardest to reduce to a single instance -- so the operator is absent where it would be most informative. Reaching them means either the accessors growing a form the guard can compare (`gaps().count() > 0`), or the sweep learning to mutate the method body, and the first is a design change to the report rather than to this tool.

Only ONE direction of the threshold is mutated, and that is deliberate rather than an omission: tightening (`> 0` to `> 1`) is a question `widen` cannot ask, but LOOSENING (`> 0` to `>= 0`) is identical to `widen` -- the guard becomes always true. So the three operators cover never-true, always-true and one-step-tighter, and the shape still unasked is a threshold moved several steps, or one moved on a comparison between two counters (`enc > opened + 3`), which no fixture in this tree would distinguish anyway.

N17 again, and it is now the live constraint: the sweep compiles and runs the suite 61 times. Layers of this shape do not compose indefinitely -- a fourth operator, or a leg count that doubles, and the per-leg crate narrowing stops being enough. The cache this wants is "which tests touch `reasons()` at all", which is derivable from the same static gates that already read the enum.

`verdict_assertion_lint` requires the pin to be in the SAME function, which is right and also blunt: a test that legitimately delegates its report-building to a helper AND asserts through that helper is accepted only because the helper itself pins. A test that splits the pin and the containment claim across two helpers would red with nothing wrong. No such test exists today; the rule is written to be corrected by a real case rather than by anticipation.
changes_bullets: R311y728 pays both carries R311y727 opened, and neither by touching the tests it complained about: N19 became a gate and N18 became a third mutation operator.

N19 -- `scripts/lib/verdict_assertion_lint.py` (run-ci Layer C0). `reasons()` answers with a SET, so `contains(&VerdictReason::X)` holds while every OTHER leg fires too. A test built that way cannot notice a guard that ran away, which is exactly what R311y727 measured: five plane legs killed by ONE test each on the widen axis against sixteen apiece elsewhere, and the thin ones were thin because their own witnesses only claimed containment. The rule is that a test reading the verdict list must, somewhere in the same function, pin the WHOLE list.

THE GATE'S OWN POPULATION WAS WRONG THREE TIMES AND EACH CORRECTION IS THE FINDING. Scanning for `contains(&VerdictReason::X)` missed a test looping `for leg in [..] { assert!(reasons.contains(&leg)) }` -- the argument is a variable there. Keying on `reasons()` missed the whole `wz-analyze` half, which reads the same list through the `Outcome::reasons` FIELD. And the pin test itself was twice too narrow: requiring the literal `reasons` inside the assertion missed a pin held in a local named `exchanges_alone`, and requiring `vec![` missed `Vec::new()`, which is the STRONGEST pin there is because it says every leg is quiet.

Thirteen violations were measured and all thirteen paid, in `wz-capture` (report.rs 3, lib.rs 8) and `wz-analyze` (2). Each got an equality against the whole list beside its existing claim; the containment claims stayed where they read better.

N18 -- the `boundary` operator in `verdict_leg_mutation.py`. `sever` is the guard never true and `widen` is the guard always true; both are EXTREMES, and a guard wrong by a step sits between them untouched. `> 1` where `> 0` was meant keeps firing on every fixture that trips the leg hard and goes quiet only on the capture holding a single instance. Apparent-size versus disk usage, or a scan reaching further than `du` does -- unresolved, and it means the percentage is approximate. Fine for a refusal threshold, wrong to quote as a reclaim figure.

What answers it is `--stamp` / `--file`: mark the moment, run the gates, remove what the gates did not touch. The criterion is usage rather than age or size.

A comment saying "only after a full gate" is an obligation written as prose and this workspace has measured what becomes of those, so the reap MEASURES what it is about to remove and refuses over 60% of the tree -- which is exactly the shape a partial-build reap takes.

The tool's own contract was got wrong twice, both times in silence. A guessed stamp filename made `stamp` report success while `reap` answered "no stamp". Passing the TARGET path where cargo-sweep wants the PROJECT path failed inside a pipeline, and `pipefail` turned it into exit 1 with no output at all. Round 1760.decision_summary: R311y733 (N25) builds a reaper for the build artefacts the gates no longer touch, and the round's own headline diagnosis turned out wrong under it: a count of duplicate executables measures how wide this workspace's feature matrix is, not how much of the tree is dead.
verification_bullets: BOTH REFUSALS WERE PROBED BEFORE THE TOOL WAS USED IN ANGER. A reap with no stamp is refused and says to stamp BEFORE the gate rather than after. A reap taken immediately after stamping -- nothing rebuilt, so nothing touched -- reported "would remove 26.28 GiB, that is 109% of the tree" and refused on the 60% limit. That second probe is the hazard itself: it is what a reap after a partial build looks like, and the tool stops rather than deleting the tree.

THE GUARD ITSELF WAS BROKEN AND THE PROBE THAT FOUND IT WAS THE `report` LINE. It printed "target: 0.0B" next to "8.4 GB of executables", which cannot both be true. `crates/target` is a symlink into `~/.buildcache/`, `du -sk` measured the link, and the refusal divides by that number -- so the share was always 0 and the guard passed unconditionally. Fixed by following the link AND refusing outright when the size cannot be taken, since a safety check computed against zero is worse than no check.

The tool's contract was wrong twice, and both failures were SILENT. A guessed stamp filename let `stamp` report success while `reap` answered "no stamp" -- the two halves disagreeing with no error anywhere. Passing the target path where cargo-sweep wants the project path made it fail inside a pipeline, which `pipefail` turned into exit 1 with NO output at all; the cause was only visible by running the inner command by hand.

The numbers behind the decision, each measured here rather than quoted: target 24 GB; `debug/deps` 710 executables under 277 names, 433 duplicates (60%), 8.4 GB; `cargo -Z gc` refused on stable; `--time 1` and `--installed` "would clean: nothing"; `--maxsize 4000` would delete 20.4 GiB; 689 of the 710 executables built on a single day.
`shellcheck -S style` is clean on the new script, and Layer 0 covers it from now on.

THE FULL WORKFLOW RAN AND THE NUMBER IS 10.5 GB. Stamp, then `run-ci.sh` with no arguments (135 lanes, 71 minutes, all pass), then reap: 24% of the tree, under the limit, applied -- 48.5 GB down to 38.0 GB. The same tool refused the same tree at 109% an hour earlier, so the guard tells the two situations apart rather than always saying one of them.

AND THE ROUND'S HEADLINE DIAGNOSIS WAS WRONG, which the reap is what exposed. "433 duplicate executables, about 5 GB of copies nothing can run" counted DISTINCT FEATURE COMBINATIONS, not garbage: after the full gate the duplicate count went UP to 1404 of 1748 (80%) while the tree got SMALLER, because every one of those copies is an artefact some lane had just used. Duplicate count is a measure of how wide this workspace's feature matrix is, not of how much is stale.

What is actually stale is what the gates do not touch, and that is the only thing the reap removes: 10.5 GB of it here, none of which was needed -- `cargo test -p wz-capture --no-run` finished in 13s afterwards without recompiling, and Layer 0 and C0 pass.
So the working-set size of this tree is about 38 GB, measured rather than guessed, and anything above that is what accumulates between reaps.

carry_forward_bullets: The reap is still a heuristic at its core and now says so at the line that holds it. Making it exact means `--message-format=json` on all 939 cargo invocations, which is a refactor of the gate rather than of this tool, and which introduces a failure mode -- a missed injection -- that is quieter than the one it removes. Worth doing only if the cost of a wrong reap ever stops being "a rebuild".

The lane-count precondition reads a LOG, so it inherits whatever the log says. A lane that passes without logging its pass line, or a future run-ci that renames "INFO  Layer X pass", breaks the count in the safe direction (refusal) but with a message that points at the wrong thing.

Still nothing calls the reap automatically. The precondition now makes an automatic call SAFE where it was not before -- it would simply refuse after a partial run instead of deleting the tree -- so wiring it into the round boundary is a smaller step than it was this morning.
changes_bullets: R311y734 answers a question put to R311y733's reaper: why is it not deterministic, and is it the right shape. The honest answer to the first was "three places" -- an mtime comparison, a 60% threshold someone chose, and a written rule saying to run the full gate first. This round removes the third and demotes the second.

THE PRECONDITION IS NOW CHECKED. A reap requires a `run-ci.sh` log, newer than the stamp, in which the number of lanes that PASSED equals the number `run-ci.sh` REGISTERS. Both numbers are read from the tree -- `grep -c '^run_layer '` against the log's own count -- so it is the tree agreeing with itself rather than a threshold. A partial run cannot satisfy it: `--layer 0 --layer C0` logs 1 lane against 135 registered.

FULL DETERMINISM WAS INVESTIGATED AND REJECTED WITH REASONS, each measured. cargo WILL name its artefacts exactly, even cached ones: `cargo test --no-run --message-format=json` reported `filenames` for 92 units of which 92 were `fresh: true`. Collecting that across a gate run would replace the mtime heuristic outright -- and it needs the flag on all 939 cargo invocations in `run-ci.sh`, where a single missed injection silently marks that lane's output unused. That trades a heuristic for a quieter failure.

`--unit-graph` (nightly 1.98 is installed) does not help: it describes units logically -- pkg_id, features, profile, target -- and names no file and no hash, because the hash is cargo's internal computation and is not exposed. A `rustc-wrapper` is worse still: a fresh unit never invokes rustc, so the wrapper cannot see the artefacts that matter most.

The residue is stated in the file rather than hidden: the reap still rests on cargo-sweep's mtime comparison, so a unit cargo re-used without touching its fingerprint could be removed. The cost of being wrong here is a REBUILD, not a wrong answer -- which is why the heuristic is worth keeping while the precondition is worth enforcing.
Round 1761.decision_summary: R311y734 replaces the reaper's written rule with a checked precondition -- a full-gate log whose passed-lane count equals the registered one -- and records why full determinism was investigated and rejected: cargo can name every artefact exactly, but only through a flag that would have to reach all 939 cargo invocations, where one miss fails quieter than the heuristic it replaces.
verification_bullets: THE PRECONDITION WAS PROBED IN BOTH DIRECTIONS. A stamp with no gate since is refused. A stamp followed by a PARTIAL gate (`run-ci.sh --layer 0`) is still refused, and the message names the counts: 135 registered against what the log holds. With the stamp placed just before the existing full-gate log, the reap accepts it and says so -- "proof of a full gate ... (135 lanes)".

THAT POSITIVE PROBE ALSO EXERCISED THE SECOND NET, unplanned and usefully. With the stamp moved artificially into the past the reap passed the precondition and then reported 104% of the tree, which the share limit refused. So the two layers are not redundant: the precondition establishes that a full gate ran, the limit catches a stamp that does not describe it.

A PROBE OF MY OWN WAS WRONG FIRST, and the tool was not. `touch -d "$(date -r LOG) -1 minute"` set the stamp to 22:20 rather than 12:18, because `-1` was read as a TIMEZONE OFFSET and `minute` discarded. The refusal that followed was correct about the stamp it was given; only the second attempt, with `-d "@$(( $(stat -c %Y LOG) - 60 ))"`, was a real test of the positive path.

`shellcheck -S style` clean. The measurements behind the rejected alternatives: 939 cargo invocations in run-ci.sh (496 test, 245 clippy, 154 build); `--message-format=json` reports 164 filenames across 92 units, all fresh; `--unit-graph` unit keys are dependencies/features/mode/pkg_id/platform/profile/target and nothing else; sccache stands at 8060 hits against 9058 misses, so discarding the tree and rebuilding is not the cheap option it looks like.

carry_forward_bullets: The reap now happens automatically only when a round runs the FULL gate, which is rare -- most rounds run lanes they touched. So the automation is correct and mostly idle: it will decline for many rounds in a row and reap on the occasional full-gate round. Whether that cadence is enough to keep the tree bounded is unmeasured; it needs several rounds of history before anyone can say.

Nothing makes a round run the full gate. If the tree grows faster than full-gate rounds occur, the reap never fires and the only signal is the decline line repeating. A round that notices `sweep-target.sh report` crossing some size could ASK for a full gate, but that is the threshold this round deliberately avoided inventing.
changes_bullets: R311y735 closes N26: the reaper now runs at the ROUND boundary, and it needed no threshold of its own to be safe there.

`round-runner.sh` stamps before each round and reaps after it. What makes that safe unattended is R311y734's precondition rather than anything added here: a reap requires a run-ci log, newer than the stamp, whose passed-lane count equals the number run-ci.sh registers. Most rounds run a PARTIAL gate and therefore cannot satisfy it, so the reap declines and the tree is untouched; the rounds that do run the full gate get their artefacts reaped automatically.

THE AUTOMATION CARRIES NO NUMBER ANYONE CHOSE. It does not check disk pressure, or a size cap, or a round count -- each of which would have been a threshold invented for the occasion. It asks the one question that already has an exact answer and acts on it.

IT SAYS WHY IT DECLINED, in one line, every time. A reap that skipped in silence would read as "there was nothing to reap", which is the failure this workspace keeps finding in its own gates. The declining message carries cargo-sweep's own words -- "no FULL run-ci log newer than the stamp" or "REFUSING -- 104% is over the 60% limit".
`--no-reap` turns the whole thing off; it is on by default because an opt-in automation is the thing N26 already was.
Round 1762.decision_summary: R311y735 closes N26 by reaping at the round boundary, which R311y734's precondition made safe to do unattended -- and the automation needed no threshold of its own, because the question 'did a full gate run since the stamp' already has an exact answer.
verification_bullets: THE HOOKS WERE PROBED WITHOUT RUNNING A REAL ROUND, by lifting the two functions out of the runner verbatim and calling them. A stamp followed by no full gate declines with the reason and the caller survives. `--no-reap` produces no output and touches nothing. With the stamp placed before the existing full-gate log the precondition PASSES and the second net catches the result at 104%, which is the two layers doing different jobs in the same call.

THE FIRST VERSION OF THE HOOK KILLED THE RUNNER, and the probe is what found it. Under `set -e` a command substitution that exits non-zero ends the shell before `rc=$?` can read it -- and a declined reap exits non-zero BY DESIGN, so the ordinary case would have ended the round loop after the first round. Fixed with `out="$(...)" || rc=$?`, and the reason is written at the line.
That is the shape worth keeping: the automation's failure mode was not "reaps the wrong thing" but "stops the loop on the normal path", and only running it revealed that.
`shellcheck -S style` clean on the runner. `--help` lists `--no-reap`.

carry_forward_bullets: THE EXACT REAP HAS NOT SUCCEEDED ONCE. Its refusals are probed, its collector is probed, and the path where it actually deletes on cargo's declaration is untested until a full gate runs with `WZ_ARTIFACT_LOG` set. Nothing schedules that: `round-runner.sh` does not set the variable, so rounds still fall back to the mtime path. Wiring it there is a one-line change and is deliberately not made until the exact path has been seen to work once.

The keep-set covers `debug/deps` only. `debug/build/` (1.6 GB of build-script output), `.fingerprint` (11387 entries) and `incremental` are left alone, because cargo's artefact messages do not name them and deleting what nobody declared is the failure this round exists to avoid. They are the next place to look if the tree keeps growing.

`grep -qxF` per file against the keep-set is O(files x keep), which is fine at 6305 x 219 and will not be at 10x that. A sorted `comm` would be the shape; it is not worth doing until the exact path has run once and the real sizes are known.
changes_bullets: R311y736 pays N28: the reaper can now decide on cargo's OWN declaration of what a build produced, instead of on cargo-sweep's mtime comparison. R311y734 rejected this and the rejection was wrong on two of its three grounds.

WHAT THE REJECTION GOT WRONG, measured. "Injecting `--message-format=json` into 939 cargo calls breaks the output run-ci parses" -- it does not: run-ci greps `^test result: ok. N passed` (53 guards) and `: test` from `-- --list` (5), and BOTH come from the test binary rather than from cargo, so the flag leaves them untouched. "One missed injection is a quieter failure than the heuristic" -- a missed injection deletes that lane's output and it gets REBUILT, which is the same cost mtime being wrong already carries, and it is checkable besides.

NO INJECTION WAS NEEDED. `run-ci.sh` defines `cargo` as a SHELL FUNCTION, which reaches all 939 call sites -- measured: zero of them go through `command cargo`, an absolute path, or a `bash -c` subshell, and the `( cd crates && ... )` subshells inherit functions. The function runs the original command untouched and then re-queries the same build with `--message-format=json --no-run`, so nothing about the gate's output can change. The re-query costs 0.089s warm, about 80 seconds across a full gate.

`scripts/lib/artifact_filenames.py` reads that JSON and prints every declared path -- `filenames` plus `executable`, because a test target's binary is not always repeated in the former and it is the artefact the reaper most needs to keep. It refuses an empty read: a collector that silently contributes nothing to the keep-set is how a reaper deletes a live lane's output.

`sweep-target.sh` takes the exact path whenever an artefact log is present, and says which basis it used. It does not consult cargo-sweep there at all -- scanning a 24 GB tree for mtimes costs minutes and answers a question that path is not asking.

ARGUMENT RECONSTRUCTION IS DRIVEN BY MEASUREMENT: cargo REJECTS a repeated `--no-run` and a repeated `--message-format`, so each is added only when absent, and everything after `--` is dropped because the test filter behind it is the binary's business and the flag may not follow it.
Round 1763.decision_summary: R311y736 pays N28 by reaping on cargo's own declaration rather than on mtime -- and records that R311y734's rejection of this was wrong on two of its three grounds, both checkable and neither checked at the time.
verification_bullets: THE COLLECTOR WAS PROVED NOT TO DISTURB THE GATE. Layer C1bt passes with collection off and with it on, and the collected log names 219 paths of which 202 are under `debug/deps` -- rmeta, rlib, so, and the extensionless test binaries, so cargo's declaration covers every artefact kind the reaper deletes.

THE EXACT PATH SHIPPED WITH A SAFETY HOLE AND A PROBE FOUND IT BEFORE IT RAN. The first version deleted straight away, which walked around the share limit entirely: an artefact log covering ONE lane names a few hundred files and condemns everything else in deps/. It now measures the condemned set first, and with a single-lane log it reports "would remove 6305 file(s), 15.0GB -- 83% of the tree" and REFUSES. The log's size is not evidence of its coverage, and that is the sentence the refusal now enforces.
`artifact_filenames.py` refuses an empty read (exit 1, named). An artefact log that names nothing under `debug/deps` is refused with the reason.

WHAT IS NOT YET VERIFIED, stated rather than implied: the exact path has never RUN to completion, because doing so needs a full gate with `WZ_ARTIFACT_LOG` set -- 71 minutes plus the 80 seconds of re-queries -- and that has not happened yet. Every refusal on the way there is verified; the successful reap is not. The next full gate is what settles it.
`shellcheck -S style` clean on both scripts.

Round 1764.decision_summary: R311y739 pays N36 by ledgering R311y737 and R311y738 -- three commits that were pushed with no ChangelogEntry -- and records that a shared cargo binary replaced under the tree is a hazard the schema-pin hook caught before it could migrate the store.
verification_bullets: THE MNEMOSYNE BUMP WAS NOT A CHOICE, IT WAS AN ACCIDENT THE HOOK CAUGHT. The shared `~/.cargo/bin/mnemosyne-cli` had been replaced by ANOTHER SESSION with a schema-46 build while this repository pinned 44. `pre-commit` refused every commit BEFORE the store was migrated -- which is precisely the point R311y401, y406 and y416 each missed, all three surfacing on hosted CI instead. Rev and ceiling moved in ONE commit; cli and mcp were installed at the same rev and confirmed through `~/.cargo/.crates.toml` rather than `--version`.

ORDERING FACT worth keeping: `install-mnemosyne-mcp.sh` reads the rev from HEAD, not from the working tree, so the pin commit must land BEFORE the mcp install -- the reverse of the order the operating guide reads as natural.

carry_forward_bullets: THE FAN IS PROVED ON ONE PLANE, and the type system carries the rest. `dispatch_event` hands `MappingSpaces` to all eight consumers, so a future consumer that declared a bare `&HashMap` would not compile -- but only the Push plane has a test that an `M=0` alias actually resolves end to end. The other seven are argued from the shared resolver, not measured. Per-plane witnesses are the honest next step.

`SubscriberRegistry::peer_keyexpr_table()` survives with NO production caller left -- only a test and two comments. It is an honest introspection read, and it is also the shape that produced this defect: a strictly weaker accessor sitting next to the correct one. Either it earns a caller or it should go.

A relay face still refuses every `M=0` alias, and that is currently correct because `LinkstateForwarder` / `RouterForwarder` declare no aliases of their own (measured: `absorb_keyexpr_into` is the only writer, and it writes the peer's table). The day a forwarder declares one, its `resolve_wireexpr` call sites become the same defect this round closed.
This round did not move the 85-atom REMAINING WORK count, and should not be read as having done so: it fixes a defect that spans many of those atoms' planes rather than completing any one of them.
changes_bullets: THE DEFECT, and it announced itself in prose for 135 rounds: `wireexpr_resolve.rs` carried the sentence "Resolving OUR ids is not built yet" together with the reason it mattered -- zenoh PREFERS the id the peer declared and stamps it `Mapping::Receiver` (`dispatcher/resource.rs:625`), so the moment wz called `send_declare_keyexpr` a zenoh peer began naming that id back at us with `M=0`. The resolver answered `None` and every caller dropped the message.

The table was never the missing piece: `SessionActions::outbound_mappings` has been written by `send_declare_keyexpr` and pruned by `send_undeclare_kexpr` since R234. What was missing was any path from it to the inbound registries, whose only table was the peer's.

`MappingSpaces` now carries the two spaces side by side, which is zenoh's own `FaceState` shape (`remote_mappings` + `local_mappings`, selected on the bit at `dispatcher/face.rs:126-127`). `resolve_wireexpr_in` reads the arm the `M` bit names and NEVER the other; `resolve_wireexpr` survives as the peer-only wrapper for callers with genuinely one space -- a relay face absorbs the peer's declarations and emits none of its own, so refusing `M=0` is its correct answer, not a degraded one.

OUR space is a TRAIT (`OwnMappingSpace::resolve_own_mapping`), not a second table. `SessionLinkActions` implements it by delegating to the R234 `resolve_outbound_mapping`, so there is exactly ONE copy of the fact and a retraction is visible to the receive path the instant it happens. A mirrored `HashMap` inside the registry would have been filled at declare time and never told about the prune.

THE WHOLE OBSERVER FAN MOVED, not the Push plane alone. All 27 dispatch entry points across the eight consumer registries (subscriber, queryable, remote-subscriber, remote-queryable, liveliness, liveliness-subscriber, liveliness-get, local-token, reply, query, switchboard) now take `impl Into<MappingSpaces<'a>>`, and `ApplicationLayerObserver::dispatch_event` hands over `subscribers.mapping_spaces()` instead of the bare peer table. A `From<&HashMap>` conversion yields `peer_only`, so the ~150 existing call sites compile unchanged and mean exactly what they meant before.

`Session::new` installs the actions bundle as the session's own space automatically, for the reason R236 moved the zid install there: the fact is authoritative at construction, and making the application ask for it only creates a way to forget. The install needs `SessionLinkActions<R, T>: Send + Sync + 'static`, stated as one honest bound on the composite.
Round 1765.decision_summary: R311y739 builds the half of keyexpr resolution that `wireexpr_resolve` said was NOT built: an `M=0` alias names OUR id space, the live session had no way to read it, and every such message was dropped -- while the PASSIVE analyzer had resolved both spaces correctly since R311y701.
verification_bullets: BOTH HALVES WERE FALSIFIED, not merely run. Reverting `dispatch_push` to `peer_only` killed 3 of the registry tests; deleting the `Session::new` install killed 2 of the 3 wiring tests. In both probes the ANTI-VACUITY twin stayed green, which is what says the suite is measuring the space rather than the presence of some table.

THE DISCRIMINATOR IS A COLLISION, deliberately: every two-space test puts the SAME id in both tables under DIFFERENT literals. A wrong-space read therefore returns the sibling's string and fires the WRONG subscriber -- caught as a wrong answer, not as silence. Both upstreams number from 1, so this is the realistic failure, and it is why answering out of the wrong space is worse than answering nothing.

WIRED IS NOT DRIVEN, so the wiring proof is end-to-end: `Session::new`, then `send_declare_keyexpr(7, "home/temp")`, then an inbound `M=0` Push for id 7 fires the subscriber. A `Some(..)` field assertion would have passed against an install of the wrong object, a table that never fills, and a resolver that ignores the install.
THE RETRACTION TEST is the one a mirrored table fails: after `send_undeclare_kexpr(7)` the same alias stops resolving with no second install, because the registry reads the live table.

changes_bullets: THE RED CAME FROM R311y739 AND IT WAS A REAL PORTABILITY WALL, not a lane artifact: `SubscriberRegistry::own_mapping_space` was typed `alloc::sync::Arc<dyn OwnMappingSpace + Send + Sync>`, and on ARMv6-M (Cortex-M0/M0+) `alloc::sync` does not exist at all -- it is gated behind `target_has_atomic = "ptr"`. Right about the danger -- naming the wrong bytes as a message's fields is worse than naming none -- and it left a LIVE TAP, which feeds incrementally, with no field walk after the first offer.

FIXED by rebasing rather than refusing. The offer's base is now a NUMBER (`stream.fed[dir]` read before the increment, not compared to zero); the frames this offer produced are shifted into its coordinate space for the duration of the `on_plaintext` call and shifted back after it, so every other reader of the stream still sees absolute offsets.

THE WINDOW IS COMPUTED FROM A COUNT, NOT FROM `before`. The `frames_per_flow` cap loop runs between the framing and the offer and discards from the FRONT, so after a trim the index `before` names a frame that is no longer there. `added` survives that; the offered window is the last `added` entries.

A MESSAGE THAT SPANS THE BOUNDARY IS STILL NOT WALKABLE, and is now named rather than lumped in. Its head is in bytes nothing holds -- a recovered QUIC stream is framed, not buffered -- so no coordinate can address it. `messages_straddling_offers` counts it; `appends_not_walked` narrows to the offer where the whole window straddled. Two findings, two counters: one says a listing is missing a section, the other that it is missing a line.

AND THE EXPORT WAS SHORT. MEASURED: six of `QuicStreamFeed`'s seven fields were emitted in the JSON and `appends_not_walked` was not -- the one counter that says a `--fields` listing is short could not be read by a consumer at all, which is the failure the emit's own comment argues against one line above it. Both it and the new counter are emitted now.

changes_bullets: THE GAP WAS TOTAL AND SILENT. Every InterestOwned wz had ever emitted carried `TO` and only `TO` -- `build_liveliness_token_interest` was the sole body-header composer and its bitset was a literal `KE|TO|R|N|M`. A zenoh router forwards a subscriber declaration to a face ONLY if that face's own `remote_interests` holds one with `options.subscribers()` matching the resource (`hat/router/pubsub.rs:120-125`; `queries.rs:255-259` for the queryable half), so a wz face peered with zenohd saw an empty `RemoteSubscriberRegistry` no matter how many subscribers the far side declared -- with no error anywhere, and indistinguishable from `nothing matched yet`.

THE KIND BITS ARE NOW A TYPE. `InterestKinds` carries `SUBSCRIBERS` 0x02 / `QUERYABLES` 0x04 / `TOKENS` 0x08 -- the bits zenoh declares at `zenoh-protocol/src/network/interest.rs:248-251` and wz's own generated `InterestBodyOwned::su`/`qu`/`to` read -- with `BitOr` for a union and NO `empty()`, `Default` or `from_bits`. The empty set is UNREPRESENTABLE rather than runtime-rejected, because there is no honest `CodecError` for it: the encoder would happily write the byte, so the refusal is a protocol judgement. `AGGREGATE` is deliberately absent, not merely unused -- it is not a kind, and wz stages no aggregate reply (see liveliness-token's residual).

N AND M STAY DERIVED, WHICH IS WHAT UPSTREAM DOES. The private `build_restricted_interest` composes `KE|<kinds>|R|N|M` and takes the kind bits alone; `RESTRICTED`/`NAMED`/`MAPPING` come from the attached wireexpr exactly as `Interest::options` adds them (`interest.rs:198-209`). A caller able to set them independently could emit `R=0, N=1`, which the protocol comment at `interest.rs:131-136` forbids. `build_interest_subscribers` / `_queryables` / `_kinds` are the public doors; the two liveliness builders became wrappers on the same SSOT.

THE EMIT SITE DIVERGES FROM ZENOH, DELIBERATELY AND RECORDED. zenoh sends the SUBSCRIBERS interest from `declare_publisher_inner` (`api/session.rs:1370-1377`) and the QUERYABLES one from `declare_querier_inner` (`:1428-1435`). wz's `declare_publisher` / `declare_querier` are infallible by-value handles with no id and no undeclare, so they can carry neither a failed emit nor the `Interest(Final)` that retracts one -- emitting there would leak an interest on the peer for the session's life. It rides `Publisher/Querier::declare_matching_listener` instead, which allocates through `alloc_next_interest_id`, rolls the watch back and returns `Err(MatchingListenerError::Wire)` on a failed emit, and whose `undeclare` Finals the id BEFORE removing the watch.

THE RECONNECT CACHE HAD TO GROW A VARIANT, and it carries the TYPED kinds. zenoh holds `remote_interests` PER FACE, so a reconnect hands us a new face with an empty set and every surviving listener would fire off a registry the peer had stopped feeding. `CachedDeclaration::MatchingInterest` replays it. The field is `InterestKinds`, not `u8`: a `u8` could hold 0 or a stray R/N/M/A bit, letting the replay emit a message no live declare path could -- the cache must not be able to say more than the send could.

A CLOSED CHANNEL STOPS THE LOOP, and that is the only non-spinning reading rather than a convenience. `changed()` errors the moment the last sender is dropped and does so on every subsequent poll, so a loop that treated the error as "keep running" would busy-wait forever. Making it a stop also makes the sender an RAII handle, which is what a caller who dropped it meant.

THE TRANSITION IS DRIVEN, NOT JUST REPORTED. The arm calls `dispatcher.stop()` before returning `Stopped`, exactly as the link-loss arm calls `notify_link_lost()`. THE BX LOCK WAS THE REAL COST OF THIS ROUND, and the fix is outside this repo so it is recorded here rather than committed. `~/.claude/remote-build/bin/bx` held an EXCLUSIVE flock across the command with fd 9 open, so any daemonising grandchild inherited it — and `~/.cargo/config.toml` sets `rustc-wrapper = "sccache"`, whose server never exits. Measured: a run at 17:26:56 spawned that daemon, finished normally, and every later bx run in the repo blocked in `flock` for ever, with no cargo process to see and no output to read (bx writes the command's output to its log, not stdout). I killed three runs on TWO WRONG DIAGNOSES — "cargo build is the bad shape" and "two concurrent bx runs contend" — both asserted from symptoms without once checking. `lsof "$lock"` named sccache in one call.

Fixed at the owner's direction, and the shape matters: SHARED lock by default, EXCLUSIVE only for `--fresh`. The exclusive-always form was over-strong because cargo already locks its own build directory (target/{debug,release}/.cargo-lock), so concurrent runs cannot corrupt each other — the one thing that genuinely cannot race a build is `--fresh`'s `cargo clean -p`. Plus `--close` (drops the fd before exec, which is exactly the case flock(1) documents the flag for) and `-w 300 -E 199` so a residual wedge prints its holder and fails instead of hanging. Verified: a run that spawned a NEW sccache daemon left the lock with zero holders, and a second bx completed while the first still held the shared lock. Backup at bx.bak-y785; it is a single file, not a git repo.

THE LESSON THAT GENERALISES: a lock is held by whoever holds a descriptor, not by whoever took it. Any `( flock N && cmd ) N>lock` in this workspace has the same defect the moment `cmd` can spawn a daemon.

Types UNGATED in `driver_loop.rs` beside `ReassemblyDropReason`, the established precedent for a feature-independent observer type. `MulticastPeerId` carries the wire zid as a `Copy` value rather than a slot index, and that is forced rather than stylistic: the peer is GONE when an observer sees the event and its index is already recycled, so an index would name whoever comes next.

Two reasons, and the distinction is load-bearing. `Closed` = the peer SAYING it left (zenoh forwards the Close's own reason byte, `multicast/rx.rs:310-313`; pico `multicast/rx.c:513-536`). `LeaseExpired` = this node INFERRING it from silence (zenoh hard-codes `close::reason::EXPIRED`, `multicast/transport.rs:401`; pico `multicast/lease.c:110-133`). Both upstreams keep them apart; an application that conflates them cannot tell a clean shutdown from a dead link.

Wired at FOUR sites — AP and MCU, announced and inferred. The reassembly-aware `multicast_rx` Close arm and sweep SSOT cover both profiles' reassembly builds at once; the non-reassembly arms in `wz-runtime-tokio multicast_glue` and `wz-session-lwip multicast_drive` are the twins. Reporting in only one build would make a membership view depend on a feature that has nothing to do with membership.

`sweep_with`'s callback widened to `(idx, MulticastPeerLost)` rather than adding a third method: the index is this node's private slot key (the reassembly host aborts chains with it), the departure is the only half an application can act on. `close_by_src_with` is the announced twin and fires ONLY inside the `Some` arm, so a Close from an address holding no peer cannot manufacture a departure.
Read BEFORE `evict()` in both paths, which is the only ordering that works — `evict()` clears the zid, so reading after would report an empty peer and the loops could not tell.

changes_bullets: SubscriberRegistry::has_local_matching (pubsub.rs) - the session-local half. TWO filters, both taken from `local_publish` so a true here predicts a real delivery rather than a table entry: the subscriber's own `allowed_origin` must permit a local origin, and the two keyexprs must INTERSECT as patterns (both sides may be wildcards, so it is `keyexpr_intersect_patterns`, not the one-sided `matches` the dispatch path runs against a literal sample).

The subscriber-origin filter follows PICO, not zenoh, and the atom's P= is why: pico gates its local count on `_z_locality_allows_local(sub->_allowed_origin)` (vendor/zenoh-pico/src/net/filtering.c:386-397) while zenoh reads only the keyexpr (zenoh/src/api/session.rs:1876-1897) and can therefore report a match no local publish would reach. The stricter answer is also the one that agrees with this registry's own delivery rule.

Publisher::get_matching_status and the aliased twin now OR the two halves, each gated by the publisher's `allowed_destination`. That is pico's `state = (targets == NULL && local_targets == 0) ? ACTIVE : OFF` (filtering.c:71) with each half admitted by `allow_local` / `allow_remote` (:66, :261-262).

The WATCH was made to agree, which is where the change stops being local to one method. `declare_matching_listener_seeded` seeds registration with the same combined verdict the poll reports; `reevaluate_matching` is driven from the local declare and undeclare sites (pico's `_z_write_filter_ctx_add_local_match` / `_remove_local_match`, filtering.c:87-101); and `dispatch_declare_with_local` carries the local half into the INBOUND path too. That last one is not decoration: without it a watch held true by a local subscriber is flipped false by an unrelated remote undeclare.

The local half is PASSED IN rather than mirrored. The local subscriptions live on `SubscriberRegistry` and the watches on `RemoteSubscriberRegistry`; they are sibling fields of `SessionObserver`, so the production fan supplies the predicate under a disjoint borrow and the fact keeps one home. The un-suffixed entry points delegate with a `false` local half, which is the honest answer for a caller holding no local table.
