wz multicast could not leave its own subnet, and nothing said so.

`transport-link-udp` asked for this round in its own words: "REMAINING:
nothing named on the dial/accept axes; the atom stays PARTIAL pending a fresh
impl-axis read against zenoh-link-commons rather than a carried list." So the
read started from the UPSTREAM surface rather than from wz's list -- which is
the shape the north star's debt 60 names, that every grading axis so far
departs from a wz atom and none from zenoh's.

The axis nobody had graded was the LOCATOR CONFIG surface. zenoh's UDP link
declares three keys and no more (`zenoh-link-udp/src/lib.rs:108-112`):
`iface`, `join`, `ttl`. wz honoured one. The string "join" and the call
`set_multicast_ttl_v4` occurred ZERO times in the workspace.

`ttl` is the one that bounds deployment rather than convenience. The OS
default multicast hop limit is 1 -- measured on this tree before the fix, by
binding a wz group socket and reading `multicast_ttl_v4()` back -- so every wz
multicast deployment was confined to one subnet, with no configuration that
could change it. A node that cannot cross a router is not a replacement for
one that can.

carry_forward_bullets: THE PRIORITY IS NOW TEMPORAL WITHIN A BATCH WINDOW AND NOWHERE ELSE, and that boundary is the honest statement of what this round bought. wz writes synchronously on the calling thread: with `transport-batching` off, or with the window closed, each message is framed and handed to the link immediately, so there is no queue for a later high-priority message to overtake it in. zenoh has no such gap because its pipeline is ALWAYS on -- the tx task is the only writer. Closing it in wz means an async TX task owning the link, which is an architecture decision (it reaches the MCU sync-pump profile too), not an increment.

Round 1871.decision_summary:
wz carried the QoS priority band on the wire and then ignored it in the schedule.

The `transport-qos` atom's own registered residual says it in as many words: "the
WIRE layer is bit-exact, but the entire scheduling layer is absent ... there are
NO per-priority TX queues and therefore no temporal priority at all". It has said
so since R311y440 and no round had taken it. This is the residual with the widest
blast radius in the whole catalog: `Priority` is a first-class public API on
`Publisher` / `put` / `Query`, an application that asks for RealTime gets the
ext_qos byte it asked for, and gets no scheduling for it.

MEASURED FIRST, before any design. A batching window that staged a Background PUT
and then a RealTime PUT put `["Background(sn=0)", "RealTime(sn=0)"]` on the wire --
arrival order. After the change the same body reads
`["RealTime(sn=0)", "Background(sn=0)"]`.

THE SHAPE CAME FROM UPSTREAM, READ DIRECTLY, NOT FROM THE REGISTRY LINE. zenoh's
transmission pipeline holds one `stage_in` PER PRIORITY and its consumer pulls
`for (prio, queue) in self.stage_out.iter_mut().enumerate()`, returning the FIRST
priority holding a batch (`io/zenoh-transport/src/common/pipeline.rs:899-914`,
tag 1.5.0 / 49c8a53). Its producer indexes `stage_in[priority as usize]` and
collapses to `(0, Priority::DEFAULT)` when the pipeline is not QoS
(`pipeline.rs:813-819`) -- which is exactly the non-QoS arm wz needs, so the
feature-off and no-negotiation builds fall out of the same shape rather than
being bolted on. zenoh-pico has no counterpart at all: one `_wbuf`, one
`_batch_state`, one `_batch_count` per transport
(`vendor/zenoh-pico/src/transport/common/tx.c:132`), so this is a zenoh-parity
gain and a pico superset.

wz's stand-in for per-priority staging was flush-on-priority-change: one open
frame, drained whenever the next message's band differed. That kept the frame
boundary honest -- a frame is one (priority, reliability) conduit -- while making
the wire order the ARRIVAL order and costing one extra frame per interleave.

The sn=0-on-both is itself the reading: each band mints from its OWN ring, so the wire order was never an SN artifact -- it was the schedule.

carry_forward_bullets: THE WIRE HALF DID NOT MOVE, AND THE REASON IS A DIVERGENCE THIS ROUND FOUND WHILE READING UPSTREAM. zenoh feeds the RESOLVED mode to the outbound Query too (`api/session.rs:2316`), so a zenoh default get transmits Latest; wz keeps eliding. It keeps eliding because wz's consolidation wire byte is PICO's numbering and zenoh's is one higher across the board: pico writes its API enum raw, NONE=0 / MONOTONIC=1 / LATEST=2 (`protocol/codec/message.c:412` over `constants.h:184-188`), while zenoh numbers Auto=0 / None=1 / Monotonic=2 / Latest=3 (`commons/zenoh-codec/src/zenoh/query.rs:38-44`). A wz `Latest` therefore reads as `Monotonic` to a zenohd. It is UNOBSERVABLE today -- the field is requester-side only and zenoh's router never consumes it (0 `consolidation` occurrences under `zenoh/src/net/routing/`, measured) -- which is exactly why it survived, and transmitting a resolved mode over a byte known to be wrong would turn a latent divergence into a live one. Moving it wants a foreign witness on BOTH planes (a real zenohd and a real pico), because the two upstreams disagree and wz claims to replace both. This is the atom's next increment and it is a wire round, not an increment on this one.

Either build that fixture or accept the pin as upstream-matched-only; do not read it as load-bearing in the meantime.

THE `_time` CARVE-OUT IS THE ONLY ONE EITHER UPSTREAM HAS, and wz deliberately did not invent an `_sn` twin even though the `@adv` recovery GET carries `_sn` and no `_time`. Both upstreams pin `None` at the call site instead, and wz now does the same. If a future round is tempted to widen the carve-out, the reason not to is that the pin is the upstream shape and the carve-out is not a general "internal GETs are exempt" rule.

THE THIRD CONSECUTIVE ROUND FOUND PRE-EXISTING TESTS ASSERTING BEHAVIOUR UPSTREAM LACKS -- y833's `_anyke`-less `@adv` GET, y834's aligner fixture answering outside its query, and now eight fixtures riding a default zenoh does not have. Three in a row is a class, not a coincidence, and the common shape is a TEST that hand-rolls a request PRODUCTION would build differently. The remedy each time was to move the fixture onto the constructor production uses. There is no gate that finds these; they surfaced only because a contract change made them red. A sweep that compares every test's request construction against the production SSOT would find the rest before the next contract change does.

Round 1872.decision_summary:
wz's default get delivered every reply where zenoh's delivers one per keyexpr.

The `query-consolidation` atom has named this residual since R311y321 and left it
open across fifteen rounds: "wz's Rust default is None where zenoh's is AUTO ->
Latest ... the wz Rust API default remains a named, un-taken decision". It is the
DEFAULT path of `get()` -- the call a zenoh application makes when it names no
options at all -- so the divergence is not a corner, it is the ordinary case.

MEASURED FIRST, AS A VALUE. A SessionLocal get naming no mode, against a queryable
answering `hist/key` twice with a stamped old and a stamped new, delivered
`[[111,108,100],[110,101,119]]` = `[b"old", b"new"]`. zenoh delivers `[b"new"]`.
The tree already CONTAINED the divergence as a green assertion -- a test named
`query_without_consolidation_still_delivers_every_reply` whose message read "the
default get must not consolidate", which was wz's default and never zenoh's.

THE RULE IS BOTH UPSTREAMS', READ DIRECTLY, WHICH IS WHAT MAKES IT THE PROTOCOL'S
RATHER THAN ONE IMPLEMENTATION'S HABIT. zenoh's option default is
`QueryConsolidation::DEFAULT = AUTO` (`zenoh/src/api/query.rs:43-46`) and `get()`
resolves it before anything else: `Auto if parameters.time_range().is_some() =>
None`, `Auto => Latest` (`api/session.rs:2247-2252`, tag 1.5.0 / 49c8a53), keyed
on the `_time` selector parameter (`api/selector.rs:145`) and tested with
`is_some()`, so even a MALFORMED range holds the resolution at None. zenoh-pico
carries the identical rule client-side before encoding
(`vendor/zenoh-pico/src/net/primitives.c:567-573`). Of the three request paths wz

The level is the sole gate on the Fragment First/Drop chain-boundary markers, and an InitAck exceeding the InitSyn's level is one both references refuse outright, which is the rule wz itself enforces as an initiator. The divergence is reachable by a stock upstream build: zenoh-pico compiled with Z_FEATURE_FRAGMENTATION=0 sends no patch extension at all, and a real zenohd answers such a peer 0 where wz answered 1.

carry_forward_bullets: THE QUERY ROUTE IS NOT CACHED where the Push route is. `route_targets` serves Push from a generation-stamped per-keyexpr cache; `route_query` runs the scan every time. That is CORRECT rather than merely cheap, and the reason is the invalidation: the generation is bumped by subscription deltas and face removals, and a queryable declare/undeclare bumps NOTHING -- so a cached query route would go stale silently. Caching it needs the generation to cover queryable deltas too, at which point every Push cache entry is also invalidated by queryable churn. The trade was not measured; it is a round.

QueryTarget AND CONSOLIDATION ARE RELAYED VERBATIM, NOT HONOURED ROUTE-SIDE. wz fans a query to EVERY matching queryable; zenoh's BestMatching picks one by distance (`hat/router/queries.rs:1100-1107`) and its consolidation modes are applied on the route. A querier asking for one answer therefore gets N through wz, which is a divergence in the direction of MORE work rather than a wrong answer -- and that is exactly the shape this tree keeps having to be told is still a divergence.

RESPONSE ext_qos / ext_nodeid ARE NOT REWRITTEN on relay. The Response is cloned, its request id re-stamped and its keyexpr re-literalized, and every extension rides through untouched. Whether a routed reply should carry the RESPONDER's node id or the router's is a question this round did not ask.

THE `complete` MERGE HAS NO TEST OF ITS OWN. `covering_queryable_info` folds every covering face's QueryableInfo when advertising, and the fold is exercised only incidentally by the single-queryable advertisement cases -- a probe that replaced the merge with "first contributor wins" would pass the whole suite. The witness needs two faces whose queryables differ in `complete` on one advertised keyexpr.

THE SAME-IMPL ROUTER e2e HAS NO QUERY LEG. `wz_router_forward.rs` is three wz processes over the Push plane; the query plane's e2e is the pico interop pair only. That is the stronger witness and it is the one that exists, but it means a build without the pico CLI gates the query plane on unit tests alone -- Layer E5 SKIPs the interop legs green when the CLI is absent.

changes_bullets: STATE (routing.rs). FaceRoute gains the query-plane twins of what it already held for subs and tokens: `qabls` (id -> resolved keyexpr + QueryableInfo), `local_qabls` (what this table advertised to this face, and under which id), `qabl_interests` (the QUERYABLES-kind gate), and `pending_queries` (the router-minted request ids sent TO this face). RouteTable gains `pending_queries` (one entry per inbound query: src_face, src_rid, outstanding), one monotonic id source for both the query key and the per-destination request id, and a `queries_routed` counter kept SEPARATE from the Push forward count because the two have different units -- a Put counts one per destination, a query one per query.

FAN-OUT (`route_query`). Three things a naive forward would get wrong, each of which is upstream's own behaviour. (1) It mints its OWN request id per destination, because a querier's id is unique only within its face and two faces routinely both use 0 -- zenoh mints from `face.next_qid`. (2) It re-literalizes an aliased query, because a destination never saw the querier's DeclareKeyexpr; the helper is the new `request_build::reliteralize_request`, the exact twin of `reliteralize_push`, with the same load-bearing verbatim arm for an already-literal request. (3) An EMPTY route is answered with an immediate ResponseFinal rather than dropped -- zenoh's own `if route.is_empty()` arm, and the same "a requester is entitled to a termination" rule R311y773 applied to declare-final.

RETURN PATH (`route_response` / `route_response_final` / `close_one_answerer`). A reply is looked up in the ANSWERING FACE's pending map, not a table-wide one, so a peer cannot answer another peer's query by guessing an id; it is then re-stamped with the querier's own request id and re-literalized in the responder's alias context. The querier is closed by exactly ONE ResponseFinal, after the LAST outstanding answerer -- zenoh gets that count from `Drop for Query` over an Arc, and this is an explicit counter instead because the accounting has to survive a destination face DEPARTING mid-query, which a refcount can only express by making each face own a clone.

DEPARTURE (`remove_face`). Both directions. A departing ANSWERER counts down every query it owed, closing the querier if it was the last -- otherwise a z_get whose only responder crashed hangs to its own timeout, the very failure the empty-route arm refuses to cause. A departing QUERIER has its pending entries dropped along with every destination's mapping into them, so a late reply cannot resolve to a querier that is gone. Its queryables are retracted to the faces that were told about them, on the same rules the token retraction already used.

ADVERTISEMENT (`propagate_qabl_declaration` / `propagate_qabl_forget` / `dump_current_queryables`). The queryable plane is now advertised on the token plane's two rules -- a CURRENT interest is dumped, a FUTURE one registers -- because a zenoh ROUTER forwards a queryable declaration only to a face that registered a QUERYABLES interest. The one field the token twin has no counterpart for is QueryableInfo, and the dedup is where it matters: two faces covering one advertised keyexpr collapse to ONE declaration, so its info must be the MERGE of theirs, else a `complete` the second contributor had is silently dropped.

FEATURE. `routing-routes` now selects `declare-queryable` + `codec-request` + `codec-response` + `codec-response-final`, in both wz-session-core and wz-runtime-tokio. Splitting the query half into its own atom was considered and rejected: the plausibility test needs a user who wants this router WITHOUT query routing, and `routing-routes` is already AP-only (alloc + session-unicast, "an MCU router is a far-future profile"), so the footprint that argument would buy is not one anybody is short of.

Round 1878.decision_summary: A wz `--router` was a router a `z_get` could not traverse, and the failure was not a slow answer but a permanent one: the RouteTable had no Request arm at all, so a query reached no queryable AND got no ResponseFinal, while zenoh-pico's z_get blocks on a condvar the reply dropper signals. Queryable routing had been recorded as a NON-GOAL of this atom on the argument that "a queryable advertised from here would invite a Request this table has no arm for" -- true of the table, never true of the protocol, and this round removes the premise rather than disputing the logic. The table now carries both planes from one set of per-face state, the way zenoh's dispatcher does: DeclareQueryable builds a query route, an inbound Request fans out under router-minted request ids, replies come back re-stamped with the querier's own id, and exactly one ResponseFinal closes the querier once the last answerer finishes -- or immediately, if nothing matched. The foreign witness is by execution: a real zenoh-pico z_get reaches a real zenoh-pico z_queryable through a wz --router in 50ms, and an unmatched one is closed in 50ms rather than waiting out pico's own ten-second timeout.

carry_forward_bullets: A CARRY-FORWARD CLAIM OUTLIVED THE CODE IT DESCRIBED, and this round is the second half of that class rather than a new one. R311y840's carry said "QueryTarget AND CONSOLIDATION ARE RELAYED VERBATIM, NOT HONOURED ROUTE-SIDE ... its consolidation modes are applied on the route". The target half was true; the consolidation half was never true of a zenoh ROUTER, and nothing measured it before it was written down. What makes this the sharp instance is that the false half was load-bearing for a round's plan: it named work that did not exist. Nothing gates a carry_forward bullet against upstream.

THE QUERY ROUTE IS STILL NOT CACHED where the Push route is, and this round did not change the reason -- but it did change the arithmetic. `route_query` now runs `query_fit` over every face per query, which is strictly more work per scan than the old bool: each candidate is walked for its includes relation as well as its intersects one. The invalidation argument R311y840 gave still stands (a queryable declare/undeclare bumps no generation, so a cached query route would go stale silently), so the trade is unchanged in shape and larger in size. Still a round, still unmeasured.

THE DISTANCE KEY IS THE PEER'S OWN CLAIM AND NOTHING VALIDATES IT. zenoh's router HARDCODES `distance: 1` for a client-face queryable (`hat/router/queries.rs:1512`) and takes the real hop count from its linkstate net; wz's RouteTable has no linkstate net, so it uses the distance the peer DECLARED. That is the only hop information available to it and it is meaningful when the face is itself a relay -- but it is unverified input affecting a routing decision, and a peer that declares distance 0 wins every tie. Whether that is a divergence worth closing, or one to state and keep, is a round nobody has run.

THE `complete` MERGE STILL HAS NO TEST OF ITS OWN. This is R311y840's carry, unmoved, and this round made it MORE reachable rather than less: `covering_queryable_info` folds every covering face's QueryableInfo when ADVERTISING, and now that `complete` selects a route the fold's correctness has a downstream consequence it did not have before. A probe replacing the merge with "first contributor wins" still passes the whole suite. The witness needs two faces whose queryables differ in `complete` on one advertised keyexpr.
RESPONSE ext_qos / ext_nodeid ARE STILL NOT REWRITTEN on relay -- R311y840's carry, untouched.

THE NEW ORACLE CLASS IS PROVISIONED BUT THIN. `zenoh-core` currently has exactly one adjudicating leg and two binaries. `z_get --target` and `z_queryable --complete` are the only foreign controls in this tree for the query plane's policy surface, and several nearby questions now have an oracle that could answer them and no leg that asks: consolidation modes end to end, `z_querier` versus one-shot `z_get`, and a queryable whose completeness FLIPS while a querier is running.

NOTHING MEASURES WHICH CHANGED CRATES HAVE A NON-DEFAULT MODULE THE CHANGED-CRATE RUN SKIPS. R311y839's carry, and this is its THIRD consecutive instance: C1bz runs on default features, `routing.rs` is behind `routing-routes`, and the only reason this round can report 358 -> 358 rather than guessing is that the feature gate was interrogated by hand again. Three rounds is past the point where the standing rule ("a class that leaks more than twice gets a gate") applies.
changes_bullets: SELECTION (routing.rs). `FaceRoute::matches_queryable` -- a bare bool -- becomes `query_fit`, returning `Option<Option<u16>>`: outer None means no queryable here intersects the query and the face is not a destination; `Some(None)` means it is a destination that cannot answer alone; `Some(Some(d))` means it can, at the nearest such queryable's declared hop distance. `route_query` builds the candidate list from that, sorts it NEAREST-COMPLETE-FIRST then by face id, and branches on `read_request_target`. The state was already there and unused: `record_declare` has read `QueryableInfo` off the DeclareQueryable ext since R311y840, and nothing consulted the `complete` bit it stored.

COMPLETENESS IS PER QUERY, NOT PER QUERYABLE, and that is the part a naive implementation gets wrong. `query_fit` ANDs the declared flag with `keyexpr_includes_target` -- zenoh's `complete && qabl_info.complete` where the left operand is `DEFAULT_INCLUDER.includes(queryable_ke, queried_ke)` (`hat/router/queries.rs:1464`, `:1510`). A queryable on `demo/a` that declared itself complete INTERSECTS `demo/*` but does not COVER it, so it cannot serve that query alone; treating the flag as a property of the queryable rather than of the pairing would silence every other answerer for a question none of them could fully answer.

THE TIEBREAK HAS NO UPSTREAM COUNTERPART AND NEEDS ONE HERE. zenoh sorts its route set by distance (`queries.rs:1520`) with a STABLE sort over an insertion-ordered `Vec`, so equal-distance entries keep a deterministic order for free. wz scans `faces: HashMap<u64, FaceRoute>`, whose iteration order is randomised per process, so the sort key is `(distance, face_id)` -- without the second field the router would answer the same query from a different peer on each run. Measured, not assumed: the probe that drops it reds.

THE All FALLBACK IS LOAD-BEARING, not a nicety. When no candidate can answer alone there is no single right answer, so BestMatching degrades to All (`dispatcher/queries.rs:252-262`). The probe that removes it reds TEN cases -- every one of R311y840's own routing tests, because their queryables carry no info ext and are therefore incomplete by zenoh's omit-on-DEFAULT.

ORACLE PROVISIONING (build-zenohd.sh, wz-integration-tests). The decision is made on completeness and NEITHER counterparty already provisioned can express it: zenohd is a router and declares no queryable, and zenoh-pico's `z_queryable` takes `z_queryable_options_default()` whose `complete` is hardcoded false (`session/queryable.h:42`) with no flag to change it. `build-zenohd.sh` now builds the CORE `zenoh-examples` `z_queryable` + `z_get` from the same pinned checkout and installs them under a `zenoh_` prefix, so which implementation a leg spawned is legible at the call site; `zenoh_core_example_binary` is their resolver, on the same panic-not-skip discipline as `zenoh_ext_example_binary`.

A NEW CORPUS CLASS, on the reasoning the zenoh-ext entry already states. `zenoh-core` is not `zenohd`: folding it in would make every claim in this family read `wz->zenohd` against a counterparty that is not the router. Kinds `wz->zenoh` / `zenoh->wz` join KINDS, KIND_CLASS and -- because that fact lives in two places -- the CLAIM_RE alternation, where they must follow the hyphen-suffixed `wz->zenoh-ext` / `wz->zenoh-c` since alternation is first-match.

LANE OWNERSHIP. The new leg is Layer E5z, run in the job that PROVISIONS zenohd, not beside E5. E5 lives in a job with the pico CLI and no zenohd, so a placement there would have put a zenohd-family prereq behind a pico-family guard and the leg would have SKIPped green on every hosted run while Layer A4 went on counting its proof as executed. ci.yml asserts both binaries exist before the lanes start, alongside the zenoh-ext ones.

Round 1879.decision_summary: A wz `--router` read every query's QueryTarget and then ignored it, which is not a slower answer but a different one -- and the failure value proved sharper than the fan-out cost R311y840 recorded as the risk: under a real zenoh z_get the querier came back holding the INCOMPLETE queryable's reply, because consolidation keeps whichever answer arrives first and the authoritative one was merely one of N racing. zenoh's compute_final_route branches three ways and the branch a plain z_get takes by DEFAULT is the narrowest: BestMatching asks the single nearest queryable that can answer the whole keyexpr alone, falling back to All only when none can; AllComplete filters to those queryables; All fans out. The table now computes that decision from state it was already holding and throwing away -- record_declare has read QueryableInfo off the wire since R311y840 and nothing consulted it. Completeness is computed PER QUERY, not per queryable, which is upstream's own `complete && qabl_info.complete` over an includes relation rather than an intersects one. The round also WITHDRAWS half of the clause it set out to close: consolidation is not applied route-side by a zenoh router either, so relaying it verbatim was already conformant and the recorded divergence never existed. The foreign witness needed an oracle class this tree did not have, because neither zenohd nor zenoh-pico can declare a queryable complete at all.

changes_bullets: THE READER (wz-session-core json5.rs, new). A hand-rolled JSON5 parser, `alloc`-only, the READ twin of the emit-only `json` module -- no `serde_json` / `json5` dependency, for the reason that module already states. The subset is the one zenoh configs use and the reference file documents: `//` and `/* */` comments, bare identifier keys, single-quoted strings, trailing commas, `\uXXXX` with surrogate pairs, line continuations. Everything outside it is REFUSED with a byte offset rather than guessed at, NaN / Infinity included, because a config parser that silently accepts what it cannot read is how a node comes to ignore half its own file. `Json5Value::Number` holds the number's SOURCE TEXT rather than an `f64`, and that is the design decision worth naming: a config carries `batch_size: 65535` and `lease: 10000`, those are a u16 and a u64 at the far end, and routing them through a binary float would put the one place an exact integer can be lost inside the parser -- on a target where floats may not exist.

THE INGEST (wz-runtime-tokio zenoh_config.rs). `ZenohNodeConfig::from_json5` returns a `ZenohConfigIngest` of three parts, and the second and third are as load-bearing as the first: the merged config, the honoured keys the document actually NAMED, and every key it carried that wz does not honour. `named` is not decoration -- `qos` resolves to zenoh's `true` for a document that never mentions it, so a caller acting on the merged value alone would carry a decision the operator never made, and the argv expansion is exactly such a caller. An absent OR `null` key takes zenoh's default, because null is zenoh's own spelling of "left unset" and its resolved config writes one for every key it did not set.

ONE KEY TABLE, TWO DIRECTIONS. `HONOURED_CONFIG_KEYS` is the SSOT for the reader, the emitter and the census, and `every_honoured_key_is_actually_read` drives each entry to a non-default value and requires the ingest to move -- so an entry added to the table without a reader would report itself honoured while doing nothing, which is the one outcome the ignored list exists to prevent.

THE ACCEPTANCE BOUNDARY, WHICH THE FOREIGN WITNESS DICTATED. `UNHONOURED_UPSTREAM_CONFIG_KEYS` (97) plus the honoured 14 is the upstream surface, and `upstream_knows` refuses any leaf outside it. The DESCENDANT half is not looseness: several upstream keys are opaque subtrees that serialise as one `null` leaf when unset (`connect/retry`, `metadata`, `plugins`), so a config filling one in carries leaves below the path the resolved tree shows, and refusing those would refuse valid configs. Stated rather than hidden: zenoh's own check is finer -- it deserialises with `deny_unknown_fields` and so refuses a bogus field INSIDE `connect/retry` too, where wz accepts anything under a known opaque node.

THE CLI (wz-ap-demo). `--config <file>` EXPANDS into argv rather than reaching past it into the runtime, so there stays exactly one configuration path and the translation is a pure function over strings, testable with no session, socket or file. mode+listen picks `--router` / `--peer` / `--listen`, connect picks `--connect`, and the transport trio rides along; a role already on the command line is never second-guessed, which is the precedence zenohd itself uses. Feature-gated as `zenoh-config` -> `wz/zenoh-config-emit`, named in the demo's `preset-ap-full` because Layer A5 refuses a demo key the preset cannot reach, and deliberately NOT in `preset-ap-client`, whose footprint is a measured baseline.

LANE OWNERSHIP, AND ONE LANE THAT HAD NEVER RUN. Layer Z gains the four new legs and the demo build gains `zenoh-config` on the single-line feature list `feature_closure.py` scrapes. It also gains `zenoh_config_emit_zenohd_interop`, the R311y579 emit-direction sibling, which was registered in NEITHER run-ci.sh NOR ci.yml and has therefore run on no hosted CI since the round that wrote it -- measured by grep, and it passes, so the fix is a lane entry rather than a debt item. Layer C1ay gains the argv-expansion tests behind their own `--features zenoh-config` invocation, because a default-features run compiles the module out and would report a cheerful `0 passed`.
Round 1880.decision_summary: wz could not read the configuration file the deployment it is meant to replace already has, and that is the operator-facing half of "drop-in" nothing in this tree had built. R311y579 taught wz to WRITE a stock zenoh config, which serves a wz deployment standing a zenohd up next to itself and does nothing at all for one standing wz up INSTEAD of it: every wz setting arrived as one of ninety bespoke command-line flags, measured by running the demo, and `--config` was not among them -- it was accepted and IGNORED, producing output identical to a nonsense flag. This round builds the read direction: a hand-rolled JSON5 reader in wz-session-core (the twin of the emit-only `json`), `ZenohNodeConfig::from_json5` sharing ONE key table with `to_json5` so the two cannot drift, and `wz-ap-demo --config` expanding the file into the argv every existing branch already parses. The round also builds the first gate in this tree that STARTS FROM UPSTREAM: every other coverage lane begins at a wz atom and asks whether it is proven, so nothing has ever asked what fraction of zenoh's own surface wz answers to. The denominator here is a real zenohd's own resolved config -- 111 leaf keys, obtained by execution rather than by parsing DEFAULT_CONFIG.json5 -- of which wz honours 14 and NAMES the other 97 in a pinned SET. The sharpest thing the round measured changed its design rather than confirming it: the first cut accepted any key it did not model and merely reported it, and a real zenohd handed the same file REFUSES TO START ("unknown field `link_unknown_to_wz`, expected one of `unicast`, `multicast`, `link`, `shared_memory`, `auth`"). Accepting it is the worse drop-in failure of the two, because a typo the operator's old node caught would run silently under wz with the setting never applied, so wz's acceptance boundary is now zenoh's.
verification_bullets: MEASURED FIRST, BY VALUE, BEFORE ANY CODE. `wz-ap-demo --config <stock config>` was run against the unchanged tree and produced output BYTE-IDENTICAL to `wz-ap-demo --totally-unknown-flag xyz`: the flag was not rejected, it was ignored. The same file handed to a real zenohd was honoured (`ss` showed the process LISTENing on the port the file named, and its resolved-config dump carried the mode, the endpoint and the scouting flag). So the gap was not "wz reads it differently", it was "the file is an input to nothing".

THE DESIGN WAS CHANGED BY THE WITNESS, NOT CONFIRMED BY IT. The first cut accepted an unmodelled key and reported it; the first run of the foreign leg failed with zenohd's own refusal ("unknown field `link_unknown_to_wz`, expected one of `unicast`, `multicast`, `link`, `shared_memory`, `auth`", commons/zenoh-config/src/lib.rs:1277). That is the round's sharpest measurement: wz was the more permissive of the two on exactly the axis where permissiveness costs the operator a silently-unapplied setting. The boundary was moved to match, and `a_config_key_zenohd_refuses_is_one_wz_refuses_too` now pins both halves against one file.

FOUR FOREIGN LEGS, ALL BY EXECUTION AGAINST A REAL zenohd 1.5.0. (1) the differential oracle -- one hand-written JSON5 file, both implementations resolve it, thirteen honoured keys compared value by value at the same paths, plus the fourteenth (`connect/endpoints`) asserted EMPTY on both sides so a reader that invented a value fails as surely as one that dropped one; (2) the census; (3) the acceptance boundary; (4) the drop-in, `wz-ap-demo --config` and nothing else, dialling a port that exists in no argv and no default. zenohd's own resolved config is parsed with WZ'S OWN JSON5 reader, which is deliberate rather than convenient: the parser has to survive a document it did not write, emitted by the implementation being replaced.

FOUR DAMAGE PROBES, EACH REDDING ONLY ITS OWN CLAIM, ALL COUNTS MEASURED. Dropping `connect/endpoints` from the ingest reds ONLY the drop-in leg -- and it does so at 20.24s, the full deadline, which is the measurement that the 0.26s green run was a real session rather than a fast lie. Round 1881.decision_summary: R311y842 taught wz to READ the stock zenoh config an operator already has, and its own report called all fourteen keys it ingests "honoured" -- a statement true about the reader and false about the node, because eight of the fourteen were read and then DROPPED at the demo boundary. That is a worse position than not reading them: the report is the surface an operator checks, so `--config z.json5: honoured [..., "transport/link/tx/lease"]` printed by a node that goes on to announce its own hard-coded ten-second lease is a silent misconfiguration wearing a confirmation. The round measured the claim before acting on it and found the carry that named it PARTLY WRONG: the carry said "the demo has no flag for them", and `--compression`, `--no-admin-read`, `--config-queryable`, `--config-writable` and `--config-write-permit` were all already there, so five of the eight needed a mapping rather than a feature. Six now reach behaviour -- compression and the three adminspace keys through flags that existed, and `transport/link/tx/batch_size` / `transport/link/tx/lease` through two new ones, which are the two that reach the WIRE: they are InitSyn and OpenSyn fields, so a dropped one is not a setting that failed to apply but a value the peer is TOLD and the operator was not. `demo_session_init_params` carried them as literals (65535 / 10_000) and now takes a `TransportTuning` threaded through all five run modes. The remaining two are NAMED rather than fixed: `scouting/multicast/enabled` is reachability and the demo's `--scout` is a role, so mapping one onto the other would rewrite the operator's topology, and `timestamping/enabled` has no sink at all (`Timestamp` does not occur under `wz-ap-demo/src/`). The gate that keeps the two halves together is a CONTROL/VARIANT table over every honoured key: a key whose expansion changes nothing must be named in `CONFIG_KEYS_THE_DEMO_DROPS`, and the table is coverage-checked against `HONOURED_CONFIG_KEYS` in both directions, so a fifteenth honoured key cannot be added without stating what the demo does with it. Because an argv gate alone would go green on a flag the binary does not parse, a second test follows the file through `TransportTuning::from_argv` -- the same call `main` makes -- into the params the node announces, with a no-config control in the same test; and the drop-in e2e leg, whose wz-side config had carried only an endpoint, now carries the two wire values and the compression offer, so a REAL zenohd adjudicates them. The round also paid off the hosted red the previous push left: Layer Z opens by building the demo with a large feature set, rebuilds it twice mid-lane, and RESTATES the opening list verbatim to restore it -- and R311y842 added `zenoh-config` to the opening line only. The restore line's own comment had predicted exactly this ("a drift between the two lines would be silent"); the prediction was correct and was not a gate, and Layer C0f now compares the first and last feature sets in that lane mechanically.

carry_forward_bullets: THE UNHONOURED LIST IS STILL TWO KINDS UNDER ONE NAME, AND NOTHING SEPARATES THEM. This round moved ten keys wz could already act on; 87 remain and the list's doc still says only "wz models the subset it can act on". Nobody has swept the remaining 87 for the same defect, and the sweep is cheap and mechanical in the way this round's was not: cross the unhonoured keys against the demo's flag surface and against `WzConfig`'s fields. `connect/retry` is the strongest known candidate — `--connect-retry <init_ms>,<max_ms>,<factor>` exists and `WzConfig::connect_retry` is a `RetryPolicy` carrying exactly zenoh's three — and it was DEFERRED here for a reason worth stating: it is an opaque SUBTREE that resolves as one `null` leaf when unset, so honouring it changes what the census's own denominator counts (R311y842 measured that filling a subtree pushes leaves down under it). It needs the honoured-key matcher to handle a subtree, which is a different shape from the ten here.

A DRAFT OF THIS CARRY CLAIMED FOUR FLAGS WERE FEATURE-GATED AND THE MEASUREMENT REFUTED IT, which is worth recording because it is the class R311y841 and R311y843 both named. The draft said `--namespace`, `--shm`, `--multicast-qos` and `--interest-timeout` all sit behind cargo features; reading the parse sites showed `--shm` and `--namespace` are parsed unconditionally, and the other two are handled by the precondition work this round did. The draft was written from a "nearest preceding `#[cfg]`" grep, which is proximity rather than scope — a filter that answers a question next to the one asked. Nothing in this tree checks a carry bullet against the tree, and this is now the third instance in four rounds.

WHAT THE ROUND DID NOT CLOSE ON THAT AXIS: the demo still ignores an unknown flag silently (unregistered debt 213). A build compiled without a feature no longer receives the flag at all, because the expansion withholds it — so the reported-but-not-applied case is now a WITHHELD case, which is honest in the argv and still invisible in the `honoured` line the operator reads (unregistered debt 208, unchanged and now carrying more keys).

THE TWO IMPLEMENTATIONS DISAGREE ON A DEFAULT AND ONLY ONE SIDE IS WRITTEN DOWN. `transport/shared_memory/enabled` resolves to `true` on a real zenohd and wz's `--shm` is opt-in. The struct carries zenoh's default so the FILE reads correctly, and the expansion acts only on a named value so no invocation changes — but a wz node started with no config at all still differs from a zenoh node started with no config at all, on a transport capability. Whether wz should default SHM on is a decision no round has taken, and the census cannot raise it: it compares a file's values, not two implementations' silences.

THE ORACLE COMPARES VALUES AND NOT EFFECTS. All 24 keys agree between wz's read and zenohd's resolved tree, which establishes that wz read the file the way zenoh does. It does not establish that wz then DOES what the value says — `queries_default_timeout` reaching `--query-timeout-ms` is checked as an argv string, and only `id` and `namespace` are checked as far as a demo that parses them and opens a session. The ten have no equivalent of the wire assertion R311y843 built for `batch_size`/`lease`, and for several of them (a TLS path, a scouting budget) the effect is only observable in a scenario no leg stages.

THE `metadata` SUBTREE IS THE OTHER SHAPE THE CENSUS CANNOT HOLD. The oracle's fixture carries `metadata: { name: 'strawberry' }` and the ingest reports `metadata/name`, while the census denominator has `metadata` — the same subtree effect that makes `connect/retry` awkward. It is handled today by the census using a config that fills nothing in, which is correct and is also a limit: the denominator is the surface of an EMPTY config, and an operator's real file has a larger one.

A FLAG'S PRECONDITION IS A FACT ABOUT THE BINARY THAT NOTHING ENUMERATES. This round found three kinds by tripping over them one at a time — a cargo feature, a sibling flag, an endpoint scheme — and each was found by running the demo, not by reading it. The list in the expansion is now correct for the twenty-four keys mapped today and there is no gate that DERIVES it: a twenty-fifth mapping whose flag rejects on some fourth condition would be caught only if the drop-in leg happens to stage that condition. What would derive it is a reader over `main.rs` that collects every `requires` rejection and the flag it guards, and compares that set against what the expansion can emit.

THE DROP-IN GATE COVERS ONE INVOCATION, NOT THE SPACE OF THEM. It stages a connecting client on tcp with `--publish`. A key applicable only to a listening node, a `tls/` link, a `--query` invocation or a `--scout` one is named in the fixture and its flag is WITHHELD there, so the leg proves the withholding does not break the node and proves nothing about the flag being right when it IS emitted. The census unit fixtures supply those preconditions, but they check the argv string rather than the binary.

R311y842 built the only gate in this tree that starts from UPSTREAM — a real zenohd's own resolved config, 111 leaf keys obtained by execution — and reported that wz honours 14 of them and names the other 97 in a pinned SET whose doc says "These are not defects. wz models the topology-and-transport subset it can act on." That sentence turned out to be two sentences wearing one coat: "wz cannot do this" and "the reader has not been taught this", and the list did not distinguish them. Ten of the 97 are the second kind. Every one has had a wz-ap-demo flag for rounds — `id` is `--zid`, `namespace` is `--namespace`, `queries_default_timeout` is `--query-timeout-ms`, `routing/interests/timeout` is `--interest-timeout` (whose parse site NAMES that upstream key in its own comment), `scouting/timeout` is `--scout-timeout-ms`, `transport/multicast/qos/enabled` is `--multicast-qos`, `transport/shared_memory/enabled` is `--shm`, and the three TLS paths are `--tls-ca` / `--tls-cert` / `--tls-key` — so an operator could get the behaviour by typing it and not by handing over the file they already have, which is the whole of what "drop-in" means. The census is now 24 of 111. The round was driven RED-FIRST by the gate R311y843 built one round earlier: promoting the ten to `HONOURED_CONFIG_KEYS` before implementing anything made `every_key_the_reader_calls_honoured_reaches_the_demo_or_is_named_as_dropped` fail naming exactly those ten, and `every_honoured_key_is_actually_read` demand a per-key fixture for each — so the work list came out of a gate rather than out of a reading. Upstream's own defaults were taken the same way R311y842 took the surface, by EXECUTION rather than from `DEFAULT_CONFIG.json5`: five of the ten resolve to `null` on a running zenohd (so they are modelled `Option`, and `to_json5` omits them rather than asserting a default zenoh does not have), `transport/multicast/qos/enabled` resolves to `false`, and `transport/shared_memory/enabled` resolves to **`true`** — where wz's `--shm` is opt-in, a divergence in DEFAULT that the field records and the expansion sidesteps by acting only on a value the document named. Both directions are adjudicated by a real zenohd over all twenty-four keys: the differential oracle compares wz's read against zenohd's resolved tree key by key, and the emit leg's fixture now sets all ten so `to_json5`'s new branches are read back by the same binary. That emit work found the shape it had to avoid by being told: a first cut of the reader's twin emitted a second top-level `"transport"` object, and zenohd refuses a DUPLICATE field as flatly as an unknown one — which is also how a doubled `queries_default_timeout` in the oracle's own fixture was caught, by zenohd refusing to start rather than by review.

The round's sharpest finding was its own regression, and it was found by RUNNING the binary rather than by any gate. Four of the ten flags exit(2) when a precondition is unmet -- `--scout-timeout-ms requires --scout`, `--query-timeout-ms requires --query`, and `--interest-timeout` / `--multicast-qos` each requiring a cargo feature -- and a fifth precondition surfaced later still: `--tls-ca` opens its file EAGERLY, so a `tcp/` connect whose config merely carried a CA path died with `No such file or directory (os error 2)`. Those rejections are right for a HAND-TYPED flag, where silence would lose an instruction the operator gave directly. They are wrong for a key arriving inside a file full of keys wz cannot all act on: the first cut turned a VALID stock zenoh config into a node that refuses to start, which is strictly worse than the "reported and ignored" it replaced and is the exact failure this whole axis exists to remove. The expansion now withholds a flag whose precondition is unmet -- a cargo feature, a sibling flag on the command line, or the endpoint SCHEME -- and the drop-in e2e leg was widened to name every honoured key a connecting client can carry, so the class has a gate that runs the real binary instead of only the string the expansion builds.

Round 1883.decision_summary:
R311y844 closed ten keys of the shape "wz already does this, the reader was
never taught it" and read the remaining 87 as the other kind — things wz
cannot do. Three of them were not. `scouting/multicast/address`,
`scouting/multicast/interface` and `scouting/multicast/ttl` are the same
class as y844's ten, in its sharpest form yet, and the sharpness is worth
stating precisely: the socket layer has taken the group, the interface and
the TTL as PARAMETERS since R311y454 (`UdpDriver::bind_multicast_v4(group,
port, McastSocketConfig { iface, ttl, .. })`), so wz could always have joined
another group. What it could not do was be TOLD to. `wz-ap-demo`'s
`SCOUT_GROUP` was `Ipv4Addr::new(224, 0, 0, 224)` compiled in, and the doc
above that constant named this very upstream key while reasoning "Not a CLI
knob: an address the peers do not share discovers nothing, and zenoh exposes
the override in its config, not its scouting API." That was right about where
the knob belongs and wrong about the consequence, because wz's config reader
could not reach it either — so the sentence closed the question instead of
opening it, which is debt-47's shape (a comment read as a judgement, halting
the next investigation).

Why these three ahead of the other 84: a node that cannot be told where to
look is not merely missing a setting, it cannot JOIN a network whose scouting
group has moved. Discovery is the first thing that has to work for a drop-in,
and every other capability is downstream of it. The competing candidate,
`connect/retry/*`, was measured and set aside honestly rather than silently:
`RetryPolicy` already ports upstream's 1000/4000/x2 faithfully and
`WzConfig::connect_retry` is wired to `RedialSchedule`, but its only sink sits
in the `--router-hat` arm behind a non-default feature, so its blast radius is
narrower than a scouting socket every mode uses.

The surface total does not move. All three are resolved leaves of a real
zenohd, so this is a MOVE between the two halves of the partition rather than
a widening of it: 111 stays 111, and the census goes 24 -> 27 honoured.

Upstream's shapes were taken by reading the types that ship, not the comments
in `DEFAULT_CONFIG.json5`: `address` is a `SocketAddr`
(`ScoutingMulticastConf`, zenoh-config/src/lib.rs:500), NOT a locator string,
so `udp/224.0.0.224:7446` is not what the key carries and a value without a
port is one zenoh itself refuses. wz refuses it too, at both boundaries, and
the reason is not tidiness: the failure mode of accepting `"224.0.0.99"` is a
node that starts, prints the key among its honoured ones, and is alone.

Round 1884.decision_summary:
R311y846 closed the half R311y843's carry named and could not take: wz can now
be FOUND. Every scouting path wz had was an initiator — active asks and dials,
static bypasses the ask, and even the deferred "passive" mode of §2.4.2 is an
asker that re-asks on a period. Nothing in the tree ever ANSWERED a Scout, so a
stock zenoh peer running its default `scouting/multicast/listen: true` could not
discover a wz node at all; it had to be handed `connect/endpoints`. For a
drop-in replacement that is the wrong way round, because the thing a drop-in
must not require is that the existing network be reconfigured.

Why this ahead of the other 84 PARTIAL atoms: y843 argued discovery is the first
thing that has to work and everything else is downstream of it, then closed only
the arm where wz is the one looking. A node that can find peers but cannot be
found participates in exactly the topologies someone configured by hand — which
is the state the config axis has been measuring its way out of for four rounds.

THE VOCABULARY WAS PART OF THE DEFECT, and this is debt-47's shape one level up
from a stale line number. The inventory row `scouting-passive` read
"beyond-zenoh/pico -- neither has a passive (listen-only) scouting mode". The
first half is true of wz's passive mode (a periodic re-scout with a Cooldown
dwell, §2.2) and the parenthetical is false of zenoh, which ships
`Runtime::responder` and turns it on by default. One row carried both claims, so
"answering a Scout" had no name in the mode enum, no atom, and no sink for the
upstream key — and every reading of that row said the axis was ahead of
upstream rather than behind it. The row is corrected in place (a reason is
current state, not ledger) and the answering arm registered as its own atom.

The responder is NOT a state machine, and that is a design conclusion rather
than a shortcut. One datagram in, at most one out, nothing carried between them;
upstream's own `responder` is a bare loop around `recv_from` with no state
(orchestrator.rs:1112-1191). The scouting FSM exists because the INITIATOR has
states worth naming. So the decision is a pure function in wz-session-core and
the socket loop is the runtime's — the same IO split `scouting_glue` documents,
earning the same two things: the gates are testable without a multicast route,
and the reasons for NOT answering are values rather than log lines.

Three gates, each taken from upstream by reading it: it must be a Scout
(:1154 — answering a Hello turns one question into a storm), `what` must include
our role (:1155, and a client scouting for routers must not be handed a peer's
Hello), and it must not be our own echo. The third diverges in MECHANISM and the
divergence is forced: upstream compares source addresses because it sends scouts
from a different socket than it listens on, while wz's `bind_multicast_v4` does
both and sets IP_MULTICAST_LOOP. The gate here is the ZID — and the obvious
cheap alternative was measured and rejected rather than shipped, because
"refuse a datagram whose source port is the group port" would refuse a second wz
NODE scouting from its own group socket, which is the wz-to-wz discovery this
exists to enable.

The reply is UNICAST to the asker (:1168), not to the group, and the loopback
e2e's scouter socket deliberately never joins the group so that its receive
SUCCEEDING is the proof of that rather than a liveness check.
verification_bullets: THE FOREIGN WITNESS, and it is the whole claim in one line: a stock zenohd, its
argv carrying `--cfg mode:"peer"` and its own listener and NOT ONE reference to
wz, discovers a wz peer and opens a session to it.
`cargo test -p wz-integration-tests --test zenohd_scouts_wz_interop -- --ignored`
= 1 passed. wz binds `tcp/127.0.0.1:0`, so the KERNEL picks the port and the only
path from that number to zenohd's dialer is the Hello wz put on the group.
MEASURED BY DAMAGE, NOT ASSUMED: with the responder moved to another socket the
run produces no SCOUT ANSWERED and no face at all.
THE FIRST DAMAGE PROBE WAS INVALID AND SAYING SO IS THE POINT. Moving only the
GROUP (224.0.0.225:7446) still answered every scout, because Linux
IP_MULTICAST_ALL delivers by PORT to a wildcard-bound socket regardless of which
group it joined — the same property this tree already records for the
`locator-iface` pin. Only moving the PORT is a discriminator, and that is the
probe whose silence is quoted above.
AND THE POSITIVE RUN READ WRONG TWICE BEFORE IT READ TRUE. It passed in 0.10s
against a leftover wz peer from an earlier manual run, then failed for 30s
against the same leftover: zenoh dedupes scouted peers by ZID
(orchestrator.rs:1032-1050), so a fixed `--zid` makes a second node carrying it
get "Already connected scouted peer" and never be dialed. The test now derives
its zid per process, the barriers print their elapsed times, and the face
assertion reads the LINE's zid and requires 32 hex chars — a zenohd's 16-byte
ZenohIdProto — so another wz node can no longer stand in for the foreign witness.
`cargo test -p wz-session-core --features codec-scout,codec-hello --lib
scout_responder` = 8 passed. Each gate has BOTH arms on ONE identity, so a
responder that answered everything fails: `what` = CLIENT and ROUTER are refused
where PEER is answered, and the same masks against a ROUTER identity flip the
verdict, which is what proves the gate reads OUR role and not a constant. The
self-echo case carries `ROUTER|PEER`, a mask that INCLUDES our role, so it passes
gate 2 and is refused only for being ours. The wire layout is pinned against
upstream's WRITER (`zenoh-codec` scouting/hello.rs:52-66), not against our own
reader, because a round trip through one codec cannot catch a field order both
halves share.
`cargo test -p wz-runtime-tokio --features scouting-responder --test
scouting_responder_multicast -- --ignored` = 2 passed over real group sockets.
The scouter never joins the group, so its recv SUCCEEDING is the unicast proof.

coverage table driving `listen` to `false` (the NON-default) so a reader that
hardcoded "always answer" fails there rather than reporting the key honoured.

Round 1885.decision_summary:
R311y847 pays off the hosted red the pre-push hook refused to let R311y846
publish over, and it is filed separately because it is a DIFFERENT round's debt
that happened to land on this round's axis.

Run 32097227053 on commit 761c9557 failed one step, Layer Z, on one assertion:
`wz_reads_a_stock_zenohd_config.rs:565` — "the drop-in fixture must name every
honoured key a connecting client can carry". R311y845 moved three keys into
`HONOURED_CONFIG_KEYS` (`scouting/multicast/{address,interface,ttl}`) and did not
add them to that fixture, so the coverage assertion that exists to stop the gate
narrowing is what caught it. It caught exactly what it was built for.

The reason this is not an ack-and-defer: R311y846 adds a FOURTH key to the same
list, so the same assertion would have failed again for a second reason, and the
standing rule's "read it, then decide whether it is your axis" resolves to yes.
Acking would have published a change that widened an already-red gate.

The fix is the fixture, not the gate. All four keys are named there now, and the
choice of values is the substance: each is upstream's own default and
`listen: false` matches the `enabled: false` already in that document, because
this leg's node is a CLIENT that dials an endpoint and must be on the group in
neither direction. That is what makes the four keys reach nothing in this
invocation, which is the property the fixture is for — every one of them carries
a command-line precondition this node does not meet, so an expansion that emitted
any of them would hand a valid operator config to a binary that exits(2).

ON, and the pre-push hook's build is not that build. R311y845 learned
the same class from the other side (verified only with features on,
missed the arm where off) and the SAME round then shipped this face of
it. Two faces, five days, no gate that sees either: C1bf exists and
caught it, but only on hosted, one push later. The cheap local form is
to run C1bf's own loop over the hazard class before pushing a change
that adds a `#[cfg(feature)] pub` field -- the audit inside C1bf
already computes that class mechanically, so the input exists.
2. The freshness lint's own message offers a branch ("raise the carried
number") that is WRONG for a fixture which spawns the binary, and
nothing in the gate distinguishes the two cases -- it asks the reader
to. Raising the number is always the path of least resistance and is
always available. Worth a gate that can tell "reads the path" from
"runs the binary", because the failure mode of the wrong branch is
silent: the count goes up, the lint goes green, and a stale binary
fakes a red in a foreign-interop test forever.
3. `get_best_match` is now REGISTERED (the scouting-responder residual)
but not implemented and not tested. On a multi-homed host wz answers
Scouts from the group socket's interface rather than the one nearest
the asker, so a scouter on a second subnet can receive a Hello whose
source address it cannot route back to. Single-homed CI cannot see
this; it needs a two-interface fixture, which this tree has no shape
for yet.

existed and no lane runs `domain-*` by NAME -- the A3 census is the
only thing that reads them. The other three carried census rows
(domain-routing omits 9, domain-storage 13, domain-transport 5) are

same unexamined state this one was in until a gate happened to look.

Round 1886.decision_summary:
R311y848 — the responder round shipped four reds, and each one is a
different gate saying the same thing: a feature was added to the tree
without being added to the tree's own registers.

The four are not four bugs. `scout_listen` landed as a `#[cfg(feature =
"scouting-responder")]` field on `PeerOpts`, and every register that
names the parts of this workspace had to learn it: the struct's OTHER
initialisers (two test fixtures), the domain census that says which
atoms `domain-scouting` composes, the inventory row's impl-axis tag,
and the freshness lint's count of fixtures that spawn the demo. The
round moved the code and left all four behind.

The build break is the sharpest and is the exact MIRROR of R311y845's
lesson, which that same round had already paid for. y845 learned "a
feature verified only with features ON hides the arm where it is OFF";
here the field was verified only with features OFF -- the default-feature
`cargo test -p wz-ap-demo` the pre-push hook runs does not build the
`scouting-responder` arm at all, so two initialisers missing a required
field compiled clean locally and reded on C1bf's `--all-features`. The
class is one class with two faces: a cfg-gated field is only checked by
the build that turns its cfg on, and the hook's build is not that build.

The A3 tag is a smaller error with a larger tail. The reason string was
written as prose ("The ANSWERING half...") where the gate reads the
first token as an impl-axis tag, so the atom entered the register
UNGRADED. Fixing the token exposed a SECOND A3 failure underneath it
that the tag error had been masking: `domain-scouting` did not list
`scouting-responder`, which means the aggregate feature a consumer
reaches for to get "scouting" composed everything EXCEPT being findable
-- the precise capability the round was added to provide.

The freshness lint is the one case where the gate's two branches had to
be told apart rather than obeyed. Its message offers "add the assert" or
"raise the carried number", and the second is correct only for a fixture
that merely READS the binary path. `zenohd_scouts_wz_interop` spawns it
and asserts a stock zenohd finds what it advertises, and a demo built
before this round has no `--scout-listen` at all -- so a stale binary
there does not weaken the proof, it REPRODUCES the exact red the test
exists to detect, and sends the next reader into the responder hunting
for a defect that is in the build. The assert is the answer.

carry_forward_bullets: 1. THE CLASS, and it is now worth a gate: a config-expansion precondition that
reads only the TYPED command line is blind to the role the FILE supplies.
Two keys had it — `connect/retry` (found while wiring it) and R311y846's
`scouting/multicast/listen` (found by asking the same question of a shipped
key, and it had been broken since the round that added it). Both were
invisible to every existing test because every fixture typed the role, and
the one invocation that does not is the one a drop-in performs. What would
catch the next one mechanically: for each honoured key with a role
precondition, expand the SAME file twice — once with the role typed, once
with it supplied by `mode:` — and require the same flags out. The existing
coverage table already enumerates the keys, so the input exists; nothing
iterates it that way yet.
2. `connect/timeout_ms` and `connect/exit_on_failure` remain unhonoured, and
the reason is now recorded in the list itself rather than left to be
rediscovered: wz matches their peer DEFAULTS exactly (retry forever, do not
exit), so honouring them means building a bounded give-up and a process exit
that wz has no substrate for. Their `listen/*` twins are the same shape.
That is a different debt from "the reader was never taught a key", and the
four of them are the cheapest remaining slice of the census only if someone
first decides wz should be able to give up at all.
3. The client `--reconnect` supervisor still takes NO config input. This round
deliberately routed `connect/retry` to the two arms that own a connect list,
because `retry_period.rs` declares the client supervisor's parity target as
pico's CONSTANT delay while `connect/retry` is zenoh's exponential. Feeding
the zenoh key into the pico-parity substrate is a divergence DECISION, not a
fix, and it wants stating rather than doing quietly. Until it is decided, a
`mode: "client"` operator config carrying a retry block reaches nothing —
the drop-in fixture pins that as the current answer.
4. `ZenohNodeConfig` lost `Eq` this round. Any future key carrying a float will
find the bound already gone, which is fine, but the reverse is now a trap: a
caller that WANTS `Eq` cannot get it back without dropping the float, and
nothing records that except the derive's own doc comment.
5. The census is 29 of 111 honoured. The remaining 82 are not one queue: they
split into "wz does it and the reader was not taught" (the y844 class, cheap
and this round's kind), "wz does the default and not the alternative" (item
2), and "wz has no such behaviour" (access_control, auth, plugins,
downsampling, the tx queue sizes). Nothing yet sorts them, so "82 left"
reads as one number over three very different costs.
changes_bullets: 1. crates/wz-ap-demo/src/args.rs — `parse_connect_retry`'s gate widened from
`router-hat-router` to `any(router-hat-router, routing-peer)`, the UNION of
its consumers (the R311y845 rule: cfg on the consumer set, never
`allow(dead_code)`). Its `use` of `RetryPolicy` widened in the same shape —
missed on the first cut and caught by building a combination that has
`routing-peer` without `router-hat-router`, which is the same mistake one
level down. Its test module's gate widened to match.
2. crates/wz-ap-demo/src/main.rs — the `--peer` arm now runs that parse and
passes the result, aborting on a malformed value exactly as the
`--router-hat` arm does.
3. crates/wz-ap-demo/src/runner.rs — `PeerOpts::connect_retry` (not an Option,
not cfg-gated: the mesh always re-dials, so there is always a schedule), fed
to the accept loop's `retry:` AND to the peer's `WzConfig` via
`with_connect_retry`. The second is not redundant: that instance is what the
`--config-queryable` admin GET renders, and a node that ran one cadence
while REPORTING another would make the operator's own introspection confirm
the wrong answer. The false comment at the `retry:` site is replaced with
what was measured.
4. crates/wz-runtime-tokio/src/zenoh_config.rs — `connect/retry` honoured:
`ZenohNodeConfig::connect_retry: Option<RetryPolicy>` (ONE Option for the
subtree, because a running zenohd renders `retry` as a single `null` — so
`None` is exactly that null and three Options would invent a surface the
census denominator lacks), a `want_f64` reader (upstream types the factor
`f64`, so `2` and `1.5` are both valid and `want_u64` would refuse the
second), the parse merging a PARTIAL block against zenoh's own defaults,
the `to_json5` emit, and the key moved from `UNHONOURED_UPSTREAM_CONFIG_KEYS`
to `HONOURED_CONFIG_KEYS`. Census 28 -> 29 of 111.
`Eq` dropped from `ZenohNodeConfig` and `ZenohConfigIngest`, keeping
`PartialEq`: `Eq` promises reflexivity and the subtree carries a float.
`RetryPolicy` is `PartialEq`-only for that reason already, so the bound
was going to fall at whichever key first carried a real number. Nothing
keyed a map or set on either type (checked).
`HONOURED_SUBTREE_LEAVES` — the three fields inside the honoured subtree,
kept OUT of the census list and used only by the `ignored` report. An
exact-match list rather than a `starts_with` rule, decided by measurement:
a real zenohd handed `connect: { retry: { period_init_mss: 250 } }` starts
and drops the field silently, so a prefix rule would swallow the same typo.
wz does not refuse it either (that would be stricter than the acceptance
boundary the census pins) — it REPORTS it, which upstream never does.
5. crates/wz-ap-demo/src/args.rs (expansion) — `connect/retry` ->
`--connect-retry <init>,<max>,<factor>`, emitted only for a run mode that
owns a connect list, and the precondition checks the command line AND
`added` (the drop-in fix above). The value is re-parsed by
`parse_connect_retry` downstream on purpose, so a file reaches the same
acceptance boundary a command line does and the policy lives in one place.
The identical `rest`-only bug in R311y846's `listen_expanded` is fixed the
same way.

`a_partial_connect_retry_block_fills_the_rest_from_zenoh_defaults` (an
unstated ceiling must not become 0, which is a hot loop);
`a_typo_inside_the_retry_block_is_reported_rather_than_absorbed`;

`the_retry_schedule_reaches_only_the_modes_that_own_a_connect_list`
(including the drop-in case, which FAILED when first written);
`being_findable_survives_a_config_that_supplies_the_role_itself` (R311y846's
key, which also FAILED when first written).
7. crates/wz-integration-tests/tests/wz_reads_a_stock_zenohd_config.rs — LEG 5,
`the_retry_schedule_a_stock_config_carries_is_the_one_the_node_runs`: two
runs of the demo from stock config files differing in ONE block, compared by
how often each re-dials a dead port. The first four legs stop at the
boundary — they show wz READ the value — and this is the one that shows the

to the drop-in fixture (which must name every honoured key) and to the two
coverage tables the demo's expansion gate compares against.
8. scripts/run-ci.sh — Layer Z's guard for that file raised 4 -> 5. It is an

Round 1887.decision_summary:
R311y849 — a peer that could be told how fast to reconnect, by a file, and
two capabilities that were unreachable from the only invocation a drop-in
actually performs.

The round started at the config census, which is the one open BREADTH axis
whose denominator comes from running the upstream binary rather than from
wz's own atoms. `connect/retry` was in the unhonoured half. What made it
worth taking before its 82 siblings is that a deployment's answer to every
restart is a reconnect: routers go down, and the operator who widened
`period_max_ms` because their router boots slowly gets 1s/2s/4s from wz with
nothing logged to contradict them. Discovery has to work for a drop-in
(R311y846); so does the pacing of the thing a network does after discovery.

Measured first, because "wz already does this" was the expected shape and it
was only two thirds true. A peer dialling a dead port re-dialled at 1s, 2s,
4s and connected the moment a listener appeared — so the SCHEDULE was right
and matched zenoh's defaults exactly. Then `--connect-retry 300,300,1` on
that same peer produced 1s and 2s: the flag was accepted and dropped.
`--connect-retry banana` did not refuse either, which is the sharper half —
the parser documents "a malformed value is REFUSED, never degraded to the
default", and the arm that dials never called it.

The cause was a COMMENT. `runner.rs:3768` read "a peer node parses no
`--connect-retry` (the flag belongs to `--router-hat`, the run-mode that owns
a connect list)", and its premise was simply false: `--peer <addr>` binds AND
dials every `--connect`, takes a comma-separated list, and paces its re-dials
by that very field. This is the R311y838 shape and this round is its second
instance — a divergence written down as a decision, which stops the next
reader from investigating. R311y838's lesson said code comments are read as
judgements; here the judgement also named the wrong subject, and the gate that
would have caught it (the flag's own parser) was cfg'd out of the arm that
needed it.

Then the wiring exposed a second, worse defect, and it was NOT the one being
looked for. The expansion's precondition asked whether `--peer` was on the
command line. But when the operator names no role, the FILE supplies it, and
that `--peer` is pushed into `added`, never into `rest`. So the schedule would
have been honoured for everyone EXCEPT `wz-ap-demo --config their.json5` and
nothing else — the single invocation the whole config path exists for. Asking
the same question of R311y846's key returned the same answer: a drop-in config
carrying `scouting/multicast/listen: true` came up with no `--scout-listen`,
so the node that round made findable was invisible on precisely the path that

Round 1889.decision_summary:
R311y851 — wz exports its dissection through TWO consumption surfaces, they
carry different halves of it, and the half a product LINKS was the thinner
one. The four analysis planes now cross the C ABI.

The state, measured rather than recalled. `wz-analyze` — the command line, a
person at a terminal — reaches the keyexpr plane, the node plane, the query
plane and the payload plane. `wz-capi-dissect` — the C ABI a framework links
against — exported five functions, and between them they answered one
question: what the TRANSPORT did. Per-flow frame counts, the health
counters, and one message's field tree if the caller already had its bytes.
Which keys carry the traffic, who the participants are by zid, whether a
query was ever answered and how fast, what the samples declare: none of it
had a symbol.

None of it was missing from the library either, and that is the part worth
naming. `wz-capture` is `wz-capi-dissect`'s own dependency, so all four
planes were compiled into every build of that cdylib. This is the same class
as an atom compiled into a preset with no flag to reach it — R311y846's
`--scout-listen` and R311y850's `preset-ap-full` are the two most recent —
and it stood because there is a gate that compares the demo's features to
the registry and NOTHING that compares wz's two analysis surfaces to each
other. A capability a consumer cannot call is one it does not have.

The emit went into `wz-capture`, beside the types, and not into either
consumer. Two consumers each rendering their own view of the same table is
how the surfaces came to disagree in the first place; one document beside
the planes is what a third consumer reaches instead of writing a fourth
rendering. It is hand-rolled for the same reason the summary beside it is —
this crate commits to zero third-party dependencies and that ABI commits to
not forcing a JSON dependency on its caller — and it escapes through the
workspace's one escaper, because a keyexpr and a locator are both bytes a
peer chose.

`null` and an empty table are kept apart, on the rule `exchange`'s own doc
already states: a plane that cannot be fed is ABSENT rather than empty. The
query and payload planes need the network codecs to have any record to
correlate, so in a build without them the two keys answer `null`. Emitting
`{"rows":[]}` there would tell a reader this capture held no queries, which
is a claim about the capture made on the evidence of the build.

One thing found on the way and fixed here rather than deferred: Layer C0 has
been red on hosted CI since R311y849, because that round's LEG 5 lives in a
`zenohd`-family fixture and its function name does not carry the token
libtest's `--skip` matches. That red is the FIRST step of the
`validate + verify + test` job and it had skipped 35 layers behind it,
`cargo test --workspace` and `cargo clippy --deny warnings` among them. It
is one round's own debt and it is repaired here for a reason specific to
this round: pushing on top of it would have made THIS change's workspace
verification unreadable in exactly the same way.

carry_forward_bullets: 1. THE PRODUCT DEFECT IS OPEN and it is on the replacement axis, not a
gate's: a wz peer without `router-connect-reconcile` dials each configured
address once and never again, while rendering zenoh's retry schedule in its
own admin config. `preset-ap-client` is such a build. Upstream retries
forever by default for every mode with a connect list, so a drop-in whose
router restarts does not come back. Registered as
`debt-peer-redial-behind-a-router-feature`. The fix is a decision about which
feature owns the peer re-dial -- the capability is misnamed rather than
miscoded -- and it moves the A5 preset census, the domain census and the
footprint lanes with it.
2. A test that asserts a BEHAVIOUR gets its feature guard; a test that
asserts a behaviour's SCHEDULE did not. The two guards this helper already
had catch a build that cannot read the config or cannot run a peer. The third
kind -- a build that runs the peer and cannot re-dial -- was invisible because
the leg's own vacuity assertion produced a plausible complaint. That is the
[[feedback_a_red_test_can_be_the_test_asserting_a_behaviour_upstream_lacks]]
class pointed inward: the behaviour was missing from OUR build, not from
upstream, and nothing enumerates which features a leg's assertions actually
need. The `#[ignore]` reason is where a human writes it and nothing reads it.
3. R311y849 measured this leg's arms with a demo it had built for a wider
feature set than the lane builds, and recorded the numbers as the leg's. Both
statements were true and they were about different binaries. Worth a habit
rather than a gate: when a probe's number becomes a test's expectation, the
probe should be re-run at the LANE's feature set before the round closes --
the lane's build command is in run-ci.sh and can simply be pasted.

Round 1890.decision_summary:
R311y852 — a wz peer dials each configured address ONCE and never again, and
the leg that would have said so blamed the wrong subject.

Layer Z has been red since R311y849 on that round's own LEG 5, the leg whose
whole point is that an honoured config value CHANGES what the process does.
Its control arm — a stock config with the `connect.retry` block deleted, so
zenoh's own 1s/4s/2.0 applies — produced ONE dial attempt in six seconds
where three were expected, and the leg's vacuity guard called that "a node
that did not run".

The first hypothesis was timing, and it was wrong. A window timed from
`spawn` spends the process's startup, and a loaded CI runner has more of that
than a dev box; the leg now opens its window on the FIRST dial and prints how
long startup took. That is a real improvement and it did not fix anything:
the measurement came back "first dial after ~50ms" and still one attempt.

What is actually true, measured at Layer Z's own feature set on this host: a
wz peer does not re-dial AT ALL. The loop that reconciles a desired peer is
built under `any(router-connect-reconcile, transport-multilink)`
(`accept_loop.rs:1645-1659`), and only the first of those reconciles a peer
that never connected — `transport-multilink` paces link RE-ADDS for an
aggregated session. Layer Z's demo build had the second and not the first, so
the schedule was discarded at `let _ = retry;`. Control: 1 attempt. Same
binary rebuilt with `router-connect-reconcile`: 3. `--connect-retry
300,300,1` on the build without it: also 1, which is what settles it — the
cadence was not being paced wrongly, there was no re-dial to pace.

This is a REPLACEMENT gap, not a lane problem, and the round says so rather
than closing it quietly. Upstream's `peer_connector_retry` retries forever by
default for every mode that owns a connect list. wz's `preset-ap-client` — a
peer, the tier a drop-in would use — dials once and gives up, while its admin
config renders zenoh's retry schedule, so introspection confirms a cadence
the node does not run. An operator whose router restarts gets a peer that
never comes back. `preset-ap-full` carries the feature and is unaffected.

Fixing THAT means deciding which feature owns a peer's re-dial. The
capability is misnamed rather than miscoded — it is `router-*` and every mode
with a connect list needs it — and renaming or re-gating an atom moves the
A5 preset census, the domain census and the footprint lanes with it. That is
a round, and it is registered as one (`debt-peer-redial-behind-a-router-
feature`) rather than improvised at the end of this one.

What this round does instead is make the two things that were LYING tell the
truth: the lane now builds a demo that can re-dial, and the leg refuses to
report a number when it cannot. The demo prints its own feature set, so the
guard reads the build rather than assuming it — the same shape the two
guards already in that function take for `zenoh-config` and `routing-peer`,
and the reason those two never cost a round to attribute.
