Round 1892.decision_summary:
R311y854 — the selector reaches the linked surface, and the surface delta stops
being a paragraph in a memory file and becomes a gate.

Two halves, and the second is the one that lasts.

THE CAPABILITY. `wz-analyze --select` has narrowed the census planes since
R311y616 — a three-valued predicate over records, with terms a person types
(`key`, `kind`, `bytes`, `time`, `delay`) — and the C ABI a framework links
could only ever ask for the whole capture. `wz_dissect_pcap_census_where` takes
that expression, and everything under it was already public on `wz-capture`
(`Filter::parse`, `aggregate_where`, `exchanges_where`, `payloads_where`), so
this is another instance of the class R311y851 measured: compiled in, no symbol.

Three planes narrow and the node plane does not, because a node is not a record
the selector's terms describe — the same choice the command line makes. The
document now SAYS which, per plane, rather than leaving a consumer to infer it
from surviving rows. That inference is the one way to read this wrong: a
narrowed census whose node plane still holds every zid looks like a filter that
did nothing. Each narrowed plane also carries `selection` — matched, rejected,
and UNDECIDED — because a keyexpr whose declaration went past before the tap
started cannot be judged, and a consumer that could not see that count would
read a short total as a whole one.

A malformed selector gets its OWN code rather than `INVALID_ARG`, because the
two are answered by different people: a null pointer is the caller's bug and a
selector is text an operator typed. The position comes from a second symbol,
`wz_dissect_selector_diagnose`, which compiles an expression WITHOUT a capture
and returns `{"ok":false,"at":N,"message":…}`. That is a separate call on
purpose: it keeps the memory rule uniform (OK means a string, an error means
none, with no exception to remember), and the moment a UI needs the answer is
while the expression is being typed — before there is a capture to run it
against, and long before anyone would pay four walks of a file to find out.

THE GATE. `scripts/lib/analysis_surface_parity.py`, in Layer C0. It pins which
surface reaches each analysis capability and fails in both directions: a row
whose flag or symbol no longer exists is stale, and a flag or symbol no row
names is a capability nobody said which surfaces reach. It is the same shape as
`apfull_membership.py` deliberately — that gate is why an atom compiled into a
preset with no flag to reach it is found in one round instead of six, and the
surface delta is the same class with no gate.

What it does NOT check is symmetry, and that is the design rather than a
weakness. A key log is a file path a person supplies; a bounded read is a
statement about a C caller's memory. Forcing both surfaces to hold everything
would be a worse contract than the asymmetric one. So every one-sided row
carries a REASON, and a reason that reads "OPEN DEBT" is exactly a debt this
file makes visible instead of hiding. Three of them do today.

Its first reading, which is the first time this delta has been a measurement:
8 capabilities on both surfaces, 9 CLI-only, 6 ABI-only, 3 of those open.

Round 1893.decision_summary:
R311y855 — the walk this ABI's own header has described since R311y586, and
could not perform.

`wz_dissect_pcap_summary`'s doc says it plainly: "A consumer walks the flows
here, then calls `wz_dissect_transport_message` per message it wants expanded."
Every part of that sentence was false in practice. The summary reports per-flow
frame COUNTS, so there is nothing to enumerate messages by — and a coordinate
would not have rescued it either, which is the part worth stating because it
determined the design. A stream message's bytes live in the REASSEMBLED
per-direction stream. That stream exists only inside this library; the capture
file the caller handed in does not contain the message contiguously. So no
amount of reporting offsets would have let a C consumer slice one out. The
instruction named a two-step walk whose first step this surface never had, and
whose second step it could not have supplied.

The fix therefore had to be: do the walk where the reassembly is, and hand back
the trees. `wz_dissect_pcap_fields` does that, over BOTH halves, bounded per
flow.

Three properties are load-bearing and each of them is a place a thinner
implementation would have been wrong.

ONE COORDINATE SPACE, NAMED ON THE ROW. Spans inside a tree are
message-relative; where the message sits is on the row. The two producers put
different KINDS of number there — a stream row's `message_at` is a byte offset
into the retained stream, so a span added to it is a capture coordinate, while
a datagram row's `packet` is an index and adding a span to it is meaningless.
They are small numbers all round and cannot be told apart by inspection, so
`offset_space` says which.

A ROW IS A TREE OR A NAMED REFUSAL. The walk is checked against the passive
session that framed the message, and a disagreement produces `declined` with
the reason instead of a tree. This is the guarantee that must not be lost in
carrying the field layer to a second surface: R311y687 found a live misread
with it — a batched unit's second message walked as its first — and a
confident tree about bytes nobody asked for is worse than no tree. Bytes a
bounded read trimmed decline the same way, with the reason.

BOTH HALVES. A datagram flow retains no stream, so the capture is parsed a
SECOND time and each packet re-decapsulated, and every way that second read can
disagree with the first is counted rather than skipped. This crate's own record
is why: R311y679 and the three rounds after it each added a plane that reached
the stream half and not the datagram one.

The emit went into `wz-capture` beside the types, like the census before it,
and behind a DEFAULT-OFF `dissect` feature. That gate is R311y675's decision
kept rather than reversed: the walker pulls twelve codec arms and this crate
must keep building for the MCU profiles, so an embedded consumer is not charged
for a reader only a desktop runs. The price of default-off is a module no
plain `-p wz-capture` build compiles, which is the "lane nobody runs" hazard —
so Layer C1bn now builds that arm and pins the module's tests by name.

And the gate R311y854 built did its job on its second outing, twice. It held
the field layer as a named OPEN DEBT until this round moved it, and when the
table moved it forced the three rows to be reclassified rather than quietly
left. It also caught a defect in ITSELF, below.

Round 1894.decision_summary:
R311y856 — the payload seam reaches the surface a product LINKS, and the
decoder stops living in a binary that surface must not depend on.

R311y854's gate has said since it was written that this was open, and it is the
half that matters most: `wz-analyze --payload-format demo/**=protobuf` has
decoded application payloads since R311y699, and `wz-capi-dissect` — the C ABI a
framework links — could not decode one at all. The seam the gate's own row
pointed at, `wz_capture::payload::formats::FormatMap`, was public and in the
cdylib's dependency graph the whole time. There was nothing on that side able to
BUILD one, for a reason no amount of ABI widening would have fixed: the only
decoder this workspace ships lived in `wz-analyze`, which carries
`wz-tls-record` and through it `ring`. Linking a cdylib against a TLS
implementation to walk protobuf varints is exactly the coupling the crate seam
exists to prevent, so the door could not be opened where the debt was written
down. The decoder had to move first.

WHAT MOVED, AND WHY THE RULE THAT PUT IT THERE DID NOT COVER IT. R311y699 placed
the built-ins in the composition root on the rule that "a format decoder is
exactly the kind of thing that grows a third-party dependency", and that rule is
right. It does not describe `Protobuf`, which is a hand-written base-128 varint
walk over bytes and takes no dependency at all. So the decoder, the map's
declaration DIALECT, and the decode core (`decode_payload`, the keyexpr
resolution it needs, the run-scoped `Declarations` ledger) now sit in
`wz-capture` beside the map — one implementation, neither consumer owning it,
which is the shape R311y851 settled for the census emit and R311y855 for the
field layer.

The built-ins are UNGATED where the decode core is behind `dissect`, and the
asymmetry is deliberate rather than sloppy: a decoder takes bytes and a decode
core reads a walked tree. Gating the decoder too would have been the tidier
dependency story and would have moved its five tests into a lane that
`cargo test -p wz-capture` does not run — this workspace's most-paid-for failure
shape — while buying nothing an MCU build does not already get from the linker
dropping a decoder no call site names.

ONE DIALECT, PARSED ONCE. `<keyexpr>=<format>` and `<keyexpr>:<path>=<name>`
were read by the command line's argument reader and by nothing else, so a second
surface could only have invented a second dialect — and two parsers for one
syntax disagree exactly where a deployment moves a rule out of a terminal and
into a config file. `FormatMap::declarations` already RENDERED a name
declaration in that spelling, so the canonical form existed and nothing could
read it back. `parse_declaration` is now that reader, both CLI flags go through
it, and the ABI takes a whole text of them.

TWO SYMBOLS, ABI 5 -> 6. `wz_dissect_pcap_fields_with_payloads` is the door;
`wz_dissect_declarations_diagnose` answers "is this text valid, and if not which
line" with NO capture, which is R311y854's argument for the selector arriving
for the second text a person types. A declaration this build cannot install is
REFUSED under its own code — not skipped — because a map quietly smaller than
the text that built it leaves a reader blaming the traffic for their own rule.

The JSON rendering of a decoding moved with the type, so the five-state
vocabulary a consumer branches on is written down once. That is a partial
payment on `debt-census-emit-two-renderings` rather than the widening R311y855's
carry warned this round would otherwise be.

ONE capture and never that any single arm printed something.
`fields_json::tests::a_declared_format_decodes_the_payload_and_the_spans_are_the_messages`
and `wz-capi-dissect`'s `a_declaration_reaches_the_abi_and_decodes_the_payload`

Round 1895.decision_summary:
R311y857 — the last one-sided row closes, and the row's own reason turns out to
have been wrong about what was missing.

`debt-analysis-surface-parity` had one OPEN DEBT left and it pointed the other
way from the rest: the loss and health counters, which `wz_dissect_pcap_summary`
has reported since R311y608 and which the row said the command line "has no flag
for -- capture drops, retransmits, sequence gaps, checksums, framing desyncs".

RUN RATHER THAN READ, that is mostly false. `wz-analyze --json` over a pcapng
carrying an Interface Statistics Block prints `capture_reported_drops`,
`retransmits`, `out_of_order`, `partial_overlaps`, the whole `framing` group,
the whole `sequence` group and `drops`, all unconditionally, inside the report's
`capture` object. The registry reason had outlived the code -- this workspace's
debt-47 shape, and it was found by running the binary while writing the fix the
reason asked for, not by auditing the reason.

WHAT WAS ACTUALLY MISSING IS TWO THINGS, and they are worth naming precisely
because one of them is the sharper defect:

  * `fragment_stats()` -- the fragment CHAINS (pieces, completed, expired,
    evicted, malformed, overlapping). No key of the report named any of it, so a
    reader could not tell a capture whose fragment chains never completed from
    one that carried no fragments.
  * the checksums that VERIFIED or were ABSENT. The report carries
    `ip_checksum_invalid` and `transport_checksum_invalid` and nothing else,
    which is a FAILURE COUNT WITH NO DENOMINATOR: two invalid checksums out of
    two and two out of two million read identically, and so does a capture where
    no checksum was checked at all.

THE ORDER OF OPERATIONS IS R311y856's, and it is the reason this is one round
rather than two. `health_json` lived in `wz-capi-dissect`, so adding the
command-line flag first would have shipped a second rendering of one document --
`debt-census-emit-two-renderings` widening while a parity row closed. So the emit
moved to `wz_capture::report` beside the counters it reads, the ABI now embeds
it, and `--health` is a second CONSUMER of one rendering. The two surfaces emit
the same bytes for that document, which is the strongest parity claim available:
not "both can answer" but "both answer identically".

`health_text` is beside it and is a second RENDERING rather than a second
SELECTION, which is the distinction that debt is about: both functions read the
same four accessors in the same order, so neither is free to report a figure the
other omits. What differs is only what a terminal needs -- a heading per owner,
and `not reported` where the document says `null`.

That `null` is load-bearing on both surfaces. A classic pcap has nowhere in the
format to record a drop count, so silence is not a clean bill of health, and a
reader shown `0` would believe their capture was whole on the evidence of a field
that cannot exist.

The gate now reports ZERO open rows: every surviving one-sided capability
carries a stated decision. The gate stays, which is what makes the debt closable
rather than merely quiet -- the next capability added to one surface still has to
answer "and the other?" in prose, at the row.
verification_bullets: THE MOVE IS WITNESSED BY THE TESTS THAT DID NOT CHANGE.
`wz-capi-dissect`'s `a_pcapng_reaches_the_boundary_and_carries_its_own_drop_count`
pins `"capture_reported_drops":17`,
`a_classic_pcap_reports_no_statement_rather_than_zero_drops` pins `null` AND
refuses `0`, and another pins the `dropped_by_limits` object literally. All 26
pass unchanged against the moved emit, which is the only claim that matters for
a move: the document is byte-identical.
THE DISCRIMINATOR for the new flag is
`the_two_unreachable_loss_groups_reach_the_command_line`, and it is built on the
MEASUREMENT rather than on the debt row's claim. One capture, two runs, and the
evidence is the difference on the two axes that were genuinely missing: without
the flag the output contains no `"health":`, no `ip_checksum_valid` and no
`"pieces":`; with it, all three. A build whose flag did nothing fails the second
arm; one that printed the group unconditionally fails the first. The five groups
are then each asserted present by name, so a document that lost one is not
mistaken for a capture that had nothing to report.
THE CONTROL is the classic pcap: `"health":{"capture_reported_drops":null}` and

Round 1897.decision_summary:
R311y859 — the document titled "what the dissection lost" carried every loss
except the one whose owner is this program.

R311y857 moved `health_json` beside the counters and gave the command line a
`--health` flag, under a doc heading that says the groups are ordered by WHO
LOST THE PACKET: the capture tool, this dissection's caps, and the wire. There
is a fourth owner and it had no group. A packet the decapsulator walked past is
traffic the capture holds and no row does, and the remedy for that loss is
neither a bigger ring buffer nor a raised cap — it is fixing this program.
`SkipCensus` counts nine such reasons and the health document named none of
them.

THE PROBE CAME FIRST AND IT DISCRIMINATED. Four packets, four different
reasons (ARP, ICMP over IPv4, an ethertype promising IPv4 with five bytes of it,
IPv6 whose next header is ESP). The census leg passed — the counters were
right — and the CONTROL leg passed — `CaptureReport`'s own JSON already carried
all four under `skips`. Only the health legs failed, which is what makes this a
rendering defect rather than a counting one, and the failure printed the whole
health document with nine missing reasons visible in it.

THE SHARPER HALF IS A COMMENT. Beside the one skip reason the text surface DID
name, a comment asserted that "every other skip is furniture in an
otherwise-readable capture". That is true of three of the eight. It is false of
`truncated` (a snaplen cut the packet short), of both fragment counters and of
`ip_fragment_pending` (a consumer that does not reassemble walked past bytes
that were captured), and of `ipv6_extension_chain` (ESP among them). Each of
those means BYTES THE CAPTURE HOLDS ARE ABSENT from this dissection, and a
reader who believes the comment reads a short capture as a whole one. This
workspace has measured this exact shape before — a code comment that files a
divergence as benign and stops the next investigation — and it is worse here
than in a registry reason, because a comment sits where the fix would be typed.

SO THE SPLIT IS THE FINDING AND NOT THE FORMATTING. Both renderings now carry
the nine reasons in two named classes: bytes this dissection does not hold, and
not this protocol. The judgement is encoded once, in one emit, so the two
surfaces cannot disagree about which class a reason is in.

ONE EMIT, TWO DOCUMENTS, on R311y856's order of operations. `skips_json` is
written once and read by both the capture report and `health_json`; the
alternative — a second `format!` in `health_json` naming the fields it happened
to think mattered — is exactly how the omission arose in the first place.
`skips_text` is likewise one rendering read by the capture summary and by
`--health`. No ABI revision: the header's own contract says the number tracks
the symbol set and not the JSON shape, and no symbol moved.

WHAT THIS ROUND ALSO DID IS RETIRE FOUR CLAIMS IT DID NOT ACT ON. The
analyzer/capture residual list this round was picked from names TLS key update,

closed, and the QUIC one was closed on a false premise: the list says
`QUIC_*_TRAFFIC_SECRET` entries are needed, and the rustls-family stacks emit
ORDINARY TLS labels for QUIC, which this reader already parses. Measured by
running the suite rather than by reading the code.

carry_forward_bullets: 1. THE PRE-PUSH HOOK CANNOT SEE A CONSUMER IT DID NOT CHANGE, and this round
paid for it with three hosted reds that had been standing since R311y857. The
hook tests the crates a push CHANGES; widening a public struct in crate A
breaks crate B's initializer, and B is not in that set. A `cargo check
--workspace` before the push would have caught it in seconds and is not run.
That is a gate-shaped hole with a measured cost, and it is not the same as the
deliberate "hosted CI owns the full matrix" trade -- this is a compile error,
not a feature-subset lane.
2. TWO SKIP COUNTERS CAN NEVER BE NON-ZERO AND ARE REPORTED ANYWAY.
`SkipCensus::ipv4_fragment` and `ipv6_fragment` appear in the capture document,
in the health document, and on the page, always as `0`, because nothing
constructs `SkipReason::Ipv4Fragment` or `Ipv6Fragment` -- every IP fragment
reaches the reassembly table. A field that cannot move is a claim of a check
that is not performed. Three ways out and this round takes none of them
deliberately: delete the variants and the fields; make them reachable by giving
`link::strip_transport` a non-reassembling mode that the tree actually uses; or
say at the field that they are structurally zero. The register in
`verdict_leg_mutation.py` now carries the fact so it is not lost.
3. THE VERDICT STILL DOES NOT READ `fragment_stats().expired`. A chain that was
held and then aged out of the table is bytes absent by exactly the argument
this round used for a pending one, and the pending counter is the only one the
leg sees. A capture whose fragments all expired reports itself complete once
the pieces leave the skip list -- unverified, and the next thing to probe here.
4. THE FURNITURE CLASS IS A JUDGEMENT AND IT IS ARGUED, NOT MEASURED. `not_ip`,
`not_transport` and `vsock_non_payload` are called incapable of carrying zenoh
on the grounds that every link this workspace speaks arrives as TCP, UDP or its
own link type. That is true of wz. It is an assumption about a capture taken
somewhere else -- a tunnel, an encapsulation this reader does not walk -- and
nothing tests it. The honest form is a witness that enumerates the link kinds
and asserts each reaches a non-furniture arm.
5. R311y859's carry 3 stands unchanged: the breakdown prints twice in a
`--health` run, and the two class subtotals added here make each printing one
line longer.

Round 1898.decision_summary:
R311y860 — a verdict that was true of every capture ever taken, and the build
break that had been hiding three hosted reds behind one message.

R311y859's carry 1 said the two skip classes were rendered and not judged. The
sharper statement, found by asking what the existing leg actually fires on:
`is_complete` guarded on `packets_skipped > 0`, and an Ethernet segment carries
ARP. Every capture taken on a real network skips packets, so the headline
verdict read INCOMPLETE always, and `wz-analyze` returned 1 always — the exit
code a script would branch on. A verdict true of everything distinguishes
nothing, and this one had a test pinning it: R311y715's fixture was an ARP
frame, which is exactly the case the leg should not fire on.

THE LEG NOW READS `SkipCensus::bytes_absent`, the class R311y859 named: bytes
that were on the wire and are in no row. The furniture — ARP and its
neighbours, IP that is neither TCP nor UDP, a vsock control op — is still
counted and still printed and is not judged. Measured on the shipped binary
rather than only in the suite: a two-packet furniture capture prints
`capture: complete` and exits 0, and the same file plus one truncated packet
prints INCOMPLETE and exits 1.

THE CLASSIFICATION IS EXHAUSTIVE BY CONSTRUCTION, which is the gate carry 2
asked for and a stronger one than a script. `total()` is now defined as
`bytes_absent() + not_this_protocol()`, and a test already pins `total()`
against `DissectionHealth::packets_skipped`. A tenth reason added at the door
and placed in neither class therefore drops out of the total and reds that
equality, instead of going quietly unjudged.

A BUILD BREAK WAS FOUND ON THE WAY AND IT WAS NOT THIS ROUND'S. `wz-replay`
had not compiled since R311y857 widened `wz_analyze::Request` with `health`;
its initializer was never updated. Nothing local could see it — the pre-push
hook tests the crates a push CHANGES, and that round changed `wz-analyze`. The
hosted run for R311y896 reported THREE failing jobs and all three were this one
error. Layer C0mut's refusal is worth quoting for what a gate should do with a
red tree: it declined to sweep at all, because "over a red tree every mutant is
red and this sweep would report every leg load-bearing while measuring
nothing".

THE MUTATION GATE THEN FOUND THREE COUNTERS NO FIXTURE HAS EVER REACHED.
Registering `bytes_absent` for the sweep meant one recipe per field, and three
survived: `ip_fragment_pending`, `ipv4_fragment`, `ipv6_fragment`. The first is
paid here with a fixture — a first fragment whose rest never arrives, which is
the sharpest member of the class the verdict now reads. The other two are not
unbuilt but UNREACHABLE: nothing in this tree constructs those two
`SkipReason` variants, because every IP fragment goes to the reassembly table.
They are reported in both documents as fields that can never be non-zero, which

Round 1900.decision_summary:
R311y862 — a capture holding a complete zenoh session reported itself COMPLETE
having read none of it, because the session was inside a tunnel and a tunnel was
filed beside ARP.

R311y860's carry 4 said the furniture class was argued rather than measured. It
was, and the argument was wrong in the direction that costs the most. The
sentence in the code read: none of these could have carried zenoh, because every
link this workspace speaks arrives as TCP, UDP or its own link type. That is a
claim about what wz SENDS. `not_transport` is a fact about what a capture
CONTAINS, and a capture is taken wherever the analyst is standing.

MEASURED FIRST, ON ONE PACKET. `IPv4(proto 4) / IPv4 / UDP:7447 / 48 KeepAlives`
— an ordinary IPIP tunnel — produced `complete=true`, `reasons=[]`,
`datagram_flows=0` and `not_transport: 1`. Every byte of a zenoh session was on
the wire, none of it was in a row, and the headline said the capture was whole
and the exit code said 0. For a tool whose whole job is to say what a capture
contains, that is the worst shape available: not a wrong number, a confident
silence.

THE FIX IS TWO HALVES AND BOTH ARE NEEDED. The walk now follows IP-in-IP: proto
4 and 41 mean the body is another datagram, and the parser for it is the one
already in this function, so `decapsulate` became a loop over the IP strip
rather than a second parser. Four levels, bounded, because the depth is read out
of the packet. And a tunnel this build CANNOT open — GRE, ESP, AH, L2TP and the
rest — leaves the furniture class for `SkipReason::Encapsulation`, which is
bytes absent: the packet was not short, not malformed and not furniture, it was
a carrier whose contents this reader did not open.

WHAT STAYS FURNITURE IS WHAT THE POSITIVE ARGUMENT ACTUALLY COVERS: a protocol
that TERMINATES at the host. ICMP carries no session; SCTP carries one zenoh has
no link for. A capture is still not a floor because the segment it was taken on
had pings on it, which is the regression R311y860 paid for with ARP and the
reason the split had to be a split rather than a widening.

THE RESIDUE IS PRINTED RATHER THAN ASSERTED. An encapsulation missing from the
list is still furniture by omission — this round cannot enumerate every protocol
number IANA will ever assign — so both documents now carry the protocol NUMBERS
behind each count. A reader who sees a number they did not expect under "held to
terminate at the host" has found the next entry for the list, which is the
difference between a claim that can be checked and one that must be believed.

AND THE MUTATION GATE STOPPED BEING ABLE TO GO QUIETLY STALE. Its recipe lists
are hand-written and the accessors they describe are not: `bytes_absent` grew a
sixth field here, the loop named five, and nothing would have said so — the new
counter would have been measured by no mutant while the gate printed OK. The
sweep now reads the summing predicates' own bodies and refuses when a term has
no recipe. Its discrimination was measured rather than assumed: empty as it
stands, and it names `self.unwalked_encapsulation` the moment that recipe is
removed.

Round 1901.decision_summary:
R311y863 — the tunnel this build opens was reported as one it cannot open, and
the only difference was that the sender had fragmented it.

R311y862 closed the case where a capture holding a complete zenoh session inside
an IPIP tunnel reported itself COMPLETE having read none of it. Its carry 2 said
the fix was half a fix: the walk stops at a fragment, so a reassembled carrier
reaches `transport_from_ip` and is reported as an encapsulation. It called that
"honest, but the session inside is still unread". Measured, it was not honest.

MEASURED FIRST, AS A PAIR WHOSE ONLY VARIABLE IS THE PACKET COUNT. The same 48
KeepAlives, the same `IPv4(proto 4) / IPv4 / UDP:7447` carrier: through ONE
packet, `datagram_flows=1`, 48 messages, `capture: complete`. Split across two
fragments of that same carrier, `datagram_flows=0`, `messages decoded: 0`, and
the page printed `tunnel IP protocol(s) not opened: 4`. Protocol 4 is exactly
what this build opens. The report was not conceding a gap, it was stating
something false about its own reader, and it named the protocol number so a
reader could act on it — which is the worst combination: an actionable line that
sends its reader to write a parser that already exists.

THE REASSEMBLY WAS NEVER THE PROBLEM. The chain completed, the census showed no
unfinished chains, and the whole inner packet was in hand. The walk had TWO
DOORS and lived behind one of them: `decapsulate` for a packet that arrives
whole, `transport_from_ip` for one the reassembler rebuilt. A tunnel adds header
bytes to packets that are already at the path MTU, so the fragmented carrier is
the ORDINARY case and the unfragmented one is the small-packet exception — which
is why this reads as a tool that works on a capture of KeepAlives and stops
working on a capture of data.

THE FIX IS THE WALK MOVING TO WHERE BOTH DOORS REACH IT. `walk_ip_chain` is
R311y862's loop lifted out of `decapsulate` and given the caller's already-folded
checksum verdict and already-consumed carrier count, so the depth bound is a
property of the CHAIN and not of the door it entered by.

AND THE FIX HAD TO NOT REGENERATE THE DEFECT ONE LAYER DOWN, which is R311y861's
lesson and it applied here directly. Walking a reassembled carrier can find
another FRAGMENT inside it — a tunnel ingress fragmenting a packet that was
already a fragment. The arm standing there called that impossible and booked it
as `NotTransport(4)`: furniture, the exact mislabelling this round exists to
undo. `push_fragment` is now a bounded loop that hands such a piece back to the
table, and a witness pins it.

THE TWO CONTROL ARMS ARE ASSERTED, NOT ASSUMED. A reassembled GRE carrier is
still a shortfall and still names 47; a reassembled ICMP datagram is still
furniture and still leaves the capture complete. Without them this round reads as
"make the verdict fire less often", which is the regression in the other
direction and the one R311y860 already paid for.

list. Without those two legs this round would read as "make the verdict fire less

THE BOUND IS PINNED THROUGH THE FRAGMENTED DOOR, which is what makes

Round 1902.decision_summary:
R311y864 — GRE is opened, and the reason for a GRE it cannot finish is no
longer the reason for a GRE it cannot start.

R311y862 named GRE and R311y863's carry called it the largest unread class left
after the fragmented-carrier fix, on measured ground rather than preference: a
capture taken off a VPN concentrator carries GRE, and this reader printed
`tunnel IP protocol(s) not opened: 47` at it. That is honest and it is useless
to the person holding such a capture.

MEASURED FIRST, ON THE SHIPPED BINARY, AND THE MEASUREMENT FOUND A SECOND THING.
Four fixtures, all four printing the same page: `capture: INCOMPLETE`,
`messages decoded: 0`, `tunnel IP protocol(s) not opened: 47`, exit 1. Two of
them were `gre-ip.pcap`, a complete zenoh session inside GRE, and
`gre-teb.pcap`, the same carrier with the same header length carrying bridged
Ethernet. INDISTINGUISHABLE. A reader could not tell a capture whose contents
this build could read from one whose contents it could not, because the reason
named the carrier and the carrier was the same.

THE HEADER IS WHY THIS WAS NEVER A ONE-LINE ADDITION. RFC 2784 gives GRE four
fixed bytes and makes everything after them OPTIONAL and keyed by a flag bit, so
there is no constant offset to the payload; RFC 2890's Key and Sequence are the
two that deploy. A reader that summed the flags wrongly would not refuse, it
would find an IP header eight bytes early and report a plausible session that
was never sent — which is why the witness drives all three deployed
combinations rather than the bare one.

AND THE REFUSALS ARE SPLIT BY WHAT IS KNOWN, not by where they happened. Three
headers cannot be SIZED at all — Routing Present, whose field is a
variable-length list; version 1, which is PPTP's Enhanced GRE and puts a payload
length where the flag word belongs; a non-zero Reserved0, which RFC 2784 says to
discard. For those, the payload type cannot be read, so `Encapsulation(47)` is
the whole of what is known and is the honest answer. Where the header parses and
only its payload is unwalkable, the ETHERTYPE is known, and reporting 47 there
would send a reader to add GRE support that is now present — the misdirection
R311y863 measured on protocol 4, one carrier later and avoided on purpose.
`SkipReason::GrePayload(u16)` is that second answer, and Transparent Ethernet
Bridging prints as `0x6558` rather than as a tunnel nobody opened.

THE TWO ROUNDS HAD TO BE MADE TO COMPOSE, WHICH IS NOT AUTOMATIC. R311y863 gave
the reassembly door its own walk by NAMING protocols 4 and 41 in it, so a new
carrier reaches that door only if it is named there too. A GRE header is exactly
what pushes a full-MTU packet past the path MTU, so the fragmented GRE carrier
is the ordinary case rather than the exotic one, and it has its own witness.

AND R311y862's OWN GATE FIRED FOR THE FIRST TIME ON A ROUND THAT DID NOT WRITE
IT. `unswept_summands` read `bytes_absent`'s body, found `self.gre_payload` with
no recipe zeroing it, and refused — before any test was written and while the
sweep would otherwise have reported OK with the new counter measured by nothing.
That is the check earning its keep against a stranger, which is the only way a
gate is ever really tested.

the measurement is what turned a one-line addition into a split reason. Four

one), exit 1. `gre-ip.pcap` holds a whole zenoh session and `gre-teb.pcap` holds
bridged Ethernet behind a GRE header of the SAME LENGTH, and no reader could
have told them apart.
THE DISCRIMINATOR IS THOSE SAME FOUR FIXTURES AFTER, and they now give four
different answers. `gre-ip.pcap`: `capture: complete`, `flows: 0 stream, 1
datagram`, `messages decoded: 48`, `packets skipped: 0`, exit 0.
`gre-teb.pcap`: INCOMPLETE with `0 tunnel not opened, 1 GRE payload not walked`
and `GRE payload ethertype(s) not walked: 0x6558`, exit 1 — the carrier was
opened and the page says what was inside it. `esp.pcap`: unchanged at

THE HEADER LENGTH IS DRIVEN RATHER THAN ASSUMED. `zenoh_inside_a_gre_tunnel_is_read`
runs all three deployed optional-field combinations — none, Key+Sequence, and
Checksum+Reserved1 — and asserts 48 messages and the INNER addresses in each. A

single bare-header witness would have passed while two of the three shapes
produced nonsense. The binary fixture uses Key+Sequence for the same reason.
THE TWO REFUSAL CLASSES ARE PINNED APART IN BOTH DIRECTIONS.
`a_gre_header_this_reader_cannot_size_is_a_tunnel_not_opened` drives version 1,

Round 1904.decision_summary:
R311y866 — a test that measures "while X is held" cannot express the window as a
duration, and this one had been guessing a number three times too small.

`saturated_rx_starves_tx_on_one_shared_runtime` took Layer C1j red on hosted run
32193989329, on a commit that touched nothing it reaches. That is the shape a
flake takes, and the usual next move — call it runner load and move on — would
have been wrong: the constants are wrong about each other, and the load only
decides how often it shows.

THE MECHANISM IS THREE CONSTANTS AND ONE SENTENCE. `saturate` grants each
saturating task `REACH_WORKER_MS` = 5 000 ms to reach a worker, and returns once
every one of them has reported in. Each task then held its worker for
`SATURATE_MS` = 2 000 ms — COUNTED FROM WHEN THAT TASK ARRIVED, not from when
the last one did. So the observation window opens when the SLOWEST holder
arrives and the first holder's clock has already been running. The relation the
old number had to satisfy was `hold > REACH_WORKER_MS + OBSERVE_MS` = 5 750 ms.
It was 2 000 ms. The comment above it said "long enough that the observation
window below closes first", which was a claim about a quantity nobody had
compared against the wait beneath it.

MEASURED RATHER THAN ARGUED, and it reproduces on demand. A probe that staggered
the second holder by 1 500 ms — well inside the budget the helper itself grants —
printed `holder A on a worker at 48µs`, `holder B at 1.500s`, and `at 2.250s the
TX task had run = true`, where the assertion demands false. One holder had
expired 250 ms before the window closed.

RAISING THE NUMBER WOULD HAVE BEEN THE SAME MISTAKE, LARGER. Six seconds satisfies
the inequality today, costs every run of this file six seconds, and remains a
guess about a scheduler this repository does not own — the same objection the
job-budget guard makes about `timeout-minutes`. The window is not a duration. It
is "while these workers are held", and the only thing that knows when that ends
is the test.

SO THE HOLD IS NOW A HANDLE. `Holders` is a shared flag; a holder occupies its
worker — sleeping in slices, so the thread is genuinely unavailable to tokio, the
property these tests need — until the test releases it. Every leg READS its
observation, RELEASES, and only then asserts, so a failing assertion unwinds with
the workers already free; `Drop` releases as a backstop and `HOLD_CEILING_MS`
catches a test that dies without one.

AND THE OTHER LEG IN THE SAME FILE HAD THE MIRROR OF THIS, WHICH IS THE WORSE
KIND. `saturated_rx_does_not_starve_tx_when_partitioned` asserts TX DOES run, so
a holder that expired mid-window made it pass — for the wrong reason, proving
nothing about the partition it is named for. It was never going to be noticed by
a red. Both legs now hold for the whole window they read.
verification_bullets: THE DEFECT WAS REPRODUCED ON DEMAND BEFORE ANYTHING WAS WRITTEN, as a probe that
printed rather than asserted, and it is deterministic rather than statistical:
`holder A on a worker at 48.522µs`, `holder B on a worker at 1.500257165s`, `at
2.250342972s the TX task had run = true (the assertion demands false)`,
`SATURATE_MS=2000 OBSERVE_MS=750 REACH_WORKER_MS=5000`. The first holder's 2 000
ms expired 250 ms before the window it was supposed to cover closed. The stagger
used, 1 500 ms, is well inside the 5 000 ms `saturate` grants each holder, so
nothing in the probe is outside what the helper permits on any run.
THE DISCRIMINATOR IS THAT SAME CONDITION AS A TEST.
`holders_that_arrive_far_apart_still_hold_together` stages the identical stagger
and asserts what the probe measured to be false, so a build with a duration-based
hold fails it every time rather than sometimes — which is the difference between
this and the hosted red it came from.
THE CONTROL ARM IS ASSERTED, not assumed. `a_released_holder_gives_its_worker
_back` releases and requires TX to run inside `OBSERVE_MS`. Without it "hold
forever" would satisfy every negative leg in this file while measuring nothing,
and it also pins the release path the other legs rely on to not hang runtime
shutdown.

`runtime_partition` is 16 passed / 0 failed, against the hosted run's 13 passed /
1 failed over 14 — the two witnesses added and nothing removed.
LAYER C1j PASSES (96s), which is the lane that went red on hosted run

72 test-binary results, 0 failures.
LANES, each on its own invocation: C0 pass, C1 pass. `cargo fmt --check` clean.

carry_forward_bullets: 1. THE INTER-PROCESS HALF OF THE RACE IS OPEN AND IS NOT CLOSEABLE FROM HERE. A
port handed out as a `u16` is unheld by definition, so anything else on the host
may take it before the caller binds. Closing it means the caller holding the
listener until it hands over a descriptor, which `z_open` — taking a config
string — cannot accept. What would help instead is the callers RETRYING: every
one of them asserts `Z_OK` on the first attempt, so a lost race is still a red
even though the honest answer is "try another port".
2. SIXTEEN COPIES EXISTED AND NOTHING HAD COUNTED THEM. The gate added here
refuses the seventeenth, but it was written after the sixteenth had already been
in the tree for rounds, and the only reason anybody looked was a hosted red.
Nothing in this workspace asks "which helper has been hand-copied into N test
files", and this is the second duplicated-helper class in two rounds — R311y866's
`saturate`/`hold_a_worker` pair lives in exactly one file only by luck.
3. THE SAME QUESTION R311y866 LEFT OPEN IS STILL OPEN AND THIS ROUND IS ITS
SECOND INSTANCE. Both defects were a GUESS standing where a GUARANTEE belonged —
a duration that had to outlast an unbounded wait, a port that had to stay free
across an unbounded gap — and load only decided how often they showed. A lane
that listed the shape would have found both; nothing lists it.
4. `FREE_PORT_ATTEMPTS` IS 64 AND THE LEDGER IS NEVER CLEARED. A test binary that
drew tens of thousands of ports would eventually exhaust the retry, and the panic
says so rather than looping — but no binary here draws more than a few dozen, so
the bound has never been approached and the number is a guess like the ones this
round is about. Stated because it is the same class.
5. R311y865'S WORKFLOW SPLIT IS STILL ONLY HALF GRADED. Run 32198505957 gave
`e2e-demo` its first green and `isolated-crate lanes` too, but `capi-c-arms` died

R311y867 — sixteen copies of a three-line helper, and every one of them handed
out a port it had just stopped holding.

`free_port()` bound `127.0.0.1:0`, read the port, DROPPED the listener, and
returned the number to a caller that would bind it later. The gap between the
drop and the caller's bind is a time-of-check-to-time-of-use race, and it took
Layer C1cc red on hosted run 32198505957: `z_open` answered -4 in
`a_put_on_a_session_with_no_peer_still_reaches_its_own_subscriber`
(`locality_roundtrip.rs:92`) with the other eight tests in the same binary green.

THE RACE IS INTRA-PROCESS AND THAT IS WHY IT IS FIXABLE. `cargo test` runs one
binary's `#[test]` fns on many threads and the binaries themselves one after
another, so the two callers that collide are two THREADS of one process. A probe
listener that never accepted a connection is released outright when it drops —
no TIME_WAIT — so the kernel may hand the same number to the next `bind(:0)`
microseconds later. Under load it does.

MEASURED, NOT ARGUED, AND THE CONTROL ARM IS THE MEASUREMENT. The new test
reproduces the old three lines beside the new helper and draws 256 ports from
each: the old shape returned 2 REPEATS IN 256 DRAWS on the build machine, the
new one returned 256 distinct. The repeat count is asserted to be non-zero
before the new helper is judged at all — on a kernel that never reuses a
released ephemeral port the race cannot happen and the comparison would be
measuring nothing, which is a fact about the host rather than a pass.

SO THE PORT LEDGER IS THE FIX, and the retry inside it is the part that matters:
a candidate already handed out is rejected with its listener STILL OPEN, so the
kernel cannot offer the same number again on the next attempt. Held listeners
drop together once a fresh port is found. The attempt count is bounded, because
a loop whose length the kernel decides is the shape this workspace bounds
everywhere else.

ONE COPY, NOT SIXTEEN, and that is not tidiness. A fix applied sixteen times is
sixteen chances to miss one, and the one missed keeps the flake while the round
reports it closed — the same objection `unswept_summands` raises about a
hand-written recipe list. `wz-runtime-tokio-test-support` was already a
dev-dependency of two of the three crates involved and the third already depends
on `wz-runtime-tokio`, so the shared home cost one manifest line.

WHAT IS NOT CLOSED, stated rather than implied: a process outside this one can
still take the port between the call and the caller's bind. Nothing a function
returning a `u16` can do about that — closing it needs the caller to hold the
listener until it hands the socket over, and the C ABI under test accepts a
config string rather than a descriptor.

Round 1907.decision_summary:
R311y869 — the analyzer decoded every DeclareSubscriber in the capture and had
no output that mentioned one.

WHAT WAS MISSING, stated as the question rather than as the code. Every plane
this crate had folds RECORDS: `agg` says which keyexpr carried the bytes,
`exchange` pairs a query with its replies, `payload` says what the samples hold,
`node` says which zids were talking. Four answers to "what happened" and not one
to "WHO WANTED IT" — which on a pub/sub bus is the question a person opens a
capture with, because a publisher shouting into a keyexpr nobody declared is a
live deployment doing nothing while every counter looks healthy.

zenoh puts that answer on the wire and this reader was throwing it away.
`KeyexprSpaces::absorb` matched `DeclKexpr` / `UndeclKexpr` and ended in
`_ => {}`, so six of the nine `Declare` arms — Subscriber, Queryable, Token and
their three Undeclares — were decoded and discarded. MEASURED before writing
anything: `DeclSubscriber` / `DeclQueryable` / `DeclToken` occur ZERO times in
`wz-capture`, `wz-analyze` and `wz-capi-dissect` combined.

THE JOIN IS THE PLANE, not the listing. A row in `agg` is a literal keyexpr and
a declaration usually is not: `robot/**` is the ordinary zenoh idiom, and
relating it to the `robot/1/pose` a publisher used is keyexpr MATCHING. Doing
it by prefix would invent a second notion of "part of a key" beside the one this
crate already resolves suffixes with — and the register carried exactly that
defect (R1667: "the rollup ignores wildcards; a `robot/**` subscriber and a
`robot/1/pose` publisher land in unrelated places in the tree"). So the join
runs through `wz_session_core::keyexpr_match`, the SAME matcher a wz router uses
to place a sample. An analyzer's "this subscriber covers that traffic" and a
node's routing decision are now one implementation.

TWO FINDINGS COME OUT OF IT and neither is reachable from any ranking: a
declaration nothing was published under, and traffic no declaration matches.

A PATTERN THIS BUILD CANNOT EVALUATE IS UNDECIDABLE, NEVER SILENT.
`filter-wildcards` is switchable and with it off `**` is compared literally.
`filter` turns that into a PARSE REFUSAL because a selector a person typed must
not quietly mean something else; this plane cannot refuse, because the
declaration is on the wire either way, so it does the other half of that rule.
Such a declaration lands in `undecidable`, never in `silent`, and `unclaimed`
becomes a FLOOR whose `unclaimed_exact:false` says so. "Nobody subscribed" and
"this build cannot tell" are different findings and only one is actionable.

WITHDRAWALS STAY IN THE CENSUS. An `Undeclare` stamps `withdrawn_at` and does
not delete the row. A live registry would drop it; an observer must not, or the
capture's last instant is reported as the whole of it.

BOTH SURFACES FROM THE ROUND IT LANDED — `--interests` and the census door —
which is what `analysis_surface_parity.py` exists to force, and its row is
checked by the ABI's own test rather than trusted.

Round 1908.decision_summary:
R311y870 — the plane R311y869 built read the ANSWERS. This round makes it read
the QUESTION, which is where completeness lives.

WHY THE PREVIOUS ROUND'S OWN CARRY WAS THE RIGHT NEXT ITEM. zenoh's declaration
exchange is interest-driven, and `zenoh-protocol/src/network/interest.rs:34-100`
draws it: A sends an INTEREST, B answers with declarations each carrying
`interest_id`, and a DECL FINAL carrying that same id terminates the dump. Read
directly from the checkout rather than recalled — this workspace has been wrong
about upstream from memory before.

Three facts fall out and none of them is reachable from a census of
declarations, however complete that census is.

A DECLARATION IS SOLICITED OR SPONTANEOUS. The `Declare` envelope's
`interest_id` says which, and R311y869 was already decoding that envelope and
ignoring the field. `None` is a contract state and not a missing value — a
Future-mode interest's later declarations carry no id BY DESIGN — so it is
rendered as `null` rather than as an absent key or a zero, id 0 being legal.

AN ANSWER IS COMPLETE OR TRUNCATED, and that is a property of the PAIR. This is
R311y841's rule arriving on a second axis: there, completeness turned out to be
a property of the query-and-queryable match rather than of the queryable; here
it is a property of the interest-and-DeclFinal match rather than of either. So
the request carries what became of it and the declaration carries what asked for
it, and neither is derived from the other.

AN INTEREST NOBODY ANSWERED IS A FINDING ABOUT THE PEER. Discovery asked for and
never served is invisible to a plane that counts answers, because there is
nothing to count. It is now its own population.

THE CORRELATION CROSSES THE FLOW, and this is the part a plausible-looking
implementation gets wrong. An Interest travels A -> B; its answers travel B -> A.
So a `Declare` seen travelling in `direction` answers the request
`direction.peer()` asked. Keyed the obvious way — on the direction the message
travelled — every answer would be looked up in the answerer's own id space,
found missing, and reported as an orphan, while the request sat at zero answers.
The table would look entirely reasonable. `an_interest_and_its_answers_are_
paired_across_the_flow` exists to fail on exactly that.

TWO PREDICATES ARE NARROWER THAN THEY LOOK, and each is a place a wider one
would fire on healthy captures. `unclosed` is judged only for the modes that
EXPECT a `DeclFinal` — a Future-only interest is terminated by nothing, so
calling it unterminated would report every correct session as truncated.
`unanswered` is judged only for interests that ask for a DECLARATION kind — an
interest for keyexpr ALIASES alone is served by `DeclKexpr`, which declares no
interest and moves no counter here.

Both surfaces again, from the round it landed, and the ABI's own test checks the
parity table's claim rather than trusting it.

R311y871 — R311y870 taught the interest plane to read the QUESTION. It still
did not ask whether the ANSWERS were answers to it. This round makes counting a
reply and checking it two different things, which is what turns a wrong answer
from a silence into a finding.

WHY THIS ITEM AND HOW IT WAS CHOSEN. R311y859's rule was followed before
anything was written: PROBE BEFORE PICKING. Two probes were added that assert
TODAY'S behaviour and both passed, which is what makes them a discriminator
rather than a compile error — a `demo/**` ask answered with an `other/thing`
subscriber reported `answers == 1` and `unanswered()` empty, and a
subscribers-only ask answered with a `DeclareQueryable` did the same. The defect
was established by running the tree, not by reading it.

THE UPSTREAM CONTRACT WAS READ, NOT RECALLED. A router serves an interest from
the declarations that `sub.matches(res)` accepts
(`zenoh/src/net/routing/hat/router/pubsub.rs:986`) and only for the kinds the
option bits named (`hat/router/interests.rs:60,71,82`). So an out-of-scope
answer is upstream doing something upstream does not do — a finding about the
PEER, not a shape this reader must tolerate.

TWO AXES, NOT ONE. The debt item named the keyexpr; the kind axis is the same
property and its material was already on the type. They are judged separately
because they fail separately: the KIND bits are on the wire and are decidable in
EVERY build, while the KEYEXPR inherits every "cannot tell" the coverage join
has. Folding them would have made the kind check evaporate wherever the matcher
is off.

THE PREDICATE IS INTERSECTION, AND THIS IS THE PART A PLAUSIBLE IMPLEMENTATION
GETS WRONG. The coverage join matches a PATTERN against a literal traffic key.
Here BOTH sides are patterns — `demo/*/pose` is a correct answer to a `demo/**`
ask — and reusing that matcher would report every ordinary wildcard session as a
divergence: a confident, plausible, wrong table.
`a_wildcard_answer_that_merely_intersects_the_ask_is_in_scope` fails on exactly
that.

THREE VERDICTS AND NOT A BOOLEAN, on this module's own rule. An answer this
build cannot evaluate is UNJUDGED and never MISMATCHED, because "cannot tell"
reported as "the peer is wrong" is the worse of the two errors. `answers` stays
the RAW count on purpose: it is what the peer CLAIMED, and lowering it would
hide the divergence instead of naming it.

THE FINDING IS HELD APART FROM THE TWO BESIDE IT. Silence, a truncated dump and
a wrong answer are three different facts about a peer and a reader acts on them
differently, so `mismatched` is its own population next to `unanswered` and
`unclosed` rather than folded into either.

Round 1910.decision_summary:
R311y872 — R311y865 gave the apt step a ceiling so a mirror outage would fail by
name instead of eating a whole job. The ceiling could not stop what it was
pointed at, and reported that it had. Nine jobs were red on installs that
SUCCEEDED.

THE MEASUREMENT, AND IT OVERTURNS ALL THREE BRANCHES THE DEBT ITEM LISTED. The
register entry offered "300s too tight", "the Azure mirror was dead" and "runner
network", and told the next round to measure before choosing. Measuring says the
answer was none of them. Job 95933028814 of run 32207350092:

    02:09:11  Get:1 ... Need to get 32.4 MB of archives
    02:11:06  Get:9 ... libclang-14-dev 25.2 MB
    02:16:45  Fetched 32.4 MB in 7min 34s (71.4 kB/s)
    02:16:49  Setting up cmake (3.22.1-1ubuntu1.22.04.2) ...
    02:16:51  ##[error]apt: install ... did not finish within 300s and was killed

Every package was fetched, unpacked and configured. Two seconds after the last
`Setting up` line, the ceiling announced it had killed the install. The mirror
was not dead — it was answering at 71 kB/s — and the deadline was not merely
tight, it was INEFFECTIVE.

TWO INDEPENDENT REASONS, EITHER SUFFICIENT. The invocation was
`timeout 300 sudo apt-get ...`, which puts an unprivileged `timeout` outside a
SETUID root `sudo`: the kernel refuses the signal, so `timeout` waits out a
command it cannot stop and answers 124 on its own clock. And there was no
`--kill-after`, so even inside the privilege the only signal sent is a TERM that
apt and dpkg trap ON PURPOSE, because a killed unpack is a broken package
database.

SO THE CEILING GOES INSIDE THE PRIVILEGE AND GAINS ITS SECOND SIGNAL:
`sudo timeout --kill-after=K D apt-get ...`. Composing that argv is now its own
function that PRINTS its answer, because the property that was wrong is a
property of the command line and a lane must be able to fail on it without a
mirror, a network or a root password.

AND THE DEADLINE SPLITS, because one number could not be right for both
invocations and was wrong for the second. R311y865's 29-minute outage was an
`update` retrying `Ign:` lines with no bytes moving; 300s is generous for that
and it stays. An `install` of this repo's largest package set is 32.4 MB and was
MEASURED at 454s on a slow-but-working mirror, so holding it to the same number
turns a slow success into a red. Raising ONE number to cover the install would
have tripled the silence R311y865 bought for the case it was built for, which is
the trap the register entry warned about — the split is how both stay true.

WHAT THIS ROUND DOES NOT CLAIM. The mirror really is slow. apt's own
`Acquire::Retries` and `Acquire::*::Timeout` are the fast path for a mirror that
does not answer at all, this wall clock is only the backstop for one that
answers and dribbles, and that the knobs fail fast is not measured here.

Round 1911.decision_summary:
R311y873 — `payload.rs` opens by stating this crate's rule: the encoding is the
SENDER'S CLAIM, and a claim is checked before it is believed. The payload PLANE
checks it. The FIELD layer never did — `decode_payload` picked a format by key
expression alone and ran it over whatever bytes were under one.

THE UNIT IS WRONG, AND THAT IS THE DEFECT. A `--payload-format` rule is keyed on
a keyexpr; zenoh carries `encoding` on every SAMPLE. One keyexpr therefore
carries two encodings legitimately, and `demo/**=protobuf` then walked a JSON
body with a varint reader.

MEASURED BEFORE IT WAS BELIEVED, and the measurement is worse than the
prediction. A walked `MsgPut` on `demo/a` declaring `application/json` and
carrying `{"a":1}` came back
`Refused { why: "byte 0: wire type 3 has no length rule" }` — the analyzer
blamed the BYTES. The publisher had said exactly what it sent; the rule was the
thing that was wrong, and the reader was sent to a wire with nothing to answer
for. The other half never surfaces as a refusal at all: `{` is `0x7b`, a valid
tag for field 15 wire type 3, so a body one byte different is DECODED and the
reader is handed fields no publisher ever sent. On a product whose whole output
is findings, that is the worst failure grade there is.

THE FIX ASKS THE FORMAT, NOT A TABLE HERE. `PayloadFormat` gains `encodings()`,
naming the table entries a format is FOR, and the check runs BEFORE the decoder
so a contradicting body that happens to parse cannot get through. Names and not
ids, on `shape_of`'s standing rule — an entry added upstream lands correctly
without an edit here. A default of `None` keeps the extension point compiling
for a consumer's proprietary format, so declining is an opt-out that is stated
rather than one taken by omission.

THREE THINGS ARE DELIBERATELY NOT CONTRADICTIONS. `zenoh/bytes` (id 0) is what a
publisher that set no encoding gets — the nanopb deployment this decoder exists
for — so silence is not a claim and does not veto. An `Absent` group is the same

Round 1914.decision_summary:
R311y876 — the owner read the diagnosis and asked the question the diagnosis had
not: if `apt-get update` is what is failing, why is the INSTALL not simply run.

THE STEP WAS ANSWERING ON BEHALF OF ITS OWN PURPOSE. `apt-install.sh` ran
`update` under a ceiling and returned on its failure, so the packages the step
exists for were never attempted. Run 32218773681: nine jobs, every one dead at
`apt: update` on its 300s deadline, and not one wz lane had run. R311y872's
ceiling was doing exactly what it was built to do — the fault is that a
preparatory step held a veto over the operation it exists to prepare.

WHICH IS THE DEFECT THE ROUND BEFORE THIS ONE FIXED, ONE LAYER OUT. R311y874
stopped a publisher's LABEL from vetoing a rule its own bytes refute; the label
was a claim about the payload and was allowed to stand in for it. Here `update`
is a means to the packages and was allowed to stand in for them. Same shape,
different subject, and neither was visible from inside its own file.

THE FIX IS NOT A NUMBER. R311y874's carry 6 proposed raising the 300s `update`
deadline and said plainly that raising it is a guess unless apt's own
`Acquire::Retries` and `Acquire::*::Timeout` are measured against a dead mirror.
That measurement is still not done, and this round does not need it: a failed
`update` is annotated as a warning and the install RUNS. Raising the deadline
would have left the veto standing while making it fire less often, which is the
worse outcome of the two because it would have looked like a fix.

NOTHING IS HIDDEN BY CONTINUING, and that is what makes it safe rather than
merely convenient. A stale index has exactly two outcomes: it still names
fetchable versions and the install SUCCEEDS, or it does not and the install FAILS
BY NAME with apt's own 404. There is no arm in which a package is quietly absent
and a later lane fails somewhere else for it. The staleness is annotated in both
directions, and an install that fails after a failed update says so, because a
stale index is the first thing a reader should suspect.

AND THE ANNOTATION LEVEL BECAME A PARAMETER, because the two invocations stopped
meaning the same thing to the job. A failed `install` is the step failing; a
failed `update` is a note about the index the install then used. Left as it was,
a green job would have carried an `::error::` annotation — and this workspace
reads annotations.

Round 1915.decision_summary:
The field layer read the extension header with a mask one bit too wide, so it
renamed the MANDATORY flag into the id and then could not recognise the one
extension whose whole job is to say "these bytes are not the payload".

zenoh's `iext` gives an extension id FOUR bits (`ID_MASK = 0x0F`); bit 4 is
`FLAG_M`, bits 5-6 the encoding, bit 7 the chain continuation. `walk_ext_entry`
emitted `header & 0x1F` under the name `ext_id`, and never surfaced the mandatory
bit at all. Consequences, in order of damage:

1. `zenoh::put::ext::Shm` is `zextunit!(0x2, true)`, so the marker's byte on the
   wire is `0x12`. The SHM check compared the mis-masked id against a bare `0x02`
   and never matched, so `payload_or_shm_descriptor` presented an SHM DESCRIPTOR
   as `payload` on every real capture. That is exactly the misreading R311y597
   closed, reopened one layer below it.
2. Both of that guarantee's witnesses built the marker as `0x02` -- a byte stock
   zenoh never sends -- so the fixtures certified the mistake. R311y597 even
   moved a third fixture's filler ids to `(i + 0x10) & 0x1F` to avoid colliding
   with the SHM id, which SET the mandatory flag and produced `0x12` exactly:
   two defects cancelling, with a green test over the pair.
3. Every mandatory extension read 0x10 too high (`NodeId` as 19, `WireExprExt`
   as 31), and the bit the R311y630 admission rule turns on was invisible.

The second half of the round is what the layer never had at all: extension
NAMES. `ext_header::body_ext_id` states in prose that "an id is only meaningful
together with the carrier it was read from", and the field layer was the one
consumer that could not act on it, because it walked all 19 chains through one
context-free function. A `Request` carrying `Timeout = 5000` rendered as
`ext_id 6, value 5000` -- every byte accounted for, and nothing that told a
reader that from `Budget = 5000`, which answers the opposite question about why
a query returned nothing.

Round 1916.decision_summary:
The reader did not know the first MID in the transport space, so a message it
could not name stopped it from reading the messages BEHIND that message.

`id::OAM` is `0x00` (`zenoh-protocol/src/transport/mod.rs:54`) and zenoh's own
decoder dispatches it (`zenoh-codec/src/transport/mod.rs:131`). wz had no arm
for it anywhere: `dissect_transport_message` fell to its `_` arm and rendered
the whole body as opaque `body` bytes; `parse_inbound_consuming` answered
`Unknown { mid: 0 }` with a consumed length of ZERO; `ext_admit` had no row, so
an OAM's mandatory `qos` extension was `Unjudged` rather than judged.

The consumed-zero is the one that costs frames rather than names. A batch walk
stands where the PREVIOUS message said the next one begins, so a message with
no length halts it: `passive.rs` counts the remainder as unaccounted and
breaks, and `multicast_rx.rs` walks the same way on the MCU. An OAM at the
front of a datagram therefore dropped every message batched behind it, which is
R311y605's JOIN defect one MID over.

Its wire shape is the reason a walker cannot guess it. The body's ENCODING
lives in header bits 5..6 (`iext::ENC_*`) where every other transport MID
spends those bits on flags, and the ext chain is written BEFORE the body rather
than after it. A trailing-chain walker reading this message reads the first
extension's header byte as the body.

The arm is UNGATED, alone among the decode arms, because there is no generated
body codec behind it to select: a z16, the shared chain decoder, and an opaque
run of bytes. That collapsed the `cfg(any(codec-*))` union on `decode_ext_chain`
and on `inbound`'s imports -- a union that had to be GROWN twice (R311y605,
R311y607) and was a defect each time until a feature-subset build found it.

What was NOT done, and it is a decision rather than an omission:
`is_credible_transport_header` still refuses `0x00`. That predicate answers
where a LOST stream may resume, not what a MID is, and admitting the eight OAM
header bytes was measured to take the resync scan's worst trial from 42%
recovered to 0% at 8192 bytes of noise. The decoder's reach and the resync
gate's discrimination are different questions and this round keeps them apart.
verification_bullets: Every defect was established BY TEST before its fix, each with a population
greater than zero read off the libtest summary rather than off an exit status.
The field layer: a probe building a transport OAM as upstream's writer emits it
reported `left: "Unknown"` against `right: "Oam"`, and passes after the arm
(dissect suite 41 -> 42 passed). The admissibility layer: `left: Unjudged`
against `right: Admissible`, on the leg that separates a JUDGED space from an
unreached one (ext_admit 6 -> 7). The decoder:
`a_transport_oam_is_measured_so_the_batch_walk_reaches_what_follows_it` asserts
the length BY LANDING ON A SENTINEL, so the number is the decoder's own
arithmetic; before the arm the walk reported one frame and the rest
unaccounted, after it two frames and zero.
The refusal to widen `is_credible_transport_header` is a MEASUREMENT: widened,
the seeded resync corpus fell 55% -> 39% recovered at 512 bytes of noise and
42% -> 0% at 8192, lead-in 5 -> 14 at 65536. Reverted, and the two lists are
now pinned against each other by PARTITION rather than by one count.

Round 1917.decision_summary:
The reader read one field at two different widths, and NEITHER of them was the
width the network uses.

`OamId` is a `u16` in both namespaces (`zenoh-protocol/src/network/oam.rs:16`,
`zenoh-protocol/src/transport/oam.rs:16`), and both codecs reach it through the
plain `Zenoh080`, whose integer derive is `let x: u64 = self.read(reader)?;
Ok(x as $uint)` (`zenoh-codec/src/core/zint.rs`, `uint_impl!(u16)`). It
TRUNCATES. The codec that REFUSES an out-of-range zint is a different codec,
`Zenoh080Bounded<u16>`, and neither OAM arm selects it.

wz held one error of each sign at once, which is why no single number described
the bug. `dissect::walk_oam` read the network id with `vle_u64` and rendered a
value no peer computes. R311y878's transport arm read it with the refusing
`vle_u16` on a stated belief -- "a varint that does not fit one is a message
stock zenoh REJECTS" -- that `uint_impl!` refutes.

The refusing half is the one that costs frames rather than numbers, and it cost
them in the exact place the arm was added to fix. `decode_oam` answered
`Err(VleWidthOverflow)`; an `Err` in `parse_inbound_consuming` consumes nothing;
so `passive.rs` counted the remainder as unaccounted and stopped. R311y878 moved
the batch-walk halt from the MID to one of its fields rather than removing it,
and the test that proved the MID was fixed could not see it.

The wide half is not cosmetic either, because this field SELECTS behaviour. An
id of `0x1_0001` truncates to `OAM_LINKSTATE_ID`, so every conforming peer walks
that body as a topology advertisement and folds it into its routing table.
`try_parse_linkstate_oam` compared the untruncated value and answered
`NotLinkstate` -- wz and the rest of the network disagreeing about who is
reachable, which is a failure a replacement cannot have.

The wire width and the value width are two facts, and the constant's own doc had
collapsed them: `OAM_LINKSTATE_ID` was `u64` because "the OAM codec models the id
field as a VLE `u64` (a superset)". A superset of the BYTES, not of the values a
peer acts on. That sentence is why the aliasing was never looked for.

A build error was found on the way and fixed first: with only `codec-keep-alive`
selected, `parse_inbound_consuming` bound an outer cursor nothing used, because
R311y878's `decode_keep_alive` delegate owns its own -- and `-D unused-mut` makes
that an error, not a warning. Three cfg unions had been kept identical by habit;
they are now the same list minus one arm, with the reason written down.

Third instance of one class, so it got a gate rather than a third fix. `weight`
is read narrow (R311y597) where upstream reads it plain
(`zenoh/src/net/codec/linkstate.rs:125`), and that one is NOT fixed here: the
refusing reader is GENERATED, SCE derives read width from storage type, and
sources/codecs/linkstate_weight.scxml already records upstream's truncation in
prose while declaring the other reader. It is carried by name as a MISMATCH the
new census prints, which is the pico-KNOWN_DIVERGENCES shape rather than a
silence.

Round 1918.decision_summary:
The reason a debt was carried outlived the code it was about, and the door it
shut was the one that opened in one line.

R311y879 left `LinkstateWeight.weight` as a named MISMATCH: upstream reads a
link weight as `let w: u16 = codec.read(&mut *reader)?` on the plain `Zenoh080`
(`zenoh/src/net/codec/linkstate.rs:125`), whose `uint_impl!(u16)` derive reads
the full ZInt and TRUNCATES, while wz read it with a refusing narrow reader.
The row said closing it "needs an SCE capability or a different codegen model,
not an scxml retype", because SCE derives read width from the storage type
(`sce-build/src/forge/generator.rs:11805`, verified again this round) and there
is no wide-read/narrow-store form to declare. Both halves are true. The
conclusion did not follow: the scxml declares the WIRE width, the VALUE width
belongs at the consumer boundary, and retyping the field `uint64` plus one
named truncation is exactly upstream's own model.

The price of the refusal was not the field, it was the whole advertisement, and
in both directions of the analyzer. `walk_linkstate_body` DECLINES on any parse
error, so one wide weight turned a full topology back into the opaque blob
R311y597 closed; `try_parse_linkstate_oam` answered `Malformed`, so wz's routing
table never learned a topology every conforming peer had already folded in.
The narrow reader also refuses more than a wide VALUE: `read_vle_u16` caps at
3 wire bytes, so a longer encoding stops it INSIDE the varint and leaves the
cursor astray -- a second divergence nothing had named.

The emit side is the same field's other half and it takes the OPPOSITE answer.
A reader must render what the network delivered, so it truncates; a sender can
decline to produce a message whose addressee it cannot express, so it refuses.
R311y879's carry 3 -- `OamOwned.id` is the wire width on the emit path, so a
consumer could hand `dispatch_oam` `0x1_0001` and every peer would deliver it
to `OAM_LINKSTATE_ID` -- is closed at `frame_encode::oam_body`, the one place
an `OamOwned` becomes bytes. Truncating there would send the caller's message
somewhere the caller did not ask for.

The correct fix had a cost, it was measured, and it is paid rather than
absorbed. Storing the wire width grew `Linkstate` 2_296 -> 2_680 B and the
borrowed `LinkstateList` 146_960 -> 171_536 B, and that 24_576 B tipped three
`linkstate_oam` round-trip tests into `SIGABRT` on libtest's default 2 MiB
thread. Attribution was established rather than assumed: a worktree at HEAD
passes the same tests on the same host. The margin had NEVER been measured, so
a 17% growth surfaced as a stack overflow with no number attached. Layer Q is
the control that says the cost is confined: the MCU multicast footprint reads
-24 B / -36 B, unchanged from the round before, because no MCU profile selects
`codec-linkstate`.

Round 1919.decision_summary:
Four rounds tuned the ceiling. This one measured what it was bounding, and the
measurement refutes the premise all four shared.

R311y865 bounded `apt-get update`, R311y872 fixed the kill it could not
perform, R311y874 raised the numbers, R311y876 stopped a failed `update`
vetoing the install it exists to prepare. Every one of them treated the CEILING
as the subject. R311y880 carried "the third instance of one wrong number, pay
it as its own round, and MEASURE the number rather than estimate it". The
measurement is off run 32266212482's own logs, taken between apt's `Get:`
timestamps:

    cmake-data       1913 kB in  67.5s   ~28 kB/s
    cmake            5010 kB in 187.7s   ~27 kB/s
    libclang-14-dev  25.2 MB, killed at 633s, needs ~933s by itself

At 27 kB/s the `routing-adminspace` job's 32.3 MB needs ~1200s and the
`cross-mcu` job's 142 MB needs ~88 MINUTES, which is past that job's own
45-minute `timeout-minutes`. No number is right for both, and none is right
for the second at all. So the number was never the lever: THROUGHPUT is the
variable and BYTES are the only thing this repository controls. Nobody was
looking at the bytes, because thirteen jobs carry a copy-pasted package list
that nothing owns.

The census owns it now, and the first thing it found is that `cmake` is pulled
by exactly ONE crate here -- `zenoh-pico-sys`, whose build script is the only
consumer of the `cmake` crate in the workspace -- and that four jobs reach
neither it nor the one crate that dev-depends on it. They were each fetching
6.9 MB they could not use, on every run, over that mirror.

The ceiling is deliberately NOT touched. Raising it would let the 25 MB class
through and could not help `cross-mcu` at all, which is the same
pick-a-number move this round's measurement is against; and the two levers
that do work -- caching the .debs, or not needing the 25 MB at all -- are each
their own round with their own measurement.

The 25 MB has a cause worth naming, because it is not wz's. `libclang-dev` is
needed because `sce-forge-runtime`'s BUILD SCRIPT build-depends on `sce-build`
-> `libxml` -> `bindgen`, and that build script exists to generate SCE's own
numerical-conformance fixtures. R311y22 moved wz's codegen into committed
`out/**` precisely so "a plain `cargo build` of the wz stack needs no
libxml2/SCE toolchain" (`scripts/regen-codegen.sh` says exactly that); this
build-dep is why that sentence is not true. SCE is pinned and read-only from
wz sessions, so it is a HANDOFF, and the round's last act is to make the
remaining question decidable by DATA rather than by anyone's guess: a
non-gating step that prints what libclang the runner image already ships.

R311y881 measured which lever works and then did not pull it. This round pulls
it.

The measurement stands: azure.archive.ubuntu.com delivered ~27 kB/s sustained
on run 32266212482, at which the `routing-adminspace` job's download needs
~1200s against a 900s ceiling and `cross-mcu`'s needs ~88 minutes against its
own 45-minute `timeout-minutes`. Trimming `cmake` took the first from 32.3 MB
to 25.4 MB, which is ~941s -- better and still short. No ceiling number is
right, and that is why y881 declined to pick one.

What was left was the only lever that does not depend on the mirror's mood:
stop paying it twice. apt downloads into `/var/cache/apt/archives`, which is
root-owned and outside anything `actions/cache` can carry, so every job of
every run re-fetches the same bytes. Pointed at a directory under the runner

an optimisation that can break the build is a defect.

Round 1921.decision_summary:
"Is a cold cache being red actually acceptable?" It is not, and the question
found a real defect in what R311y882 shipped one round earlier.

y882 pointed apt at a cacheable directory and wrote in its own carry that
nobody knew whether `actions/cache` saves after a FAILED job. That unknown was
not a footnote; it was the whole mechanism. The job this fix exists for is the
one a slow mirror REDS. If a red job cannot save its partial download, the
archive is thrown away, the next run starts cold, and it reds again -- the
bootstrap depends on a green run that a bad mirror will not give. A fix whose
first half is conditional on not needing it is not a fix.

The unknown was resolvable by READING the action's own documentation rather
than by waiting for a run, and it says the opposite of what the shipped shape
needs: "the cache couldn't be saved as the workflow failed in between. For such
use-cases, users now have the ability to use the `actions/cache/save` action to
save the cache by using an `always()` condition"
(actions/cache `save/README.md`). So the combined action was the wrong one, and
this round replaces it with the restore/save split the docs prescribe.

Two things had to be settled to make the split correct rather than merely
present.

WHEN TO SAVE. The upstream example gates on `cache-hit != 'true'`, which does
not converge here: a cold run that dies at 60% saves a partial archive under
the primary key, the next run restores that key EXACTLY, skips the save, and
the remaining 40% is re-fetched forever. The gate has to be "did the archive
gain anything", so `apt-install.sh` fingerprints the directory before and after
-- sizes as well as names, because a resumed download changes a file's size and
not its name -- and sets `WZ_APT_CACHE_DIRTY` for the workflow. Marked on the
FAILURE path too, before the return, because that is the path this exists for.

WHAT SAVING COSTS. Without a gate, a warm fleet re-uploads ~35 MB per job per
run into a 10 GB repo-wide cap, and the caches it evicts are the Rust ones that
make the builds fast. The dirty flag makes a warm run save nothing at all. The
key carries `github.run_id` so a save is always a NEW entry: writing to a key
that already exists is a no-op, which is the other way a partial archive
freezes.
verification_bullets: The claim that the combined action cannot save on failure is READ from
actions/cache's own `save/README.md`, quoted in the decision above, not inferred
from behaviour nobody has observed. That is the difference between this round

Each of the three new arms was damage-probed separately and each named ITS OWN
failure: removing `wz_apt_mark_dirty` from the failure path reds "the install
FAILED after downloading part of the archive"; marking unconditionally reds
"nothing was downloaded and the workflow was told to save anyway"; and a
fingerprint blind to files (directories only) reds "the archive GREW and nothing
told the workflow". Three damages, three distinct arms, no overlap.
The workflow is verified MECHANICALLY rather than by eye, and the check is the
ordering that makes the fix work: for all 13 jobs with an apt step, exactly one
`cache/restore` on the wz-apt path before the first install, exactly one save
after the LAST install, `always()` and `WZ_APT_CACHE_DIRTY` both in its `if`,
and `run_id` in its key. 13 of 13, 0 bad.
That check caught its own false positive first: `zephyr-mcu` counted two
restores, because the Zephyr SDK cache is also a restore/save split. Scoping the
check to the wz-apt path is what made the answer true rather than alarming.

NOT verified here: that a GitHub-hosted red job actually reaches the `always()`
save step. The docs say it is what the split is for; the next run is what shows
it. If the archives never grow across two reds, this mechanism is not working
and the evidence will be the cache entry list, not a guess.
