Round 1922.decision_summary:
Three open-debt items, closed together because each was the same shape one
layer apart: a fact the analyzer already HELD and no consumer read.

233 -- THE CHECKSUMS WERE RENDERED AND NEVER JUDGED. `valid` / `invalid` /
`absent` reach both surfaces, `health` prints all six, and no leg of
`CaptureReport::reasons` read one, so a capture whose every checksum failed
called itself complete. `DissectionHealth::any_checksum_invalid()` even
existed, with no caller.

The rule is NOT `invalid > 0`, and the reason is the defect R311y860 removed
from `packets_skipped`: checksum OFFLOAD makes a host's own transmit path
present-and-wrong through no fault of the wire, so a verdict on `> 0` would
fire on ordinary local captures and take the exit code with it. It fires when
this reader verified at least one transport checksum and NOT ONE passed --
nothing corroborates the headers the rows were built from, which is a FLOOR
claim and so belongs in this enumeration. The IP axis is deliberately not
asked: that checksum covers the header only, is recomputed every hop, and does
not exist in IPv6.

And it could not have been closed without the finding underneath it. EVERY
packet builder in this tree wrote a ZERO checksum, which over IPv4 is
present-and-wrong rather than absent, so the whole fixture corpus sat in the
corruption bucket. A corpus that cannot express the healthy case cannot test a
rule about the unhealthy one -- that is why 233 stayed open, and it was
invisible because nothing judged the counters.

234 -- `dropped_by_limits` WAS ZERO FOR A STRUCTURAL REASON. Neither surface
built a bounded dissection: `wz-analyze` calls `from_capture_declaring` and the
ABI's summary door calls `from_capture`, neither of which takes limits. With no
cap in place nothing can be dropped by one, and a structural zero reads exactly
like a measured one. `--bounded` gives the command line the SAME preset the
ABI's `wz_dissect_pcap_summary_bounded` already used, so the two surfaces
answer one question.

`pattern=format` and `pattern:path=name`; `FormatMap::declarations` rendered a
format rule as the BARE PATTERN, which carries no `=` and is therefore not a
declaration by the reader's own grammar -- while its own field is documented as
"How the reader wrote it". `wz-analyze` built a third spelling by hand, and
that one happened to be right, which is precisely why nobody noticed the render
was not. A round trip is the fix and the test: the writer and the reader agree
on a string without either being told what it should look like.

A BOUND NOBODY COULD ASK FOR, AND A BOUND NOBODY WAS TOLD ABOUT -- the two
halves of "a bounded read is never silent", closed on the surfaces that
lacked them.

THE CENSUS DOOR COULD NOT BE BOUNDED AT ALL. R311y748 gave the C ABI a
bounded SUMMARY and R311y884 gave the command line `--bounded`, so the
parity table records "reading under the live-tap bounds" as a capability

document a live tap actually reads: `wz_dissect_pcap_census` builds five
analysis planes over a `Dissection` whose every limit is `None`, and its own
doc says UNBOUNDED in as many words. A framework watching a running link
could cap the transport answer it did not need and not the analysis one it
did. `Dissection::from_capture_bounded` was already compiled into the
cdylib -- the same constructor the summary door calls -- so what was missing
was the entry point, which is the R311y851 shape one layer in.

AND THE CENSUS DOCUMENT HAD NOWHERE TO SAY WHAT A CAP COST. `census_json`
carried no `dropped_by_limits` group, so a plane made short by an evicted
flow read exactly like a quiet network. Adding the door without the group
would have shipped the structural-zero defect R311y746 pinned for the
summary, inverted: a bound that bites and says nothing.

away from the real gap. The parity row's residue said the ABI's bounded door
emits the summary while "the drop counters live in the HEALTH group, which
only `wz_dissect_pcap_summary` (unbounded) renders", so "a linking consumer
can bound the read and still cannot see what the bound cost". Both doors
call one `summary_json`, which embeds that group. Measured rather than
re-read: the bounded door's own document reports `"flows":1` on the 1 025-

through that door since the round it landed. This is the debt-47 shape --
a reason outliving the code -- with the sharper edge that a reader following
it would have widened the SUMMARY and left the census exactly as it was.

THE COMMAND LINE HAD THE SAME SILENCE, one flag over, and it was found by
asking what a person types. Both arms of R311y884's test pass `--health`, so

Round 1924.decision_summary:
EVERY CAPTURE THREE CRATES BUILT WAS CORRUPT, AND NOTHING WAS RED -- open-debt
item 357, repaid, with its own reason corrected on the way.

WHAT THE ZERO MEANT. Six crates lay Ethernet/IPv4/TCP packets by hand for their
tests. Three wrote a ZERO into the checksum fields. Over IPv4 that is not
absence -- neither IPv4 nor TCP has a declining form, unlike UDP, whose zero
RFC 768 defines as "not computed" -- so `wz-capture` counted every one of those
packets present-and-wrong. Measured before the fix, through the C ABI's own
summary door: a 1 025-packet capture from `wz-capi-dissect`'s fixtures reported
`ip_checksum_invalid: 1025` and `transport_checksum_invalid: 1025`, with zero
valid on either axis. Nothing failed, because no test in any of those files
reads a checksum counter. The bill falls on the NEXT test that does, and
R311y884 paid it: item 233 could not be closed until the corpus could express a
healthy capture at all.

THE ITEM'S OWN REASON WAS WRONG ABOUT WHO. It named four crates -- and
`wz-replay` was already correct, computing both sums; `wz-analyze`'s
`tests/binary.rs`, which it did not name, was correct AND carried the clearest
statement of why ("a zeroed one is not absent, it is PRESENT AND WRONG"). The
three actually broken were `wz-capi-dissect`, `wz-tls-record` and
`wz-integration-tests`. That is the debt-47 shape again, in the direction that
costs most: a list that is wrong about membership sends the repair at crates
that did not need it and leaves one that did.

A COMMENT WAS HOLDING THE DOOR SHUT. `wz-integration-tests` said, beside its
zeros: "Checksums are left zero: `wz-capture`'s TCP path does not verify them,
so computing them would assert nothing this harness is about." That path
verifies both axes and reports each as valid / invalid / absent. A false claim
about another crate, written where the next reader would take it as settled --
the same shape R311y838 recorded when a comment nailed a divergence down as
"agreed".

AND THE SECOND SHAPE, WHICH THE FIRST FIX DID NOT REACH. With the builder
corrected, `wz-capi-dissect`'s captures still reported 1 025 invalid TCP
checksums: the 1 025-flow fixture overwrites the SOURCE PORT after building
each packet, and that byte is inside what the TCP sum covers. A fixture that
edits a packet after building it has invalidated the checksum as surely as one
that never wrote it, and only the transport axis moved -- the IPv4 sum does not
cover the port, so it read clean and the two axes disagreed. That disagreement
is what named the cause.

THE ARITHMETIC NOW HAS ONE OWNER AND THE LAYOUTS DO NOT. Three copies of the
one's complement sum existed, two of them byte-identical.
`wz-packet-fixtures` owns it; the packet LAYOUTS stay hand-laid per crate, on
the argument `wz-capi-dissect`'s own fixture doc makes -- a fixture the reader
and the writer share proves only that they hold one belief between them. A sum
is not a belief. It is deliberately not `wz_capture::link`'s implementation
either, because that one VERIFIES: a fixture computing its checksum with the
function that checks it makes "these checksums are valid" tautological.

Round 1925.decision_summary:
TWO RESIDUES FROM R311y885, ANSWERED RATHER THAN REPEATED -- open-debt items
360 and 361.

THE DOUBLING, AND WHY THE NEXT PAIR WAS THE MOMENT TO STOP IT. Boundedness is
orthogonal to everything else a read door varies. R311y748 gave the summary a
`_bounded` twin, R311y885 gave the census one, and the pair that would have
come next -- a NARROWED census under a ceiling -- would have settled the
pattern by repeating it: a twin per document times a twin per selector, and the
door count doubling every time a new axis arrives.

So the preset is a PARAMETER. `wz_dissect_pcap_census_where_limited` takes the
selector and the ceiling both, and the ceiling is a small INT
(`WZ_DISSECT_LIMITS_NONE` / `WZ_DISSECT_LIMITS_LIVE_TAP`), not the limits
STRUCT the sibling doors' docs refuse: a struct freezes nine fields' layout
into the boundary, an int grows by gaining VALUES and no consumer is recompiled
for one it does not use. NONE is zero, so a zero-initialised argument reads a
file the way every door here read one before presets existed.

AN UNKNOWN PRESET IS REFUSED AND NEVER DEFAULTED. The failure mode of the other
choice is the one that cannot be seen from the outside: a consumer passing a
preset a newer build understands is handed an UNBOUNDED read while believing
its memory is capped, and nothing in the document it gets back says otherwise.

IT SUBSUMES THE THREE NAMED CENSUS DOORS AND REPLACES NONE OF THEM, and that
claim is asserted BYTE FOR BYTE rather than argued: `("", NONE)` equals
`wz_dissect_pcap_census`, `("", LIVE_TAP)` equals
`wz_dissect_pcap_census_bounded`, `(expr, NONE)` equals
`wz_dissect_pcap_census_where`, all off one capture the live-tap ceiling
actually bites. If that were merely nearly true, this ABI would have grown a
second answer to a question it already answered, which is worse than the
doubling. The three keep their symbols: a published symbol is one somebody
links.

AND THE SILENCE IS A RULE NOW, NOT THREE HABITS. `dropped_by_limits` reached
each bounded door because a test written in that door's own round says so. A
FOURTH door added without one is silent again, in the way that is hardest to
notice -- the document comes back, the planes are short, and nothing in it is
wrong. `bounded_output_parity.py` (Layer C0) reads the POPULATION from the code
-- a body that calls a bounded constructor -- and not from a `_bounded` suffix,
which is the only rule that finds the door this round added, whose ceiling is
an argument. It fails in both directions and it also checks the EMITTERS, which
is the half no per-door test can see: three doors could pass their own
assertions against one emitter while a fourth document had no group to carry.

TWO OF THE GATE'S FOUR DAMAGE PROBES FOUND DEFECTS IN THE GATE. Its first
finding was its own: the population slice ran to the next function's marker and
therefore held that function's DOC COMMENT, so
`wz_dissect_pcap_census_bounded`'s prose naming `from_capture_bounded` made the
UNBOUNDED census door read as bounded -- a population read off text that
mentions a constructor rather than off code that calls one. Then the emitter
probe went green twice: once because a comment explaining the shared emitter
contains the searched string, and again because `dropped_by_limits` is a
substring of `dropped_by_limits_json`, the emitter FUNCTION. It strips comments
and searches for the quoted KEY now. A gate adjudicated instead of obeyed, and
then hardened by the thing it got wrong.

`an_unknown_limit_preset_is_refused_rather_than_defaulted` — 2, -1 and

`a_bad_selector_through_the_limited_door_is_still_a_selector_error` — the
preset sits between the selector and the output, and validating it first would

test that exists and does not assert the key -> FAIL. All damage restored and

Round 1926.decision_summary:
A BUILDER IS CORRECT UNTIL SOMEBODY EDITS IT, AND AN EDIT AFTER THE BUILD IS AN
EDIT INSIDE THE CHECKSUM -- open-debt items 363 and 364, and the second one was
LIVE in three more places than the round that named it knew.

THE MEASUREMENT THAT CHANGED THE ROUND. Item 364 was written as a shape with
one instance, already repaired. Swept mechanically -- a local bound from a
packet builder, then index-written -- `wz-capture` had THREE more, all
rewriting the source port to make each packet its own 5-tuple, all after
R311y884 gave that builder a real checksum. So every capture those three loops
built was present-and-wrong on the transport axis at the moment this round
started, and the reason nobody saw it is the reason the class is worth a gate:
IPv4 does not cover the ports, so the IPv4 axis stayed clean and the only
symptom was two checksum counters disagreeing.

THE REPAIR IS ONE CALL, NOT A RULE TO REMEMBER.
`wz_packet_fixtures::set_tcp_source_port` writes the port and refills the sum
it invalidates, reading the addresses and the datagram length OUT OF THE FRAME
-- a caller that had to supply them could supply the wrong ones and get a
self-consistent wrong answer. It sums to the end of the IPv4 datagram and not
the end of the buffer, because a NIC pads a short frame to 60 bytes and those
bytes are outside the cover; that is the failure a caller could never see,
since the sum it wrote is the sum it would read back. Its own tests pin both
directions: the rewrite leaves the frame verifying, and the same write WITHOUT
the refill does not, so the class is not imaginary.

THE WITNESS HALF, AND WHY IT IS A POPULATION AND NOT FOUR TESTS. R311y886 left
six crates building healthy packets and three of them saying so. A crate with
no witness is one edit away from the state item 357 was found in -- correct
code, nothing looking, and the bill paid later by a test about something else.
The gate reads its population from the MANIFESTS: every workspace member
depending on `wz-packet-fixtures` is exactly the set that lays packets by hand,
so a seventh crate cannot join quietly, and each named witness must READ a
checksum counter rather than merely exist.

WHAT EACH WITNESS HAD TO BE, WHICH IS NOT THE SAME TEST SIX TIMES.
`wz-capture`'s covers TCP both directions AND the UDP builder, because that one
leaves its transport checksum zero DELIBERATELY -- RFC 768's declining form,
read as ABSENT -- so the corpus can express "declined" and "verified" and
"wrong" as three different things. `wz-analyze`'s runs the BINARY with
`--health`, so the counters under test are the ones a person sees rather than
the ones the library holds. `wz-replay`'s drives all six of its module's
captures, because the builders and the ASSEMBLY are separate claims.
`wz-integration-tests`' is the sharpest: until R311y886 that harness wrote
zeros under a comment asserting `wz-capture` did not verify them, and the only
assertions in that crate touching those captures are a damage SWEEP -- which
classifies outcomes and would have taken a wholly-corrupt corpus as its own
baseline.

`the_fixtures_this_file_builds_are_checksum_clean` (wz-analyze) — driven

`every_fixture_capture_is_checksum_clean` (wz-replay) — six captures, each

`the_synthesised_pcap_is_checksum_clean` (wz-integration-tests) — 2 and 2 on

`rewriting_the_source_port_leaves_the_frame_verifying` and
`the_port_is_inside_what_the_sum_covers` (wz-packet-fixtures) — the paired arms
that make the helper's claim falsifiable rather than assumed.

Round 1927.decision_summary:
A RED THAT COULD NOT BE READ, AND A CONTROL THAT JUDGED A KERNEL -- open-debt
items 362 and 365, plus the hosted failure this round's own CI read produced.

THE FAILING BUILD SAID NOTHING. Hosted run 32314626012 went red on Layer Qz
with one line, `Qz build deploy/zephyr-app (west) FAIL`, in zero seconds. The
`west build` behind it was written `>/dev/null 2>&1`, so the log held the
verdict and none of the evidence: a missing toolchain, a broken CMakeLists and
a compile error are indistinguishable from it, and telling them apart meant
provisioning Zephyr by hand and running it again. A whole round spent
reproducing what the failing run already knew.

MEASURED RATHER THAN FIXED ONCE, and the sweep is the reason this got a gate.
Three builds in `run-ci.sh` discarded their output: the Zephyr one, the
`sce-codegen` rebuild in Layer B (four words on failure), and the xtask build
in Layer B2 -- that last the worst of its kind, because it SKIPS rather than
fails and prints "libxml2/sce-build toolchain absent?" as a diagnosis when it
is a GUESS. A real break in the xtask read exactly like a box without libxml2.
R311y756 had already repaired a fourth site in the same file for the same
reason, which is what makes this a rule and not a habit somebody remembers.

THE GATE IS NARROW ON PURPOSE. `build_evidence_lint.py` flags a discard only on
a BUILD -- `west build`, `cargo build/test/run`, a `scripts/build-*.sh`,
`cmake --build`, `make`. The other ~55 discards in that file are `command -v`
probes and the gates' own selftests, which run a script with deliberately bad
input and legitimately care about nothing but the exit status. A rule that
flagged those would need an exemption table longer than its findings, and a
table nobody maintains is worse than no gate.

THE NEW MEMBER, ASKED OF EVERY LOCAL ENUMERATOR. Item 365 said a workspace
member joins every gate that counts crates and only Layer C1bz had been
exercised against `wz-packet-fixtures` by name. Run: Layer C1bz (whole
workspace), Layer C1cf (53 crates build clean with default features off), Layer
L (all eight lockfiles resolve), Layer C1 (`cargo test --workspace`), Layer C2
(workspace clippy), Layer 0 (shellcheck, run LOCALLY because the build host
carries 0.9.0 against the pinned 0.11.0 and emits SC2317 across this file --
the artifact `run-ci.sh`'s own header names), and `validate-workspace`, whose
citation-gate population moved 2820 -> 2821 sources. All green. The answer to
WHY nothing needed editing is the part that was unmeasured: every one of those
enumerators is DYNAMIC -- `cargo metadata`, a manifest glob, a lockfile find --
so there is no hardcoded member list anywhere for a new crate to be missing
from. That is a fact about this repo's gates, and it was not known before.

AND THE CONTROL ARM THAT TURNED A KERNEL INTO A RED. Reading the hosted run for
`e267232f` found `free_port_never_repeats_and_the_old_shape_does` failing on
its CONTROL: the runner drew 256 DISTINCT ports through the old bind-read-drop
shape, so the race the helper exists to avoid could not be provoked there. The
control was right to say so and wrong to be an assertion -- and worse, it ran
FIRST, so the property that actually matters never executed on the host where
the build runs. A failing step hides the ones after it.

Split. `free_port_never_repeats` asserts nothing about the kernel and is
deterministic by construction: `free_port` keeps a process-wide ledger, so a
repeat is impossible rather than unlikely. The control PRINTS its number and
fails only under `WZ_PORT_RACE_REQUIRE`, which is the arming shape Layer Qz
already uses for its prerequisites -- and its own draws are `Option` now, so
the one test in this file that asserts nothing about the environment also
cannot panic because of it. Swept for the class: 23 assertion messages in the
tree name a host, a kernel or a machine, and 22 are interop-oracle guards
reporting that a REFERENCE implementation failed, which is a real failure. This
was the only one judging the environment.

Round 1928.decision_summary:
AN EXTENSION THE ANALYSER COULD NAME AND COULD NOT READ -- the field layer's
ZBuf extension bodies, walked.

THE STATE THIS FOUND, AND IT WAS FOUND BY RUNNING THE SURFACE RATHER THAN BY
READING IT. A probe built a Put carrying a `source_info` extension through this
tree's OWN encoder and asked the field walker what it saw. The answer was
`"ext_name": "source_info"` and, one field later, `"value": "20a1b2c3072a"`.
So the dissector told a reader precisely which structure it was looking at and
then handed over the bytes of it. That is a stranger state than not knowing:
`ext_name` (R311y505) closed the naming half and left the reading half looking
closed too. Every `ExtZbuf` body in the tree was in it -- the walker's `enc ==
2` arm read a VLE length and then `c.bytes("value", n)`, with no dispatch of
any kind beneath it.

WHY THAT MATTERS ON THE AXIS THIS PROJECT IS MEASURED ON. A `source_info` is
where the ORIGIN of a sample is: the publisher's zid, its entity id, its
sequence number. On an analysis surface that is not a detail of an extension,
it is the answer to "who sent this". A `Query`'s VALUE is worse -- it rides an
extension and nothing else, so a dissector that leaves that body opaque cannot
show a query's payload AT ALL, whatever else it renders.

FIVE, AND THE RULE THAT PICKED THEM. A walker here is a SECOND implementation
of a layout, so one is written only where this tree already holds the first and
a test can judge the two against each other: `source_info`
(`source_info_ext::encode_source_info_ext_body`), `responder_id`
(`response_build::encode_responder_ext_body`), `query_body`
(`query_value_ext::encode_query_value_ext_body`), `wire_expr`
(`declare_ext_keyexpr::build_ext_keyexpr`), and the network `timestamp`.

The timestamp is the one that could not be settled inside this tree, and it was
settled by reading upstream rather than by resemblance: zenoh's `WCodec<(&ext::
TimestampType<ID>, bool)>` writes a `ZExtZBufHeader` and then
`self.write(writer, &tstamp.timestamp)` -- the ordinary `Timestamp` codec,
`zint(time)` then the length-prefixed id (`zenoh-codec/src/network/mod.rs:181`,
`zenoh-codec/src/core/timestamp.rs:36`). One layout with two carriers, not two
layouts that look alike, so it may share `walk_timestamp`.

WHAT STAYS OPAQUE IS A DECISION, NOT A REMAINDER. `attachment` is USER bytes
and `auth` is a negotiated method's challenge; inventing a structure there
would be worse than hex. `multi_link`, the establishment `shm` and `Join`'s
ZBuf `qos` have a layout upstream declares and this tree does not encode, so a
walker for them would be judged against nothing but its author's reading --
which is the failure the `dissect` feature's own history (R311y605) is a record
of.

THE DISPATCH IS ON THE CARRIER'S NAME FOR THE EID, NOT ON THE EID. `0x3` is
`attachment` on a `Put` and `responder_id` on a `Response`, and both are ZBuf.
A dispatch keyed on the id alone would walk a user's attachment as an identity
and report a zid nobody sent. That is R311y505's rule reaching one level
further in, and it is what the control test holds down.

AND THE GATE READ THE TESTS. Every arm names its group with a LITERAL, because
resolving the name from `ext_name`'s return value would be shorter and would
make five names invisible to `dissect_name_census.py` -- the y877 shape, where a
gate that counts names is blind to a generation form it does not enumerate. The
census then redded on a name invented in a FIXTURE (`group("chain", ..)`),
which is a reach nobody had claimed for it: it reads that file whole.
verification_bullets: Seven tests, and every fixture is minted by the encoder that IS the layout in

DAMAGE PROBE 1, the dispatch: `walk_ext_zbuf_body` forced to `None`. Exactly

DECLINE test stay green, which is right — both describe behaviour that must

Round 1929.decision_summary:
THE PUBLISHER CHOSE THE KEYEXPR AND VERY NEARLY CHOSE THE DOCUMENT --
`debt-census-emit-two-renderings`, probed rather than read, and what the probe
found was a defect rather than a difference of taste.

THE ROW SAID "THE TWO CAN DISAGREE AND NOTHING MEASURES IT", so this round
measured it. Diffing the node plane's two emitters -- `census_json::nodes_json`
and `report`'s `json_fields` -- puts SEVEN facts on the record where before
there was one adjective: `whatami` is a NUMBER in one emitter and a role STRING
in the other; `evidence` is a nested object in one and flattened in the other,
and `admissible` exists only in the shared emit; `first_packet` is absent from
the report; `flows` is a list of flow OBJECTS in one and a COUNT in the other;
the byte totals are top-level in one and under `node_bytes` in the other; a
link carries its flow in one and only two zid strings in the other; and the
report emits no `selection`. Six of those are shape, and shape is the round the
row already says it is.

THE SEVENTH IS NOT SHAPE. `census_json` puts every wire-sourced string through
`wz_session_core::json::escape_into`, and the report put THREE of them through
`format!("\"{x}\"")`: the node plane's `locators`, and the keyexpr on BOTH
interest planes. A locator arrives in a HELLO and a keyexpr in a DECLARE, so
all three are text a PEER chose, and this module's own doc has said since it
was written that "a keyexpr is attacker-influenced text on the wire, and a
writer that emitted it raw would let a publisher choose the shape of this
tool's output". The escaper existed, was documented as a correctness boundary,
was pinned character by character in this module's tests, and three fields did
not call it.

WHY THEY DID NOT, WHICH IS THE PART WORTH KEEPING. `quote_into` takes a `&mut
String`. All three sites build their field INSIDE a `format!`, where there is
no cursor to write into, and `format!("\"{k}\"")` is one character away from
correct-looking. So the safe path was unavailable in exactly the syntactic
position where the unsafe one is shortest. `quoted()` -- the allocating form --
is the whole fix, and it is a fix to the ERGONOMICS rather than to three
call sites.

THE TESTS JUDGE THE DOCUMENT, NOT THE SPELLING. A test asserting that `\"`
appears is a claim about a rendering; a publisher choosing where a field ends
is a claim about the document. So both tests hand the whole report to
`payload::json_wellformed` -- this crate's OWN RFC 8259 scanner, already shipped
for judging payloads and now reachable to judge this crate's own emit. The
damage probe is what shows the two are not one test twice: with `quoted`
reverted, the keyexpr fails on "unescaped control character in a string" and
the locator on "expected ',' or ']' in an array". Two fields, two grammars, two
ways for the same omission to break a reader.

AND THE ROW ITSELF WAS WRONG ABOUT WHERE TO LOOK. It said `wz-analyze` renders
its own view; `wz-analyze` renders nothing -- it calls `CaptureReport` in
`wz-capture`, one crate in from where the row pointed. That is the debt-47
shape again and it was found the same way, by opening the file the row named
and not finding the code there. The registry reason now carries the seven-fact
list and the correction, so the next round starts from a measurement.
verification_bullets: DAMAGE PROBE, and it is what establishes the defect was real rather than
theoretical: `quoted` reverted to `format!("\"{value}\"")`, which is exactly
what the three sites spelled before. Both tests red, and each on a DIFFERENT
grammar rule -- the keyexpr at "the report is not JSON at byte 1652: unescaped
control character in a string", the locator at "byte 1883: expected ',' or ']'
in an array". Two fields, two failure modes, so neither test is the other one
twice. Restored: both green.
The population is asserted before the document is: the interest test refuses to
proceed unless exactly one declaration was READ and its keyexpr came back
WHOLE, and the node test unless one node carries the hostile locator. Without
those, a capture the reader silently dropped would satisfy every "no injected
key" assertion by rendering an empty plane. The node test found this for real
-- the first version pushed a lone HELLO and censused ZERO nodes, because a
HELLO is read as an ANSWER and there was no SCOUT to answer.

Round 1930.decision_summary:
TWO HOSTED REDS, NEITHER OF THEM A TEST FAILING -- runs 32321994673, 32323298824
and 32324338415, read at the start of this round as the standing rule requires,
and both diagnosed to a cause rather than acknowledged.

FIRST, A CORRECTION THIS ROUND OWES ITS OWN NOTES. R311y889 landed the
Qz build's evidence preservation and left the instruction: "a Qz red after this
should finally be diagnosable from the log -- if it is not, that is the next
defect." It IS diagnosable. The first read here reported otherwise, because the
log was grepped for `Qz|FAIL|error` and the evidence line contains none of those
three words. The filter hid the answer, not the log. The line was there:

    scripts/run-ci.sh: /home/runner/zephyrproject/.venv/bin/west:
      /home/runner/zephyrproject/.venv/bin/python: bad interpreter

Two readings were wrong before that one. `gh run view --json jobs` was filtered
on `conclusion != "success"`, which includes SKIPPED, so "Provision Zephyr"
looked like the failing step when it had been skipped on a cache hit; the real
failure was the Qz step itself. And `gh run view --log` returns EMPTY for this
job while `gh api .../actions/jobs/<id>/logs` returns all 873 lines -- which is
exactly what the run's own annotation says to use, and the annotation was right.

THE CAUSE, AND IT IS THE CACHE KEY. `~/zephyrproject/.venv` is built by
`python3.12 -m venv`, so `.venv/bin/python` is a SYMLINK into the hosted tool
cache and `.venv/bin/west` is a script whose shebang names that symlink. The
cache key was `zephyr-<ref>-sdk-<sdkver>-v2` and named neither. `actions/setup-python`
is asked for "3.12", a RANGE, and which patch it hands back is the runner
image's choice: when that moved, the restored venv's symlink dangled and Layer
Qz died in 0 seconds. It came back on its own when the patch lined up again,
which is why it read as flake across two runs. The rule the key was breaking is
general -- a cache key must name every input the cached artifact depends on --
and one comment above the step already said the Zephyr job is the only user of
`actions/setup-python`, so the dependency was documented next to the key that
omitted it.

AND THE STEP WHOSE WHOLE JOB IS TO CATCH THIS REPORTED OK. "Verify Zephyr
provisioning (catch a partial cache / failed provision)" opened with
`test -x ~/zephyrproject/.venv/bin/west`. The file was present and the mode bit
was set; the interpreter was gone. `test -x` cannot fail on this defect, which
makes it not a check -- the same shape R311y887 found twice in one round, where
a rule was satisfied first by a comment and then by a function's name. It now
RUNS `python --version` and `west --version`, the cheapest things that resolve a
shebang, import a stdlib and print what they found.

SECOND RED: THE BUDGET FLOOR, WHICH IS A GATE WORKING. The e2e-demo job failed on
"job used only 29% of its 1200s budget (floor at 30%)". Nothing broke; the gate
was saying a budget a job never approaches is not a gate, and its own remedy is
to lower `timeout-minutes` in the commit that reads it. Measured over the six
runs ending at 77753278 the job costs 349, 364, 375, 378, 395 and 418 seconds --
5.8 to 7.0 minutes -- so it was STRADDLING its own floor and greening or redding
on runner noise. The job's comment had predicted this in advance: "if this job
ever drops under 6 minutes its budget should come back down." 15 minutes puts
the fastest at 39% and the slowest at 46%.

THE SWEEP, BECAUSE ONE INSTANCE IS NOT A CLASS. All four budget gates were
measured against the same run: `ci` 862s of 1800 (48%), feature-gates 1313s of
2700 (49%), routing-adminspace 738s of 2700 (27%, floor 20). Only e2e-demo sat
on its floor.

WHAT HAD NO GATE AT ALL. The budget is ONE fact in TWO places -- the
`timeout-minutes` the RUNNER enforces and the seconds `job-budget-margin.sh`
grades against -- bound only by a comment at each call site saying "the two
numbers are one fact, so move that and move this". This round moved both by hand
and nothing would have spoken if only one had. Layer C0b selftests the SCRIPT
thoroughly in both directions; the ARGUMENT it is handed was ungoverned. Move the
argument alone and the gate grades a ceiling that is not the ceiling; move
`timeout-minutes` alone and a job can be cancelled at its real ceiling with the
margin gate reporting comfort the whole way up. `job_budget_binding.py` is the
binding, and it is the same arrangement `mnemosyne.toml::[tool] pin` and
`MNEMOSYNE_REV` already have for the same reason.

neither of those, so every packet of such a file came back
`UnsupportedLinkType` and the report printed `messages decoded: 0` over a
capture that held a whole session. That reading -- a clean, empty, plausible
report -- is the one R311y603 named an under-promise when it landed `vsock`,
and it was standing on the single most ordinary way a person captures a
local zenoh deployment: both ends on one host.

than as a compile error: the constants were added first so the new legs
would BUILD and then fail, and they failed with `Err(UnsupportedLinkType(0))`.
A probe that does not compile is not a discriminator.

WHERE THE ADDRESS-FAMILY TABLE CAME FROM, since this is the part a reader
should be able to check. `AF_INET` is 2 everywhere; `AF_INET6` is the one
number that is not portable -- 24 on NetBSD/OpenBSD, 28 on FreeBSD, 30 on
Darwin -- and `LINKTYPE_NULL`'s word is in the byte order of the machine that
SAVED the file, so a reader may not assume its own. None of that was
remembered: `tcpdump 4.99.4` on this machine was handed files carrying AF 2,
10, 17, 24, 26, 28 and 30 in BOTH byte orders and asked. It read 2 as IPv4
and 24 / 28 / 30 as IPv6 in either order, and refused 10, 17 and 26 outright
-- Linux's own `AF_INET6` (10) among the refused, correctly, because this is
a BSD encapsulation Linux does not write. Reading both orders is unambiguous
rather than lenient: no member of the table is the byte-swap of another, so
at most one reading can name a family. A word neither reading answers to is
`NotIp`, which is what the Ethernet arm already says to an ethertype it does
not carry.

Round 1932.decision_summary:
TWO EXTENSION BODIES THE DISSECTOR NAMED AND DID NOT READ, both excluded
by ONE REASON THAT WAS FALSE.

`walk_ext_zbuf_body`'s own doc listed the ZBuf rows it leaves as opaque
`value` and gave each a reason. Three shared one: `multi_link`, the
establishment `shm`, and `Join`'s `qos` "have a layout upstream declares and
this tree does not yet encode, so a walker for them would be judged against
nothing but its author's reading". That rule is right — it is R311y605's, and
the round that wrote it had been burned by a hand-walked arm with no codec
behind it. What was wrong was the FACT it was applied to. `Join`'s qos table
has been written by `multicast_join::write_join_qos_ext` since R311y227 and
read back by `decode_join_qos`; the establishment `shm` has been written by
`extshm::encode_shm_init_syn_body` / `..._ack_body` for as long as the
`session-extshm` feature has existed. Both met the rule's condition and were
excluded anyway.

WHAT THAT COST A READER, in the case it is most likely to cost it. A qos JOIN
writes the DECOY `{0, 0}` into its base `next_sn` fields — zenoh's
`multicast/link.rs` sets `next_sn = PrioritySn::DEFAULT` when the real numbers
ride the extension — and every per-priority baseline a receiver seeds from is
in the ext. So a capture of a qos multicast group showed two zeros where the
announcement was and thirty-odd hex bytes where the answer was, which reads as
a peer announcing that it has sent nothing. That is the most ordinary question
a multicast capture is opened to answer.

A FALSE REASON IS WORSE THAN A MISSING ONE, and this is the shape: it does not
merely fail to close a gap, it points at the wrong side of it. Anyone auditing
this row would have gone looking upstream for a layout nobody here writes,
while the producer sat two modules away. The same class as open-debt item 47.

THE LAYOUTS, and where each number came from. Join's `qos` body is
`Priority::NUM` `(reliable, best_effort)` VLE pairs, `Control` (0) first —
zenoh `join::ext::QoSType = Box<[PrioritySn; Priority::NUM]>`, whose codec
writes the pairs back to back with no count, and `Priority::NUM` is 8 by
`1 + Background - Control`. The priority is POSITIONAL, so the walker emits it
from the index and aliases the pair's own span rather than inventing a name
table this tree has no adjudicator for. Init's `shm` body is the establishment
handshake, whose two halves ride ONE eid: `InitSyn { alice_segment }` is one
VLE, `InitAck { alice_challenge, bob_segment }` is two. The Init `A` flag says
which, and the walker cannot see it — but it does not need to: a VLE's width
is fixed by its own bytes, so after the first read the cursor is either empty
(the SYN) or the second VLE must finish it exactly (the ACK), and both cannot
hold without a zero-byte VLE.

THE CARRIER IS PART OF THE KEY, and for `shm` that is load-bearing today
rather than defensively: `Join` declares its OWN `shm` at the same id `0x2`
with the same ZBuf encoding, and THAT row is still one nothing here writes. A
dispatch keyed on the name alone would read a JOIN's opaque blob as a segment
id and report a handshake that never happened. There is a test that fails on
exactly that.

AND ONE MORE THING THIS ROUND OWED, open-debt item 387. R311y893 made the five
walked names constants of `ext_name` so a renamed row carries its arm; the
repair reached only rows that already had constants, and a NEW arm spelled as
a literal still compiled. This round wrote the sixth and seventh arms, which
is precisely when that would have regrown, so the rule is now mechanical:
`dissect_name_census.py` reads the match and FAILS an arm that is not an
`ext_name::` path.

Round 1933.decision_summary:
A TOOL THAT COULD NOT SAY WHAT IT READS, and therefore could not make its
own silence mean anything.

The set of pcap link types this dissector decapsulates was discoverable only
by reading `strip_link`'s match arms. Nothing counted them, so nothing noticed
when the number moved — `vsock` at R311y603, the two loopback encapsulations
at R311y893 — and a comment in `wz-analyze/tests/binary.rs` still said "decap
dispatches SIX link types" while the answer was nine. That comment is TRUE AS
A QUOTE, which is exactly why open-debt item 385 recorded it: a figure that
was right when written is the kind that stops the next investigation rather
than the kind that reds.

WHY THE ABSENCE COSTS MORE HERE THAN A MISSING DOC USUALLY DOES. When this
tool is handed a capture whose link type it does not read, it opens the file,
counts the packets, decodes nothing, and prints `messages decoded: 0`. That is
the SAME sentence it prints for a capture that genuinely carried no zenoh
traffic. R311y893 paid for that reading once already. The report does name the
refused type in its skip census, but only AFTER a run — and a reader who
believes the empty report has no reason to run anything again. So the honest
place for the answer is BEFORE, and `--help` is where a person looks.

WHAT WAS ADDED IS NOT THE LIST BUT THE BINDING. A list of link types in a help
string is another comment, and this round exists because a comment went stale.
So `wz_capture::link::READABLE_LINK_TYPES` is swept: every link type from 0 to
1000 is put through `decapsulate` with a 64-byte probe, and the set that does
NOT come back `UnsupportedLinkType` must equal the declared list EXACTLY, in
both directions. A new arm nobody documented reds; a documented row with no arm
reds. The help block is then pinned against the same list, also both ways. Three
surfaces, one fact.

Both gates were damaged to prove they measure, four probes in all: a row
dropped from the list reds with the missing code named; a row invented for a
code no arm reads reds with the extra one; the help with a type omitted reds
saying the dispatch reads it; the help with a type invented reds saying the
dispatch does not.

THE PCAPNG LEG, AND THE THING IT FOUND. Item 388: the loopback encapsulation
was proved in classic pcap three times and in pcapng not once — measured by
hand in the y893 session, which is the same as not measured. The two container
paths have diverged before (R311y683). The leg was written as whole-report
equality against the Ethernet baseline, the way its three siblings are, and it
FAILED — on exactly one line. pcapng has an Interface Statistics Block to
record what the capture tool dropped and classic pcap has nowhere to put it, so
one says `0 packet(s) dropped` and the other `not reported (this capture format
has nowhere to say)`. That is R311y892's deliberate distinction, and demanding
equality across containers would have demanded a defect. The leg now compares
everything else and asserts that one line SEPARATELY in both directions, which
is a stronger statement than either half.

AND ONE SHAPE THE NEW WALKER HAD NEVER MET. R311y894 landed the JOIN `qos`
table walker against fixtures carrying one extension. Real zenoh-pico does not
send that: `_z_join_encode` writes the qos header as
`_Z_MSG_EXT_ID_JOIN_QOS | _Z_MSG_EXT_MORE(has_patch)` and chains a `patch` Z64
behind it whenever fragmentation is compiled in, which is the default. The
chained shape is now a test. It PASSES — the walker was right — and the value
is that the assertion is there before a capture proves it in the field.

Round 1934.decision_summary:
AN EXTENSION THIS READER COULD NAME, ALREADY KNEW HOW TO PARSE, AND PRINTED AS
HEX ANYWAY — because a sentence beside the dispatch said not to.

zenoh's `0x3` establishment auth extension is a MULTIPLEXER, not a value. Every
configured method contributes a sub-extension keyed by its `auth::id`, the set
is encoded as an ext chain into the extension's ZBuf body, and the peer
demultiplexes by that id — upstream reads the body back as `Vec<ZExtUnknown>`
(`establishment/ext/auth/mod.rs`, the `ztake!` macro), and this tree writes the
identical shape in `auth_dispatch::AuthDispatch::mux` and reads it in `demux`.
So the body was an ext chain: the ONE structure `dissect` already had a walker
for, at the only place a reader was told to expect none.

THE REASON WAS FALSE, AND IT WAS THE THIRD OF THREE. `walk_ext_zbuf_body`'s doc
called `auth` "the negotiated method's challenge bytes, opaque by the same
rule". That sentence is true of what a METHOD's sub-extension holds — one level
down — and false of what the extension carries. R311y894 found the same
paragraph false about `Join`'s `qos` and about the establishment `shm`; with
this round it was wrong about every row it ever covered. A capture of a REFUSED
handshake therefore could not answer the only question it is opened to ask:
which method did the two ends actually try. The field layer said `auth` and
then handed over `824102aabb`, which is that question spelled in hex — and the
run that proves it is in this round's own damage probe.

WHAT WAS ADDED IS THE CHAIN, NOT A LAYOUT. `ExtCarrier::Auth` is the first
variant of that enum that names an extension BODY rather than a message,
because the method id space is a space of its own: `0x1` is `qos` on an `Init`
and `pubkey` inside its auth ext. Its rows are keyed `(method, encoding)`
rather than by method, because the ENCODING is what says which stage of the
four-message handshake an entry belongs to — usrpwd offers itself with a UNIT,
is challenged with a `Z64` nonce and answers with a `ZBuf`, all on `0x2`. A
table keyed on the id alone would name all three and distinguish none, which
for an auth exchange is the difference between "a credential went past" and
"one was offered". `walk_auth_body` is this module's own `walk_ext_chain_z` one
level down, bounded by `parse_error::MAX_EXT_CHAIN_DEPTH` — the participant's
own cap, because an observer that accepted a chain the peer beside it refuses
would report a handshake nobody had.

AND THE REPAIR FOR THE REASON ITSELF (open-debt item 389). Which rows stay
opaque, and why, was a PARAGRAPH beside a `match`; nothing read it, so nothing
could contradict it, and it stood wrong for hundreds of rounds three times
over. The dispatch is now a value — `zbuf_body_walker` returns the walker and
its group name — and the reasons are a SET, `OPAQUE_ZBUF_BODIES`, one row per
`(carrier, upstream name)`. A sweep holds the set against the dispatch in both
directions over every ZBuf row `ext_name` declares: a row must be walked XOR
declared opaque. So an upstream row nobody decided about reds, and — the shape
this class actually fails in — a row that GAINS a walker while its "it is
opaque because…" entry still stands reds on the round the walker lands rather
than three hundred later. What the sweep does NOT do is check that a reason is
TRUE; that half is still judgement, and saying so is part of the repair.

TWO GATES ANSWERED BACK, WHICH IS THE POINT OF HAVING THEM. Splitting the
dispatch out moved the block `dissect_name_census.py` anchors on, and the gate
refused with "re-anchor this regex on whatever the walker's dispatch is called
now" — its unfindable branch earning its keep. Writing the arms as bare tuples
then dropped eight group names out of the census's `name("literal"` shape
entirely, and it said that too; `walked()` exists to keep the call shape, and
that is why it is a function rather than a tuple.

wrap the `auth` arm's head AND spell its pattern as a literal — showed the gate
still reported it: `\s*` spans the newline. The premise was wrong, the check
could not be made to fail, and a check that cannot fail is furniture, so it
went. The measurement stayed, in `ARM_HEAD`'s own docstring.

THE ROWS, AND WHY THIS IS THE MOST ORDINARY THING A CAPTURE IS OPENED FOR.
`qos` is the QoS byte, mandatory on `Frame` / `Fragment` / `TransportOam` and
optional on every network message: priority in the low three bits, congestion
across bits 3 and 5, express at bit 4. "What priority was this published at,
does the publisher block on congestion, did the sample jump the queue" — three
questions, all of them inside `value: 28`. `target` on a `Request` is which
matching queryables a query is FOR, three named values rendered as `value: 2`.
`queryable_info` on a `DeclareQueryable` is the complete flag and the hop
distance a BestMatching route is chosen by, packed one and sixteen bits into
one number. All three have a producer AND a consumer in this tree, which is the
rule a walker is admitted under.

TWO OF THE THREE READ A VALUE THIS TREE'S OWN TYPED ENUM CANNOT NAME, AND THE
WALKER FOLLOWS THE WIRE. Upstream congestion has THREE states: `D_FLAG` at bit
3 is `Block`, and `F_FLAG` at bit 5 ALONE is `BlockFirst`
(`QoSType::get_congestion_control`'s `(false, true)` arm). This tree's
`crate::qos::CongestionControl` has two, so `QosLevel::congestion()` reads that
byte as `Drop`. An observer that re-rendered a peer's bytes through the
narrower vocabulary would report a publisher that drops when it does not, so
the reading is a `&str` from the wire and a test PINS the divergence — it reds
on the round the product closes it. `target` is the same shape: `QueryTarget`
carries the two values a wz `get` can ask for and upstream's DEFAULT
`BestMatching` is not one of them. Both are now registered debt (403, 404)
found BY the analyzer rather than asserted about it.

BITS NOBODY READS ARE NAMED, NOT DROPPED. Upstream's `From<ZExtZ64> for
QoSType` is `ext.value as u8`: it accepts any value and discards the rest
silently. A walk that showed three clean sub-fields for a value with bit 40 set
would be every field correct and the message misreported — `walk_oam`'s failure
in miniature — so the leftover comes back as `undefined_bits` whenever it is
non-zero, and the control leg proves a fully-read value grows no such field.

AND THE ANALYZER CAN NOW SAY WHICH BODIES IT OPENS (item 398, CLOSED). R311y895

reports `messages decoded: 0` and so does a capture with no zenoh traffic, so a
reader who cannot ask cannot tell the two apart. The extension layer has the
identical shape one level in — an unwalked body renders as `value`, which reads
as "there was nothing structured here" — and had no such question, because both
dispatch tables are private to `dissect`. `readable_ext_bodies_line` renders

`EXT BODIES READ:` block is pinned to that renderer in both directions, and the
renderer is pinned to the dispatch. Help text, renderer and dispatch are one
fact, so a body that gains a reading appears in all three on one commit.

Round 1940.decision_summary:
A REPORT THAT SHOWED A NUMBER NOBODY ON THE WIRE EVER ACTED ON.

R311y898 closed the Z64 extension axis by deciding every row: walked, or
listed in `SCALAR_Z64_BODIES` with a reason. The reason those eleven rows
share is one sentence — "the number is the whole of it" — and for SEVEN of
them upstream says otherwise in a single line each. None of the three
conversions REJECTS a wider value; each keeps a prefix and drops the rest in
silence.

WHAT UPSTREAM ACTUALLY DOES, READ DIRECTLY AT THE PINNED 1.5.0 CHECKOUT.
`From<ZExtZ64> for NodeIdType` is `node_id: ext.value as u16`
(`network/mod.rs:594-600`), so a routing context of 70000 is 4464 inside every
peer. `From<ZExtZ64> for PatchType` is `Self(ext.value as u8)`
(`transport/mod.rs:344-348`), so a peer announcing 256 is read as announcing
NOTHING. And the Request budget is `BudgetType::new(l.value as u32)` over a
`NonZeroU32` (`zenoh-codec` `network/request.rs:216-219`), which narrows AND
turns a low word of zero into `None` — the query then runs with no reply
budget at all, which is the OPPOSITE of the four billion the raw number reads
as.

THIS IS THE WORSE HALF OF THE walk_oam FAILURE, NOT THE MISSING HALF. An
unread body renders as `value` and a reader can tell nothing was opened. A
NARROWED body renders as `value` too and reads like an answer. The seven rows
were the second kind: `node_id: 70000` was reported while this tree's OWN
`ext_nodeid::read_source` — `v as u16`, the same narrowing — routed on 4464.
Both implementations agreed with each other and disagreed with the report.

THE COUNTERPART THE WALKED ROWS ALREADY HAD. R311y898 gave a walked row
`undefined_bits` for exactly this: bits a reading does not cover, named rather
than dropped. A table declaring the value IS the answer has no room for a
remainder, which is why the scalar rows had no such field. They now have it,
plus `read_as` for the value a receiver acts on, plus `absent_to_receiver` for
budget's third outcome — which cannot be derived from `undefined_bits`, since
a literal `0` discards nothing and still means "no budget".

NOTHING IS EMITTED WHEN THE VALUE FITS, and that is what makes the fields a
FINDING rather than decoration: an ordinary capture's node ids grow no second
number. Each test carries the control leg that says so, and the rows stay
listed as READ because the self-report is driven by the DISPATCH — the rule
`target` already lives under, where a walker that declines had nothing to say
rather than not existing.

AND ONE ROW READS DIFFERENTLY IN THE TWO IMPLEMENTATIONS.
`extpatch::peer_patch` is `u8::try_from(..).unwrap_or(u8::MAX)` — it
SATURATES, on purpose and with its reason written down, so a peer newer than
`u8::MAX` does not wrap to `NO_PATCH`. Stock zenoh truncates. The walker
follows the reference reader and a test PINS the disagreement, the same shape
R311y898 used for the third congestion state: it reds on the round either side
moves.

Round 1941.decision_summary:
A WITNESS WITH NO WZ PROCESS ON THE WIRE.

R311y898 gave the Z64 extension bodies their first walkers and R311y899 added
three more, so six of them stopped rendering as a bare number. Every one was
judged by exactly two things: a producer in this tree, and upstream source a
person had read. Those are not two witnesses. A walker written from a misread
of `network/request.rs` and a producer written from the same misread agree
perfectly, and a test holding the two together reports that agreement as
correctness. Open-debt item 406 filed it as the fourth instance of one axis --
390 (the ZBuf bodies), 396 (the auth chain), then this -- and said what was
missing: not the traffic, the BRIDGE.

THE BRIDGE WAS ONE SLICE, PRIVATE TO A RENDERER. `fields_json` walks every
message of a capture and prints the trees as JSON; the arithmetic that cuts a
message out of the reassembled stream lived there, private, so the only way to
reach a walked field tree from outside `wz-capture` was to parse that JSON
back. A witness asserting on a field VALUE would then be judging a string it
had re-derived. `FlowDissection::message_bytes` is now public and
`fields_json` calls it, so there is one correct slice per frame and one place
it lives.

BOTH ENDS FOREIGN, WHICH THE TWO OLDER WITNESSES COULD NOT MANAGE. The pico
and zenohd dissection witnesses tap a session between wz and a foreign peer,
so one half of every capture is wz's own encoder. Here a stock
`z_queryable --complete` dials through the tap into a stock `zenohd`, and a
stock `z_get --target ALL_COMPLETE` queries it from off the tap -- so the
router forwards a stock client's query back through the recording. No wz
process is on that wire at all. wz appears only as the reader of the
synthesised pcap, which is the right shape for grading a DECODER: a decoder
needs no seat at the table.

WHAT EACH READING IS HELD AGAINST IS NOT THIS TREE. `queryable_info`'s
`complete` against the `--complete` flag; `target` against the
`--target ALL_COMPLETE` flag; `qos` against upstream's own `QoSType::DECLARE`
and `QoSType::REQUEST` (`network/mod.rs:410-414`); `patch` against
`PatchType::CURRENT` = 1. The two flags are the sharpest of these, because a
CLI switch is not a constant this tree could have copied wrong: a reader that
mixed up `All` and `AllComplete` passes every self-witness in the workspace.

THE `patch` LEG'S SUBJECT IS A SILENCE. R311y899 made the presence of
`read_as` / `undefined_bits` / `absent_to_receiver` a FINDING -- they mean the
wire said something no peer will act on. So the only thing a conforming
capture can witness about `read_patch_z64` is that it says nothing, and that
is the half of the walker no hand-written fixture here covers. It is asserted,
and the probe that makes `narrowed_z64` speak unconditionally reds on it
alone.

AND THE FIRST RUN FOUND TWO THINGS THE ITEM DID NOT CONTAIN. The wire carried
SIX extension bodies, not the four this file first claimed -- `responder_id`
and `timeout` were there too, and the two-sided set assertion is what said so
rather than a re-reading of the fixture. The second is a defect and is filed
as item 412: a `Frame`'s `qos` is reported with `congestion` and `express`,
and upstream's frame receiver reads `ext_qos.priority()` and nothing else
(`unicast/universal/rx.rs:85`). That is R311y899's own failure one carrier
over, and it was invisible from inside this tree because wz's frame encoder
writes the same zeros a stock one does.

the test itself: `Init/qos` (a UNIT marker, no body) and `Init/patch value=1`
on each half; `Frame/qos value=0`; two `Declare/qos value=8`;

RED FIRST, AND IT WAS NOT THE RED EXPECTED. The first run FAILED on the set
assertion: the file claimed four bodies and the wire carried six. That is the
two-sided comparison doing the only job it exists for -- had the claim been a
containment check, `responder_id` and `timeout` would have gone unjudged and

FIVE DAMAGE PROBES, EACH APPLIED ALONE, EACH RED FOR ITS OWN REASON, each
reverted before the next:
1. `read_target_z64`'s `1` / `2` arms swapped -> "no `Request`'s `target` was
read as AllComplete ... A Request/target value=Some(2) read=[target=All]".
Nothing else red.
2. `read_queryable_info_z64`'s `complete` taken from bit 1 -> "no `Declare`'s
`queryable_info` was read as complete ... read=[complete=false,
distance=0]". Nothing else red.
3. `read_qos_z64`'s congestion arms reordered so `D_FLAG` reads `Drop` ->
"no `Declare`'s `qos` was read as (Control, Block, false) ...
read=[priority=Control, congestion=Drop, express=false]".
4. `narrowed_z64` made to emit `read_as` unconditionally -> the `patch` leg,
and only it: "`read_patch_z64` spoke about a value a receiver acts on AS
WRITTEN ... B Init/patch value=Some(1) read=[read_as=1]".
5. THE BRIDGE ITSELF: `message_bytes`'s `end` one byte short -> the set
assertion, `left: ["qos", "responder_id"]` against six. A broken slice
EMPTIES the capture rather than mis-reading it, and the anti-vacuity leg is
what catches that shape.
Each probe compiled and ran; none was a compile failure standing in for a

Round 1942.decision_summary:
A WIDTH THAT WAS WRITTEN TWICE, AND NOW IS WRITTEN ONCE.

R311y899 gave three Z64 rows a narrowed reading: `node_id`, `patch` and
`budget` are each read at the width a conforming receiver acts on, and the
walkers carried that width as a literal — `16`, `8`, `32`. Open-debt item 410
filed what measured those literals: one doc sentence per row. A literal cannot
be wrong in a way anything notices. If upstream widened `NodeIdType` to a
`u32`, this report would be sixteen bits wrong and every test in the workspace
would stay green.

THE ITEM'S OWN PROPOSAL WAS REFUTED BEFORE IT WAS BUILT, and the refutation is
recorded in the item rather than here: parsing the pinned zenoh checkout needs
a machine-local absolute path, which this repository forbids in a committed
file (R311y302 is the proof — a path recorded that way had rotted to a
directory that no longer existed and was cited for months). It is also not a
declared prerequisite of a clone, so the gate would SKIP-green on CI. That is
the population-of-zero failure this tree keeps paying for, bought deliberately.

SO THE FIX IS NOT A COMPARISON, IT IS A REMOVAL. Each width now comes from the
module that performs the narrowing: `ext_nodeid` exports `NodeId` and
`NODE_ID_BITS`, `extpatch` exports `PatchLevel` and `PATCH_BITS`,
`request_build` exports `Budget` and `BUDGET_BITS`, each `BITS` derived from
its own alias with `<T>::BITS`. The dissector reads those constants and its
three literals are gone. There are no longer two numbers that happen to match;
there is one constant. All three are type aliases over the primitives already
in use, so the behaviour change is nil.

THE THREE PAIRS ARE THREE DIFFERENT KINDS OF THING, which is why this binds
the WIDTH and never the narrowing rule. `node_id`'s pair is a READER that
truncates exactly as the walker does. `patch`'s pair is a READER that
SATURATES — deliberately, so a peer announcing something newer than `u8::MAX`
does not wrap to `NO_PATCH` — so a gate binding the two by value equality
would turn an intended divergence into a false red. `budget` has no consumer
in this tree at all, so its pair is a PRODUCER, and the binding runs the other
way: the builder accepts a `Budget` and the walker narrows to `BUDGET_BITS`.
One sentence about "extracting the cast width" would have covered none of
this.

AND THE RISK THE ITEM LEFT OPEN WAS AVOIDED RATHER THAN SOLVED. The item
warned that `read_source`'s signature carries a lifetime, so coercing it into a
`fn(A) -> R` helper might need an HRTB, and said to find out by compiling. That
design was not built: the item also recorded a stronger alternative — the pair
exports its width and the walker uses it — and taking it removed the place
where the lifetime would have mattered. The HRTB question is still unanswered
for the design that would have asked it, and the item says so.

Round 1943.decision_summary:
THE TRAFFIC WAS ALREADY HERE AND IT WAS THE WRONG HALF.

Open-debt item 396 said the auth walkers had no foreign witness, that the
traffic already existed in `usrpwd_zenohd_interop.rs`, and that only the
bridge was missing. R311y900 built that bridge for item 406. So this round
should have been that witness copied one axis over.

It was not, and the reason is the whole finding: in every auth interop test in
this tree WZ DIALS, and the usrpwd body carrying `{user, hmac}` is written by
the DIALER. Pointing the dissector at those captures would have graded wz's
encoder against wz's decoder — the self-witness this axis exists to escape,
and the identical mistake item 395's own caveat made when it called pubkey's
producer foreign because it lived in `wz-runtime-tokio` rather than here.

SO THE FOREIGN HALF HAD TO BE THE CLIENT. Upstream config carries
`transport/auth/usrpwd/{user,password}` (`DEFAULT_CONFIG.json5:737-742`), which
makes a stock `z_get` a usrpwd INITIATOR. It dials through the tap into a stock
zenohd holding the matching dictionary — and a configured dictionary makes auth
MANDATORY, so the captured chain is a required exchange rather than an optional
one. No wz process is on that wire; wz is only the reader of the pcap.

WHAT THE CAPTURE TURNED OUT TO BE WORTH is more than the item asked for. One
extension id carries THREE encodings across a single handshake: the
initiator's `Init` offers usrpwd as a UNIT with no body, the acceptor's `Init`
answers with a Z64 challenge nonce, and the initiator's `Open` carries the
ZBuf `{user, hmac}`. `walk_ext_entry` selects on the encoding bits before
`zbuf_body_walker` is asked at all, so a build that keyed on the name alone
would try to read the UNIT offer as a `{user, hmac}` pair. Nothing in this tree
emits all three — the acceptor's challenge is zenohd's — so this grades the
DISPATCH and not merely a walker, which is precisely what item 396 said was
missing.

WHAT IS HELD AGAINST WHAT. `user` is asserted against the username the client
was spawned with: a config value, not a constant this tree could have copied
wrong, so a walker that swapped the two ZBufs or folded a length into a value
passes every self-witness in the workspace and reds here. `hmac` is asserted
as FRAMED AND NON-EMPTY rather than by value, because it is a keyed digest and
this test holds no key — stating that limit rather than inventing an assertion
that would only re-derive the walker's own output.

AND THE CLOSURE IS NARROWER THAN THE ITEM'S TITLE. Item 396 widened at
R311y897 to cover four body walkers. Two of them now have a foreign witness;
`walk_pubkey_challenge_body` has none, at any of its three carriers, because
this capture holds no pubkey bytes at all. That residue is filed as item 416
rather than left inside a closed entry.
verification_bullets: RED FIRST, AND ON THE ASSERTION R311y900 PAID FOR. The first run FAILED on the
SET assertion: this file claimed three extension bodies and the wire held five

established — say what the capture CONTAINS before saying what any reading of

THE CAPTURE, MEASURED. Fifteen extension entries, printed by the test itself.
Both halves carry `Init`/`Open` with an `auth` chain that walked
(`auth=<1 field(s)>`). The usrpwd id appears four times at three encodings:

`user_len=23, user="wz-foreign-witness-user", hmac_len=32, hmac=<32 byte(s)>`,
acceptor `Open` enc=0.
THREE DAMAGE PROBES, each applied alone, each reverted from the index before
the next, and each red on a DIFFERENT assertion — judged by the panic message
body rather than the exit status (open-debt item 414):
1. `walk_auth_usrpwd_body` reading hmac before user -> the `user` VALUE

it was spawned with", with the swapped framing visible in the dump.
2. `walk_ext_entry`'s encoding mask narrowed to one bit -> the SET assertion,
because the ZBuf parse breaks and the auth rows vanish entirely.
3. The reported `encoding` field pinned to 2 while the parse still used the
real bits -> the THREE-ENCODINGS assertion: "no `usrpwd` entry on B's Init
with encoding 0 (the method OFFER carries no body)". This is the surgical
one: the set is intact and `user` still reads, so only that assertion can
catch it.
THE LANE. `--ignored --list` names
`the_auth_chain_walkers_read_what_a_stock_zenohd_usrpwd_handshake_wrote`.
`bash scripts/run-ci.sh --layer Ewirez` run LOCALLY (the lane is oracle-gated
and a remote run SKIP-greens it, open-debt item 413) reports all three legs by

Round 1944.decision_summary:
A CORRECT ZENOHD FAILED A TEST ONCE IN SIXTEEN RUNS, AND THE TEST WAS WRONG
TWICE OVER.

Open-debt item 417 was filed off a hosted red: Layer M's
`a_stock_zenohd_discovers_wz_by_scouting_and_dials_what_its_hello_advertised`
decided which node a face belonged to by asserting the rendered zid was 32
characters long, under a message claiming "a 16-byte ZenohIdProto". Read
directly at the pinned checkout, upstream refutes the premise:
`ZenohIdProto` wraps `uhlc::ID`, whose `Debug` is
`write!(f, "{:x}", u128::from_le_bytes(self.0))` (`uhlc-0.8.2/src/id.rs:279-283`),
and `{:x}` drops leading zero nibbles; `ID::rand()` is
`OsRng.gen_range(1..u128::MAX)` (`:88-92`), uniform. So a correct zenohd renders
short once in sixteen runs. It did, and the run went red on
`e77a27c47363d6d97990a76230cc58`.

AND THE ITEM'S OWN PROPOSED REPAIR WAS ALSO WRONG. It suggested using the byte
count "which is 16, unlike the render length". `ID::size()` is
`MAX_SIZE - (leading_zeros / 8)` (`:63-67`) — the count of SIGNIFICANT bytes.
A zid whose top BYTE is zero has size 15, once in 256. Following the item would
have moved the same defect one layer down. This is the register's own prose
outliving what it describes, and it was caught only because the round read
upstream instead of quoting the item.

SO THE RULE IS NEITHER A LENGTH NOR A SIZE. `face_zid_value` parses the
rendering into the NUMBER it denotes; rendering is lossy about width and exact
about value. And the comparison is now POSITIVE: zenohd's zid is pinned with
`--cfg id:"2e0d<pid>"` so the test names the node it expects. That is strictly
stronger than what it replaced — `len == 32` admitted ANY 32-character zid,
including a second zenohd's.

A SECOND TRAP, AVOIDED ONLY BY MEASURING. Pinning `id:"2e0db2ae"` produced a
face reading `zid aeb20d2e`: zenoh parses the config string into bytes, holds
them little-endian, and renders `from_le_bytes`, so the printed hex is the
configured hex WITH ITS BYTES REVERSED. Comparing against the config string's
own numeric value would have compared against a number that appears on no wire
— the identical shape as the length rule, one layer down again.
`configured_zid_value` carries that conversion and a unit test pins the fact.

AND LAYER C0 DECIDED WHERE THE FIX LIVES. A probabilistic defect cannot be
judged by re-running the e2e; the reproduction must be deterministic and must
run always-on. But C0 requires every `#[test]` in a binary-dep test FILE to
carry `#[ignore]`, which would have hidden the reproduction behind an oracle.
So the discriminator and its three tests moved into the library, where Layer
C1's workspace run executes them with no oracle present. The gate chose the
design; it was not a preference.

Round 1945.decision_summary:
THE SAME SHAPE, A DIFFERENT MECHANISM, AND A DIFFERENT NUMBER.

R311y903 fixed a test that read a node's identity off the LENGTH of a rendered
zid, and recorded that its sibling — `wz_scout_zenohd_interop.rs` — carried the
same shape. Item 420 was filed with an explicit warning against copying the
fix, because two things differed and either could have changed the verdict: the
assertion's stated reason is decode verification rather than identity, and the
string is printed by wz rather than by zenoh.

SO THE FIRST STEP WAS READING WZ'S RENDERER, and it refutes half the
expectation. It is `h.zid.iter().map(|b| format!("{b:02x}"))`
(`wz-ap-demo/src/runner.rs:601-605`) — FIXED WIDTH per byte. Nothing is lost to
nibble formatting here, so R311y903's one-in-sixteen does not apply and copying
it would have been the register-prose-outliving-code failure this repository
keeps paying for.

THE DEFECT IS REAL ANYWAY, ONE LAYER OUT. The WIRE is variable-length: zenoh
writes `flags |= ((zid.size() - 1) as u8) << 4` and then exactly `zid.size()`
bytes (`zenoh-codec/src/scouting/hello.rs:62-66`), and `ID::size()` subtracts

A SETUP THAT ASSUMED A SCHEDULER PROMISE NOBODY MADE, AND A FAILURE THAT SAID
ONLY `Timeout`.

`saturated_rx_starves_tx_on_one_shared_runtime` took Layer C1j red on THREE
hosted runs in a row — 32386238488, 32418058280, 32420064578 — and on two

its budget: Timeout`. That is the SETUP failing, not the property under test.

WHAT THE SETUP ASSUMED. `saturate` spawned all `count` tasks and only then
waited for `count` signals. Each task blocks its worker thread outright, which
is the whole point — it is the shape a saturated RX path has. So the helper
needed `count` tasks sitting in tokio's injection queue to be DISTRIBUTED
across `count` workers. Tokio does not promise that. A worker takes a BATCH off
the injection queue into its own local queue; if it runs the first and blocks,
anything batched behind it sits on a queue nobody is draining, and the only way
out is another worker stealing from a thread that is not running.

THE FILE ALREADY HELD THE ANSWER. `holders_that_arrive_far_apart_still_hold_
together` does it by hand: spawn one holder, wait until it is ON a worker,
then spawn the next. That test has never gone red on hosted CI while the three
callers of `saturate` have. `saturate` now does the same, which converts a
distribution assumption into a liveness one — holder `k` is not created until
`k-1` are confirmed on workers, so a free worker exists and tokio only has to
poll a ready task.

reproduced locally. Roughly 200 runs across four configurations — pinned to two
CPUs, pinned to one, six competing spin loops on the same two cores, eight
concurrent processes — produced zero failures, and an instrumented build that
printed each holder's thread id put them on distinct workers 60 times out of
60. So this round removes an assumption that is unguaranteed BY CONTRACT; it
does not demonstrate that the assumption is what broke. The item stays open
until hosted CI says otherwise.

WHICH IS WHY THE SECOND HALF OF THE CHANGE IS THE FAILURE MESSAGE. A red that
recurs on a machine you cannot reproduce on has to carry its own evidence, and
`Timeout` carries none: it does not say which holder never arrived, nor how
many did. The panic now names both — `saturating task 2 of 2 did not reach a
worker within 5000ms (Timeout); 1 of 2 had already arrived` — so the next
occurrence discriminates between "the first holder never ran" (the runtime
never started) and "a later one did not" (the free worker was not used), which

Round 1956.decision_summary:
THE ANALYZER COULD NAME A JSON PAYLOAD, VALIDATE IT, WEIGH ITS LABEL AGAINST ITS
BYTES, AND TALLY THE RULES THAT GOT IT WRONG. IT COULD NOT OPEN IT. IT CAN NOW.

`wz_capture::payload`'s opening line is that "a capture of a fleet publishing
JSON was, to this tool, a capture of some bytes". The plane that line introduced
closed half of it: a payload declaring `application/json` gets a VERDICT, and a
body that does not parse is reported with the byte it stopped at. The FIELD layer
kept the other half open for the whole of that track, because
`payload_builtin::BUILTIN_NAMES` held exactly one entry and it was `protobuf`.

THE SHAPE OF THE GAP IS THE SHARP PART, AND IT WAS VISIBLE FROM THE MECHANISMS
BUILT AROUND IT. `PayloadFormat::encodings` exists because a `demo/**=protobuf`
rule "walked a JSON body with a varint reader" (R311y873). `judge_claim` then
learned to check that label against the bytes rather than believe it (R311y874),
and the disagreement was tallied per topic (R311y875). Three rounds of machinery
whose every witness is a `protobuf` rule LOSING to a JSON label -- and the reason
it could only ever be phrased in that direction is that the format on the other
side of the collision did not exist. A reader whose fleet publishes JSON could be
told which rule not to apply, and never shown their data.

ONE GRAMMAR, NOT TWO. The walk is the SAME scanner `inspect` validates with,
running with an emitter attached: `Scanner` gains an `Option<Emit>`, `scan_json`
and the new `walk_json` are two entry points into one `scan`. A decoder with its
own reading of RFC 8259 would let this crate hold two opinions about what JSON is
-- and then the plane above could call a document well-formed that the plane
below refuses, which is a disagreement inside one report.

WHAT A ROW IS. Every value gets one, containers included, so a reader sees the
shape before the leaves: `$` is the document, `$.sensor` a member, `$.readings.0`
an element. The span is the VALUE and not the `"key": ` in front of it, because
an array element has no key and a member-wide span would give the same field two
meanings depending on what contained it -- and the key is not lost, it IS the
last path segment.

AND THE NAME STAYS OFF `PayloadField::name`, WHICH IS THE ONE PLACE THIS COULD
HAVE GONE WRONG QUIETLY. JSON carries its own member names, which is exactly the
temptation: protobuf's decoder returns `name: None` because the wire has none to
give, and a JSON decoder filling it in looks like an improvement. It is not. That
field's contract is "the DECLARED name, from `FormatMap::field_name`", and a
decoder writing it would make one field carry two provenances. The wire's name
goes where the wire put it -- in the path -- so `--payload-name` stays a rename
rather than the only source, and the usage text that said a walk "NEVER" recovers
a name is corrected rather than left to rot.

THE PATH SYNTAX IS PROTOBUF'S, DELIBERATELY. `$.a.0` uses the same `.` the
protobuf walk's `2.1` uses, so `--payload-name` keys on one syntax. The cost is
stated rather than hidden and registered as item 431: a member key containing a
`.` produces a path that reads as nesting.

Round 1958.decision_summary:
TWO OF THE THREE ITEMS R311y909 OPENED ARE CLOSED, AND ONE OF THEM WAS A
CONFIDENT WRONG ANSWER RATHER THAN A GAP.

ITEM 432 — "IT PARSED" WAS SAYABLE ABOUT BYTES THAT ARE NOT JSON. RFC 8259 §8.1
makes UTF-8 part of what a JSON text IS, and this module enforced it on one arm
and not the other: `Verdict::Text` has always been a `from_utf8` with
`Mismatch::NotUtf8` as its answer, while the JSON arm admitted any byte from
0x20 up inside a string. So one module answered the same question two ways
depending on which name the publisher used.

That is not a cosmetic verdict. `payload_decode::judge_claim` reads
`Verdict::Json` to decide whether a publisher's `application/json` label
survives being weighed against its own bytes, and a label that SURVIVES vetoes
the operator's `--payload-format` rule. So a body this reader should have
refuted could argue it out of decoding a topic.

The check goes at the top of `scan`, before the grammar, and not inside
`string`. Two reasons and the second is the one that pays: the requirement is
about the TEXT rather than about one token, and one pass at the top lets the
emitting half hold a `&str`. That DELETED two branches — `push_key`'s
placeholder name for an unprintable key and `fill`'s "N byte(s), not UTF-8"
render — because both had become unreachable. A fallback nothing can reach is
worse than no fallback: it reads as a case that happens.

The control is what keeps the fix from over-reaching, and no existing fixture
had it: a MULTI-BYTE key (`{"온도":21}`) is valid UTF-8 and must stay
`Verdict::Json`. An ASCII-only check would have passed every other test and
broken every non-English deployment.

ITEM 431 — A DOTTED KEY AND A NESTED MEMBER NO LONGER SHARE A PATH. `.` inside a
member key is written `\.` and `\` doubles, so `{"a.b":1}` is `$.a\.b` while
`{"a":{"b":1}}` stays `$.a.b`. Escaping rather than a second syntax
(`$.["a.b"]`), and the reason is mechanical rather than aesthetic:
`FormatMap::field_name` matches a path by STRING EQUALITY, so an operator who
writes the escape gets an exact match and there is no parser to teach. One path
syntax, still shared with the protobuf walk's `2.1`, which was the whole point
of the separator being `.`.

a reading — item 408's failure, one carrier over.

only for the person it is meant to help.

Round 1966.decision_summary:
CBOR IS OPENED, AND THE ITEM THAT HAD TO BE ANSWERED BEFORE THE DECODER COULD
BE WRITTEN IS ANSWERED FIRST.

Items 433 and 434 are a pair on purpose. 433 is the missing decoder for
`application/cbor` -- entry 8 of the wire table, a self-describing format this
analyzer handed to the reader as a byte count. 434 is the path question CBOR
raises and JSON does not, and its own last line says why it had to come first:
write the decoder and the answer freezes in code.

THE SYMPTOM 433 RECORDS IS NOT "NO DECODER", AND THAT IS THE PART WORTH
RESTATING. `shape_of` called `application/cbor` binary; `inspect` answers
`Opaque` for binary; `Opaque` is consistent with every claim; and
`payload_decode::judge_claim` treats a claim it cannot REFUTE as a VETO over the
operator's rule. So a `--payload-format` rule pointed at a cbor topic came back
`encoding_mismatch` with nothing decoded, and the reader was told their mapping
was wrong when the publisher's label was. That is strictly worse than having no
decoder, and it is the axis the evidence for this round is built on.

ITEM 434'S ANSWER: THE ESCAPE ALPHABET WAS ALREADY CLOSED. JSON keys are always
text, so R311y910's rule -- the key's source text with `.` and `\` escaped by
`\` -- covers every path a JSON document can produce. CBOR map keys are
arbitrary data items, and the item recorded that both naive candidates collide:
a positional index `$.0` collides with the text key "0", a marker `$.#1` with
the text key "#1", and widening the escape set for CBOR alone would give this
crate two path syntaxes.

The way out is that R311y910's rule emits `\` in exactly one position --
immediately before a `.` or a `\`. So a segment whose first character is `\` and
whose second is neither of those cannot be produced by ANY text key: the text
key `\i5` arrives as `\\i5`. That free space takes the non-text keys, one letter
each: `\i` integer, `\b` byte string, `\f` float, `\s` simple, `\t` a tag's
content, and `\x` followed by the key's byte OFFSET for a container, a tag or an
indefinite-length string.

`\x` IS THE HONEST ARM RATHER THAN THE LAZY ONE. A `--payload-name` declaration
needs a segment that is stable across messages, and a nested map key is not
that -- it has no name to be called by. So those get a locator, unique within
the document and findable in the capture, whose shape says it is a position and
not a name.

WHAT IS CHECKED AND WHAT THE RFC CALLS IT. RFC 8949 1.2 separates well-formed
from valid. The walk enforces well-formedness in full and exactly one validity
rule beyond it: a text string must be UTF-8 (3.1), which is the judgement item
432 already made for JSON on the same ground -- a capture is by definition not a
closed ecosystem. The duplicate-key prohibition (5.6) is NOT enforced, and
saying so is the point: detecting it means holding every key of every map on a
path that runs over every payload in a capture.
verification_bullets: THE WITNESS CORPUS IS THE RFC'S OWN, WHICH IS THE PROPERTY THAT MATTERS. RFC
8949 Appendix A's encoded values and Appendix F's non-well-formed ones are
copied from the document, not produced by this decoder -- a table this walk
generated would agree with whatever the walk did. 62 Appendix A vectors are
accepted with the top-level kind the RFC's diagnostic notation gives; 19
Appendix F encodings are refused; and both readers are held to the same offset
on every refusal, so a second opinion about what CBOR is would red rather than
diverge quietly.
